              "# This function performs a complete calibration, validation, and reconstruction \n# workflow for multiple geochemical elements using log transformed ICP-MS \n# calibration data and log transformed XRF datasets. For each element, it fits \n# eight univariate and, where applicable, multivariate statistical models \n# (OLS, WLS, weighted OLS, weighted WLS, Bayesian Generlised Linear Model (BGLM) \n# regression, Random Forest, PLS with LOO, and PLS with k-fold), evaluates model \n# performance using Ru00b2, RMSE, 10-fold RMSEP, AIC/BIC (where applicable), and runs \n# diagnostic tests for normality and heteroscedasticity. It produces predicted \n# vs. observed plots, residual and influence diagnostics, and saves model \n# rankings based on Ru00b2 u2192 RMSE u2192 RMSEP. The function then generates ppm-scale \n# predictions with 95% confidence intervals for new XRF data, produces site-level \n# and multi-site and multi-element comparison plots for depth and age, and outputs \n# both 8 different (unweighted, weighted OLS, WLS) and multivariate (2 PLS models, \n# RF, BGLM) models and best model-multivariate-only visualisations. Finally, it \n# compiles global summary tables (in log space and ppm space), saves per-element \n# prediction files, and organises all outputs into structured folders for \n# streamlined interpretation and reporting.\n\n# It nows includes Random Forest OOB (Out-of-Bag) - a method for estimating a \n# random forest model's performance without using a separate test set. RF works\n# by having each tree in the forest evaluate the data points that were not \n# included in its own training sample (the \"out-of-bag\" data). By averaging these \n# predictions across all trees and their respective OOB samples, the out-of-bag \n# error provides a robust and unbiased estimate of the model's generalization error.\n\n# This function fits: \n# u2022 OLS, WLS (var), weighted OLS (sd), 2-step WLS, Bayes, RF, PLS LOO & k-fold\n# u2022 R2 (true) as Sum of Squares = 1-(SSres / SS_tot)\n# u2022 writes per-element folders into your chosen directory\n# Saves:\n# u2022 Residual distribution plots (PDF)\n# u2022 Predicted vs Observed plots (PDF)\n# u2022 PLS RMSEP validation plots (PDF)\n# u2022 Influence plots (Cooku2019s distance + residuals vs leverage) as PDF\n# Writes a per-element diagnostics to a .csv file with:\n# u2022 AIC & BIC tests\n# u2022 Normality test (Shapirou2013Wilk)\n# u2022 Heteroscedasticity (Breuschu2013Pagan) for LM/Bayes\n# u2022 Unified 10-fold CV RMSE for every model (where possible)\n# Native CV metrics for:\n# u2022 RF OOB MSE & Ru00b2 \n# u2022 PLS RMSEP at best ncomp\n# u2022\tExplanations for each test in plain English\n# Makes a Best Model performance summary\n# u2022 ranking based on R2, RMSE, RMSEP where AIC & BIC dont exist (PLS, RF)\n# u2022 where R2 higher, RMSE/RMSEP lower, AIC, BIC lower is better\n# u2014 sequential R that works on a Mac.\n\n# Key features for each element:\n# u2022 OLS, WLS, weighted OLS, 2-step weighted WLS - based on existing code (Steve Roberts)\n# u2022 Bayesian GLM - using the bayesglmglm function in the arm.R package\n# u2022 Random Forest - using the randomForest.R package\n# u2022 PLS (LOO and 10-fold CV) - using the pls.r package \n# u2022 Residual plots, normality tests, heteroscedasticity tests, influence plots\n# u2022 Predicted vs observed plots colored by Site using a JCO palette\n# u2022 RF variable importance, PLS RMSEP validation plots\n# u2022 Per-model/per-element diagnostics (PDF + CSV)\n# u2022 Performance summary CSV (Ru00b2, RMSE, RMSEP, AIC, BIC)\n# u2022 Best-model table\n# u2022 README.txt file explaining criteria and rankings\n\n# Multivariate run set up\n# \n# Single-predictor models (based on existing manual code):\n# u2022\tOLS\n# u2022\tWLS (variance weighted OLS)\n# u2022\tOLS_weighted\n# u2022\tWLS_weighted\n# \n# Multi-predictor models (updated from univariate function):\n# u2022\tBayes u2192 uses ALL 6 elements as predictors\n# u2022\tPLS_LOO u2192 uses ALL 6 elements as predictors\n# u2022\tPLS_kfold u2192 uses ALL 6 elements as predictors\n# u2022\tRandom Forest u2192 uses ALL 6 elements as predictors - NEW in v. 1.1\n# \n# Ranking Logic\n# \n# Models ranked by:\n# 1.\tHighest Ru00b2 (best explanatory fit)\n# 2.\tLowest RMSEP (best predictive CV performance)\n# 3.\tLowest RMSE\n# \n# No PLS priority. \"- Weighted Least Squares (WLS)\",\n  \"- Weighted OLS (using standard deviations)\",\n  \"- Two-step WLS\",\n  \"- Bayesian Generalised Linear Model (BGLM)\",\n  \"- Random Forest (RF)\",\n  \"- Partial Least Squares (PLS) with Leave-One-Out (LOO) CV\",\n  \"- PLS with k-fold CV\",\n  \"\",\n  \"Model performance is evaluated using:\",\n  \"- Ru00b2, RMSE, 10-fold RMSEP\",\n  \"- AIC/BIC (where applicable)\",\n  \"- Normality and heteroscedasticity tests\",\n  \"\",\n  \"The workflow generates predicted vs observed plots, residual and influence diagnostics, and creates model rankings based on Ru00b2 u2192 RMSEP u2192 RMSE.\",\n  \"It then produces ppm-scale predictions with 95% confidence intervals, site-level and multi-site/multi-element comparison plots (depth and age), and compiles global summary tables in both log and ppm space.\",\n  \"\",\n  \"Random Forest OOB (Out-of-Bag)\",\n  \"\",\n  \"Random Forest models include OOB error estimation, providing a robust measure of performance without a separate test set.\",\n  \"Each tree predicts observations not included in its bootstrap sample, and OOB predictions are averaged to compute unbiased error and Ru00b2 estimates.\",\n  \"\",\n  \"Models Included\",\n  \"\",\n  \"Single-predictor models:\",\n  \"- OLS\",\n  \"- WLS (variance-weighted OLS)\",\n  \"- OLS_weighted\",\n  \"- WLS_weighted\",\n  \"\",\n  \"Multi-predictor models (using all 6 elements as predictors):\",\n  \"- Bayes\",\n  \"- PLS_LOO\",\n  \"- PLS_kfold\",\n  \"- Random Forest\",\n  \"\",\n  \"Metrics, Tests, and Outputs\",\n  \"\",\n  \"Calculated metrics:\",\n  \"- True Ru00b2 = 1 - (SS_res / SS_tot)\",\n  \"- RMSE\",\n  \"- 10-fold RMSEP\",\n  \"- RF OOB MSE and Ru00b2\",\n  \"- PLS RMSEP at optimal ncomp\",\n  \"\",\n               "To perform validation tests on **_all key elements_** in your dataset (i.e., for each of the `key_elements_icp` as the response variable `Y_test`), you need to **loop through each key ICPMS element** and run the same LOO-PLSR validation for each one.\n\nHereu2019s how to modify your code to run this process automatically:\n\n---\n\n### u2705 **Full Loop for Validation on All Key ICPMS Elements**\n\n```r\n# Define predictor and response variables\nkey_elements_xrf <- c(\"Ti\", \"Ca\", \"Mn\", \"Fe\", \"Sr\", \"Zr\")\nkey_elements_icp <- c(\"Ti_ICP\", \"Ca_ICP\", \"Mn_ICP\", \"Fe_ICP\", \"Sr_ICP\", \"Zr_ICP\")\n\n# Loop over each key ICP element\nresults <- list()\n\nfor (icp_element in key_elements_icp) {\n  \n  # Set Y_test dynamically based on current ICPMS element\n  Y_test <- df[[icp_element]]\n  \n  # Create combined data frame of predictors and response\n  data_model <- data.frame(df[, key_elements_xrf], Y_test = Y_test)\n  \n  # Run PLSR with leave-one-out validation\n  pls_model <- plsr(Y_test ~ ., data = data_model, \n                    validation = \"LOO\", \n                    jackknife = TRUE,\n                    scale = TRUE, center = TRUE)\n  \n  # Get RMSEP and optimal number of components\n  rmsep_vals <- RMSEP(pls_model)$val[1, , -1]\n  opt_ncomp <- which.min(rmsep_vals)\n  \n  # Get jackknife test results\n  jack_res <- jack.test(pls_model, ncomp = opt_ncomp, use.mean = TRUE)\n  \n  # Store results in a list\n  results[[icp_element]] <- list(\n    RMSEP = rmsep_vals,\n    optimal_components = opt_ncomp,\n    jackknife_test = jack_res,\n    model_summary = summary(pls_model)\n  )\n  \n  # Optionally print status\n  cat(\"Finished validation for\", icp_element, \n      \" | Optimal components:\", opt_ncomp, \"\\n\")\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudce6 What This Code Does:\n\n- Loops through each `key_elements_icp` (each as `Y_test`)\n- Uses the same `key_elements_xrf` as predictors\n- Runs **PLSR with LOO validation**\n- Calculates:\n  - **RMSEP** (Root Mean Square Error of Prediction)\n  - **Optimal number of components**\n  - **Jackknife t-tests** for coefficient significance\n- Stores everything in a `results` list, which you can access later for analysis.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d Example to Access Results\n\n```r\n# View RMSEP values for Fe_ICP\nresults$Fe_ICP$RMSEP\n\n# View jackknife test for Mn_ICP\nresults$Mn_ICP$jackknife_test\n```\n\nWould you like help with visualizing these results (e.g., RMSEP plots or coefficient significance per element)?"

              "The error:\n\n```\nError in df[[icp_element]] : object of type 'closure' is not subsettable\n```\n\nmeans that **`df` is being interpreted as a function, not a data frame**.\n\n### ud83dudd0d Why?\n\nIn R, `df` is a common name for a data frame, but if **you or a package accidentally redefined `df` as a function**, then `df[[...]]` tries to subset a function u2014 which fails.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Solution: Check if `df` is a function\n\nRun this:\n\n```r\nprint(class(df))\n```\n\nIf it returns:\n\n```\n[1] \"function\"\n```\n\nu2026then you've accidentally masked your data frame `df` with a function.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Fix: Rename your data frame (or reassign `df`)\n\nDo this to reassign the data frame properly:\n\n```r\ndf <- your_actual_dataframe  # replace with real object name if you have one\n```\n\nOr if you already had a proper `df` but it got overwritten, reload it (e.g., from file):\n\n```r\ndf <- read_csv(\"your_data.csv\")  # or however you originally loaded it\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83euddf9 Prevent this in the future\n\nAvoid naming your data frame `df` in long scripts or functions, because itu2019s easy to mask or overwrite. But here's a practical workaround:\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Workaround: Use depth as the common axis, but fake the secondary axis with custom ticks and labels\n\nIf `depth` and `age` are paired one-to-one (say N observations), you can:\n1. Pass them to `sec_axis()` as static `breaks` and `labels`.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd27 Example\n\n```r\n# Pick depths and ages to show on the secondary axis\naxis_df <- pred_data %>% \n  dplyr::arrange(depth) %>% \n  dplyr::slice(seq(1, n(), length.out = 6))  # ~6 axis ticks\n\n# Then:\nscale_y_reverse(\n  name = \"Depth (cm)\",\n  sec.axis = sec_axis(~ ., \n                      name = \"Age (yr BP)\", \n                      breaks = axis_df$depth, \n                      labels = round(axis_df$age))\n)\n```\n\nThis simply reuses `depth` for both axes, but swaps labels on the right for age.\n\n---\n\n### ud83eudde0 Summary\n\n| Method | Supports non-functional mapping? | Transformation? | Accurate? |\n|--------|-----------------------------|------------------|-----------|\n| `sec_axis(~ ., breaks=..., labels=...)` | u2705 Yes (manual labels) | No | u2705 (at tick marks only) |\n| `sec_axis(~ func(.))` | u274c No (must be a function) | Yes | u2705 (continuous) |\n| Interpolation with `approxfun()` | u2705 Yes | Yes | u2705 (all values) |\n\n---\n\nLet me know if you'd like this wrapped into your full plotting function."

\", element, \"_ICP_sd\"),\n      xmax = paste0(element, \"_ICP + \", element, \"_ICP_sd\")\n    ), height = 0, color = \"red\", linewidth = 0.75) +\n    geom_point(data = icp_data, aes(x = !!element_icp, y = depth), shape = 21, size = 0.75, color = \"red\", \n               fill = \"white\", stroke = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +\n    \n    # Add dual y-axis with labels\n    scale_y_depth_age(\n      age_model,\n      name = \"Depth (cm)\",\n      age_name = \"Age (cal a BP)\",\n      age_breaks = age_breaks\n    ) +\n    \n    labs(\n      title = paste0(site_name, \": PLSR \", element, \" Predictions with Confidence Interval (log_inc model)\"),\n      x = paste0(element, \" (ppm)\")\n    ) +\n    theme_classic(base_size = 12) +\n    theme(\n      plot.title = element_text(color = \"black\", size = 12, face = \"bold\"),\n      axis.title = element_text(size = 12),\n      axis.text = element_text(size = 12),\n      axis.ticks.length = unit(0.3, \"cm\"),\n      axis.line = element_line(size = 0.75),\n      axis.ticks = element_line(size = 0.75)\n    )\n\n  # Save plot\n  if (!is.null(output_dir)) {\n    file_path <- file.path(output_dir, paste0(site_name, \"_\", element, \"_log_inc_PLS_depth.pdf\"))\n    ggsave(file_path, plot = p, height = 24, width = 12, dpi = 600, units = \"cm\")\n  }\n\n  return(p)\n}\n```\n\n---\n\nLet me know if you'd like to **add age uncertainty bands** or modify the **position or style** of the age ticks!"

              "To turn your hardcoded `ggplot2` plot into a **reusable plotting function** that works for different **elements** (e.g., Ca, Sr, Zr) and **sites** (e.g., HER42PB, BI10), we need to:\n\n- Use dynamic `aes_string()` or `aes()` with `.data[[...]]` for flexible column references.\n- Pass in:\n  - The site name (to dynamically load site-specific data).\n  - The element of interest (to reference correct columns).\n  - Plot limits (x and y axis).\n- Allow saving to file with a filename that depends on element and site.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 FUNCTION VERSION\n\n```r\nlibrary(ggplot2)\nlibrary(rlang)\n\nplot_element_vs_depth <- function(site_name, element, \n                                  df_pls, df_wls, df_icp, \n                                  x_limits, y_limits, \n                                  save_path = NULL) {\n  #               "Here's a **generalized function** to calculate **x and y axis ranges** (`x_limits` and `y_limits`) for **any site and any element**, based on the structure you showed.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Function: `get_plot_ranges()`\n\n```r\nget_plot_ranges <- function(element,\n                            df_log_inc,\n                            df_wls = NULL,\n                            df_clr = NULL,\n                            df_icp,\n                            col_map = NULL) {\n  # Default column names\n  icp_pred_col <- paste0(element, \"_ICP_pred_ppm\")\n  wls_col      <- paste0(element, \"_ppm_WLS\")\n  clr_col      <- paste0(element, \"_ICP_clr_ppm\")\n  icp_col      <- paste0(element, \"_ICP\")\n\n  # Override with col_map if needed\n  if (!is.null(col_map)) {\n    icp_pred_col <- col_map[[\"icp_pred\"]] %||% icp_pred_col\n    wls_col      <- col_map[[\"wls_pred\"]] %||% wls_col\n    clr_col      <- col_map[[\"clr_pred\"]] %||% clr_col\n    icp_col      <- col_map[[\"icp\"]]      %||% icp_col\n  }\n\n  # Collect all depth vectors\n  depth_vecs <- list(\n    df_log_inc$depth,\n    df_icp$depth\n  )\n  if (!is.null(df_wls)) depth_vecs <- append(depth_vecs, list(df_wls$depth))\n  if (!is.null(df_clr)) depth_vecs <- append(depth_vecs, list(df_clr$depth))\n\n  # Collect all concentration vectors\n  value_vecs <- list(\n    df_log_inc[[icp_pred_col]],\n    df_icp[[icp_col]]\n  )\n  if (!is.null(df_wls)) value_vecs <- append(value_vecs, list(df_wls[[wls_col]]))\n  if (!is.null(df_clr)) value_vecs <- append(value_vecs, list(df_clr[[clr_col]]))\n\n  # Compute ranges\n  x_limits <- range(unlist(value_vecs), na.rm = TRUE)\n  y_limits <- range(unlist(depth_vecs), na.rm = TRUE)\n\n  return(list(x_limits = x_limits, y_limits = y_limits))\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83euddea Example Usage\n\n```r\nranges <- get_plot_ranges(\n  element = \"Ti\",\n  df_log_inc = HER42PB_PLS_ppm_pred_log_inc,\n  df_wls = HER42PB_WLS_ppm_pred_log_inc,\n  df_clr = HER42PB_PLS_ppm_pred_clr,\n  df_icp = HER42PB_ICP\n)\n\nHER42PB_x_all_depth <- ranges$x_limits\nHER42PB_y_all_depth <- ranges$y_limits\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudee0 With Custom Column Names\n\n```r\nranges <- get_plot_ranges(\n  element = \"Ca\",\n  df_log_inc = BI10_PLS_log_inc,\n  df_wls = BI10_WLS_log_inc,\n  df_clr = BI10_PLS_clr,\n  df_icp = BI10_ICP,\n  col_map = list(\n    icp_pred = \"Ca_log_pred\",\n    wls_pred = \"Ca_WLS_ppm\",\n    clr_pred = \"Ca_clr_pred\",\n    icp      = \"Ca_ICP\"\n  )\n)\n```\n\n---\n\nThis function works flexibly across:\n- Any **element** (`\"Ti\"`, `\"Ca\"`, etc.)\n- Any **site** (datasets for `log_inc`, `clr`, `wls`, and `icp`)\n- Optional **column remapping**\n\nLet me know if you'd like to batch-run this across a list of elements/sites!"

              "Here's a generalized **function** to create your Plot 1: **PLS log_inc u00b1CI & WLS vs ICP-MS** by **depth** for any site and element.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Function: `plot_log_inc_wls_vs_depth()`\n\n```r\nplot_log_inc_wls_vs_depth <- function(site_name,\n                                      element,\n                                      df_log_inc,\n                                      df_wls,\n                                      df_icp,\n                                      save_path = NULL,\n                                      col_map = NULL) {\n  # Default column names\n  depth_col     <- \"depth\"\n  icp_pred_col  <- paste0(element, \"_ICP_pred_ppm\")\n  low_rmse_col  <- paste0(element, \"_low_RMSE\")\n  up_rmse_col   <- paste0(element, \"_up_RMSE\")\n  wls_col       <- paste0(element, \"_ppm_WLS\")\n  icp_col       <- paste0(element, \"_ICP\")\n\n  # Override with custom mappings\n  if (!is.null(col_map)) {\n    depth_col    <- col_map[[\"depth\"]]      %||% depth_col\n    icp_pred_col <- col_map[[\"icp_pred\"]]   %||% icp_pred_col\n    low_rmse_col <- col_map[[\"low_rmse\"]]   %||% low_rmse_col\n    up_rmse_col  <- col_map[[\"up_rmse\"]]    %||% up_rmse_col\n    wls_col      <- col_map[[\"wls_pred\"]]   %||% wls_col\n    icp_col      <- col_map[[\"icp\"]]        %||% icp_col\n  }\n\n  # Lock x and y ranges\n  x_limits <- range(\n    df_log_inc[[icp_pred_col]],\n    df_wls[[wls_col]],\n    df_icp[[icp_col]],\n    na.rm = TRUE\n  )\n  y_limits <- range(\n    df_log_inc[[depth_col]],\n    df_wls[[depth_col]],\n    df_icp[[depth_col]],\n    na.rm = TRUE\n  )\n\n  # Plot\n  p <- ggplot(df_log_inc, aes(x = .data[[icp_pred_col]], y = .data[[depth_col]])) +\n    geom_ribbon(aes(xmin = .data[[low_rmse_col]], xmax = .data[[up_rmse_col]]),\n                color = \"lightgrey\", linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +\n    geom_lineh(color = \"brown\", linewidth = 0.5) +\n    geom_point(size = 0.5, color = \"brown\") +\n\n    geom_lineh(data = df_wls,\n               aes(x = .data[[wls_col]], y = .data[[depth_col]]),\n               color = \"gold\", linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.4) +\n\n    geom_lineh(data = df_icp,\n               aes(x = .data[[icp_col]], y = .data[[depth_col]]),\n               color = \"blue\", linewidth = 1) +\n    geom_point(data = df_icp,\n               aes(x = .data[[icp_col]], y = .data[[depth_col]]),\n               shape = 21, size = 1, color = \"blue\", fill = \"white\", stroke = 1) +\n\n    scale_x_continuous(limits = x_limits) +\n    scale_y_continuous(limits = y_limits) +\n    scale_y_reverse() +\n    labs(title = paste(site_name, \": PLS & WLS log_inc predicted vs ICP-MS\"),\n         x = paste(element, \"(ppm)\"),\n         y = \"Depth (cm)\") +\n\n    theme_classic(base_size = 12) +\n    theme(plot.title = element_text(color = \"black\", size = 12, face = \"bold\"),\n          axis.title = element_text(size = 12),\n          axis.text = element_text(size = 12),\n          axis.ticks.length = unit(0.3, \"cm\"),\n          axis.line = element_line(size = 0.75),\n          axis.ticks = element_line(size = 0.75))\n\n  print(p)\n\n  # Save to file if path provided\n  if (!is.null(save_path)) {\n    ggsave(save_path, p, height = 24, width = 12, dpi = 600, units = \"cm\")\n  }\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83euddea Example Usage\n\n```r\nplot_log_inc_wls_vs_depth(\n  site_name = \"HER42PB\",\n  element = \"Ti\",\n  df_log_inc = HER42PB_PLS_ppm_pred_log_inc,\n  df_wls = HER42PB_WLS_ppm_pred_log_inc,\n  df_icp = HER42PB_ICP,\n  save_path = \"Papers_R/2024_DeVleeschouwer/ACE_PLS/Output/PLSR/log_inc/HER42PB/P1_HER42PB_Ti_log_inc_PLS_WLS_depth.pdf\"\n)\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudee0 With Custom Column Mapping (if needed)\n\n```r\nplot_log_inc_wls_vs_depth(\n  site_name = \"BI10\",\n  element = \"Ca\",\n  df_log_inc = BI10_PLS_log_inc,\n  df_wls = BI10_WLS_log_inc,\n  df_icp = BI10_ICP,\n  save_path = \"Output/BI10_Ca_log_inc_PLS_WLS_depth.pdf\",\n  col_map = list(\n    depth = \"core_depth_cm\",\n    icp_pred = \"Ca_log_pred\",\n    low_rmse = \"Ca_log_low\",\n    up_rmse = \"Ca_log_up\",\n    wls_pred = \"Ca_WLS_ppm\",\n    icp = \"Ca_ICP\"\n  )\n)\n```\n\n---\n\nLet me know if you'd like to **bundle this with the other two plots** into a single function or pipeline."

              "The **dark grey appearance** of your `geom_ribbon()` is typically due to the **overlap of multiple semi-transparent layers**u2014especially when:\n\n1. You have **many closely spaced points**, and\n2. You use a **semi-transparent fill** (via `alpha`), e.g., `alpha = 0.5`,\n3. You set a **border color** (`color = \"lightgrey\"`) that also stacks up visually.\n\n### ud83dudd0d Why this happens\n\nWhen `geom_ribbon()` uses `alpha = 0.5`, overlapping ribbons **blend**, making areas look darkeru2014even though each individual ribbon isn't. This is especially visible if:\n\n- The dataset has many predictions (e.g. depth/age slices),\n- The `ribbon` area is wide (high error),\n- The fill is semi-transparent (`alpha` < 1) and repeated for many rows.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 How to fix or improve visibility\n\nHere are a few options:\n\n---\n\n#### **Option 1: Remove `color` or set it equal to fill**\n\n```r\ngeom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Ti_low_RMSE, ymax = Ti_up_RMSE),\n            fill = \"lightgrey\", alpha = 0.5, color = NA)\n```\n\n- `color = NA` removes the ribbon border.\n- Reduces visual stacking lines.\n\n---\n\n#### **Option 2: Use lighter fill color with less alpha**\n\n```r\ngeom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Ti_low_RMSE, ymax = Ti_up_RMSE),\n            fill = \"grey85\", alpha = 0.3)\n```\n\n---\n\n#### **Option 3: Thinner or summarized ribbon**\n\nIf you're plotting **one ribbon per observation**, it may be better to **summarize** the ribbon over a moving window, bin, or spline fit. Otherwise, ggplot draws one polygon per row, stacking up to a very dark band.\n\n---\n\n#### **Option 4: Only use ribbon for model mean + CI**\n\nIf you're using many ribbons across a dense time/depth scale, you might want to first smooth or bin the prediction (e.g. `dplyr::summarise()` or `ggplot2::stat_summary()`), then draw just one ribbon.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudca1 TL;DR Fix\n\nIf you're happy with the visual shape and just want it lighter:\n\n```r\ngeom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Ti_low_RMSE, ymax = Ti_up_RMSE),\n            fill = \"lightgrey\", alpha = 0.3, color = NA)\n```\n\nLet me know if you want a version that **automatically adapts color and transparency** based on site or element, or if you're seeing **double plotting** of overlapping ribbons from multiple layers."

              "To **plot a line through `NA` values** in **ggplot2**, you need to explicitly tell `ggplot` **not to break the line at `NA`** values. Here's how to do that:\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Solution: Use `na.rm = TRUE` **with interpolation**\n\n**However**, `ggplot2`u2019s `geom_line()` **does not interpolate across NA values by default** u2014 it **drops** them instead, resulting in broken lines.\n\n#### ud83dudd04 Options:\n\n---\n\n### **Option 1: Interpolate manually across NA values**\n\nIf you want to connect across `NA` values (e.g., for `geom_line()`), you **must fill or interpolate** them first, using something like:\n\n```r\nlibrary(zoo)\n\ndf$y_interp <- na.approx(df$y, na.rm = FALSE)\n```\n\nThen plot the interpolated column:\n\n```r\nggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y_interp)) +\n  geom_line()\n```\n\nThis draws a continuous line across what were previously `NA` values.\n\n---\n\n### **Option 2: Use `geom_line(na.rm = TRUE)` to skip NA segments**\n\n```r\nggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +\n  geom_line(na.rm = TRUE)\n```\n\n- This **removes** `NA` rows.\n- But it **will still break** the line at those gaps (i.e., no interpolation).\n\n---\n\n### u26a0ufe0f Why `geom_line()` doesn't interpolate by default\n\n`ggplot2` behaves this way because it's designed for data-accurate plottingu2014plotting a line through unknown (`NA`) values could mislead. So it breaks lines instead of assuming continuity.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Recommended approach for your case\n\nIf your goal is to **draw modelled or predicted lines continuously** through a time/depth series, and you know gaps are small/insignificant:\n\n```r\nlibrary(zoo)\n\nHER42PB_PLS_ppm_pred_log_inc$Ti_ICP_pred_ppm_filled <- na.approx(HER42PB_PLS_ppm_pred_log_inc$Ti_ICP_pred_ppm, na.rm = FALSE)\n\nggplot(HER42PB_PLS_ppm_pred_log_inc, aes(x = SH20_age, y = Ti_ICP_pred_ppm_filled)) +\n  geom_line()\n```\n\nLet me know if you'd like to apply this to **multiple elements or sites in a loop** u2014 I can help automate that too."

              "To draw a line through datapoints while **ignoring `NA` values** in `ggplot2`, you can simply pass your data to `ggplot()` and use `geom_line()` u2014 by default, `ggplot2` will **automatically omit** `NA` values when drawing lines, as long as you donu2019t group data in a way that breaks the line.\n\nHereu2019s a minimal working example:\n\n```r\nlibrary(ggplot2)\n\n# Sample data with NA\ndf <- data.frame(\n  x = 1:10,\n  y = c(1, 2, NA, 4, 5, NA, 7, 8, 9, 10)\n)\n\n# Plot with geom_line ignoring NA\nggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +\n  geom_line(na.rm = TRUE) +  # removes NAs for the line\n  geom_point()               # shows all non-NA points\n```\n\n### Key Points:\n- `geom_line(na.rm = TRUE)` tells ggplot to **remove rows with NA in `y` or `x`** when drawing lines.\n- Without `na.rm = TRUE`, you might get warnings or the line may break at `NA` values.\n- If your data has **multiple groups**, make sure to use `group =` inside `aes()` accordingly to ensure the line connects as expected.\n\n### Optional: Remove rows manually (if needed)\nIf `na.rm = TRUE` doesnu2019t behave as you want, you can manually remove `NA` values before plotting:\n\n```r\ndf_clean <- na.omit(df)\n\nggplot(df_clean, aes(x = x, y = y)) +\n  geom_line() +\n  geom_point()\n```\n\nLet me know if your data is grouped or time-series u2014 the method can vary slightly."

              "For **grouped data**, drawing lines while **ignoring `NA` values** in `ggplot2` works similarly, but you must:\n\n1. **Specify the grouping variable** in `aes(group = ...)` or `aes(color = ...)`.\n2. Use `na.rm = TRUE` inside `geom_line()` to skip `NA`s **within each group**.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Example with grouped data\n\n```r\nlibrary(ggplot2)\n\n# Sample grouped data with NA values\ndf <- data.frame(\n  group = rep(c(\"A\", \"B\"), each = 6),\n  x = rep(1:6, 2),\n  y = c(1, 2, NA, 4, 5, 6, 2, NA, 3, 4, NA, 6)\n)\n\n# Plot with group-specific lines, skipping NA values\nggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, color = group, group = group)) +\n  geom_line(na.rm = TRUE) +\n  geom_point()\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d Notes:\n\n- `group = group` tells `ggplot2` to draw separate lines per group.\n- `na.rm = TRUE` in `geom_line()` ensures that `NA` values **donu2019t break the line drawing**.\n- The `geom_point()` (without `na.rm = TRUE`) will automatically skip `NA`s but plot the rest.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudca1 Optional: Interpolation vs Skipping\n\n- If you **want the lines to connect across `NA` values**, thatu2019s **not the default**; you'd have to interpolate or fill the values yourself.\n- By default, `ggplot2` **breaks the line** at `NA`, even with `na.rm = TRUE`.\n\nTo truly **connect across NA gaps**, you'd need to **remove `NA` rows manually**:\n\n```r\ndf_no_na <- df[!is.na(df$y), ]\n\nggplot(df_no_na, aes(x = x, y = y, color = group, group = group)) +\n  geom_line() +\n  geom_point()\n```\n\nLet me know if youu2019d prefer interpolation, smoothing, or linear fill instead of skipping!"

**Ti_ICPMS** is the response variable.\n  - Other elements (e.g., Ca, Fe, Sr, Mn, etc.) measured by ITRAX are predictor variables.\n- All data are numeric and cleaned (no missing values).\n- The response variable is continuous.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudce6 **Required Package**\n```r\ninstall.packages(\"pls\")  # Run this if you haven't installed it yet\nlibrary(pls)\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudcca **Example Workflow**\n\n```r\n# Load libraries\nlibrary(pls)\n\n# Simulate or load your dataset (replace this with your actual data)\n# Assuming `data` is a data.frame with predictors (ITRAX) and response (ICP-MS)\n# Ti_ICPMS is the response, and the others (e.g., Ca, Fe, Sr, Mn...) are predictors\n# Example:\n# data <- read.csv(\"your_data.csv\")\n\n# Split into predictors (X) and response (Y)\nX <- data[, c(\"Ca\", \"Fe\", \"Sr\", \"Mn\", \"Zr\", \"Rb\", \"K\", \"S\")]  # ITRAX elements\nY <- data$Ti_ICPMS  # ICP-MS measured Titanium\n\n# Perform PLS regression (10-fold cross-validation for model tuning)\npls_model <- plsr(Y ~ ., data = data.frame(X, Y), validation = \"CV\")\n\n# Summary of the model\nsummary(pls_model)\n\n# Plot root mean squared error of prediction (RMSEP) to choose number of components\nplot(RMSEP(pls_model), legendpos = \"topright\")\n\n# Choose optimal number of components (e.g., based on RMSEP or explained variance)\n# Suppose optimal is 3 components:\nncomp_opt <- 3\n\n# Predict Ti using the model\npredicted_Ti <- predict(pls_model, ncomp = ncomp_opt)\n\n# Plot predicted vs actual\nplot(Y, predicted_Ti, xlab = \"Measured Ti (ICPMS)\", ylab = \"Predicted Ti (from ITRAX)\", main = \"PLS Calibration\")\nabline(0, 1, col = \"red\")\n\n# Calculate R2 and RMSE\nr2 <- cor(Y, predicted_Ti)^2\nrmse <- sqrt(mean((Y -               "Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression is often **better than Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)** regression for **covariant systems** like geochemical data due to several key reasons:\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd01 1. **Multicollinearity in Covariant Data**\nGeochemical datasets often have **highly correlated predictors** (e.g., concentrations of elements like Si, Al, Fe, etc.). In OLS:\n\n- High multicollinearity leads to **unstable coefficient estimates**, making interpretation and prediction unreliable.\n- OLS tries to invert \\( X^TX \\), which becomes **ill-conditioned** when predictors are collinear.\n\n**PLS advantage**:\n- PLS projects the predictors into a **lower-dimensional space** that captures directions with high variance **and** high covariance with the response.\n- It handles multicollinearity naturally by **compressing information** into fewer, stable latent variables.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d 2. **High-Dimensional Data / Few Samples**\nIn geochemistry, datasets may have:\n- **Many variables (p)** (e.g., dozens of elements)\n- **Few observations (n)** (e.g., limited rock samples)\n\nOLS fails when \\( p > n \\), or is overfit when \\( p \\approx n \\).\n\n**PLS advantage**:\n- Can handle \\( p > n \\) situations by using only a **small number of latent components**, avoiding overfitting.\n- More **robust to noise** in high-dimensional settings.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd04 3. **Focus on Predictive Power**\nOLS minimizes the **error in fitting** \\( Y \\) given \\( X \\), but doesnu2019t consider how well the model **predicts** new data.\n\n**PLS advantage**:\n- It extracts components that explain **maximum covariance** between predictors and the response, enhancing **predictive performance**.\n- Better suited when the goal is **prediction** rather than purely inference.\n\n---\n\n### ud83euddea 4. **Interpreting Complex Geochemical Relationships**\nGeochemical data are influenced by overlapping geological processes (e.g., weathering, metamorphism), often leading to:\n\n- **Hidden structure** in the data\n- **Non-orthogonal effects**\n\n**PLS advantage**:\n- Captures **underlying latent processes** through components\n- Enables more **meaningful interpretation** of complex, overlapping geochemical trends\n\n---\n\n### Summary Table\n\n| Feature                        | OLS                           | PLS                               |\n|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|------------------------------------|\n| Handles multicollinearity     | u274c No                         | u2705 Yes                             |\n| Works with \\( p > n \\)        | u274c No                         | u2705 Yes                             |\n| Good for prediction           | u26a0ufe0f Sometimes                  | u2705 Strong predictive performance   |\n| Dimensionality reduction      | u274c No                         | u2705 Yes                             |\n| Robust to noise in \\( X \\)    | u274c No                         | u2705 Yes                             |\n\n---\n\n### ud83eudde0 In Practice\nFor a geochemist building predictive models from element concentrations:\n\n- Use **PLS regression** when your **predictor matrix is highly collinear**, **noisy**, or has **more variables than samples**.\n- Reserve **OLS** for cases where variables are uncorrelated and the dataset is well-conditioned.\n\nLet me know if you want a visual comparison or a sample code to illustrate this!"

              "In **regression**, the axes depend on whether youu2019re looking at the **model itself** or at a **diagnostic plot**. Here are the two common interpretations:\n\n---\n\n# u2705 **1. Scatterplot of Observations + Regression Line**\nThis is the most common plot when visualizing regression.\n\n- **X-axis:** the **predictor variable(s)** (often just one variable in simple regression)\n- **Y-axis:** the **observed response variable** (the outcome you're trying to predict)\n\nIf you add predictions to this plot:\n\n- The regression line shows the **predicted values** \\(\\hat{y}\\) for each \\(x\\).\n\n### Example:\n- X-axis: hours studied  \n- Y-axis: exam score  \n- Regression line: predicted exam score for each hour value  \n\n---\n\n# u2705 **2. Plot of Predictions vs Observations**\nSometimes you create a plot comparing predicted values to actual values to assess accuracy.\n\nTwo common formats:\n\n### **A. y-axis = observed values, x-axis = predicted values**\nUsed to evaluate how well predictions match reality.\n\n- **X-axis:** predicted values \\(\\hat{y}\\)  \n- **Y-axis:** observed values \\(y\\)  \n- A perfect model u2192 points lie on a 45u00b0 line.\n\n### **B. y-axis = residuals, x-axis = predicted values**\nUsed for diagnosing model issues (nonlinearity, heteroscedasticity, etc.)\n\n- **X-axis:** predicted values \\(\\hat{y}\\)  \n- **Y-axis:** residuals \\(e = y - \\hat{y}\\)\n\n---\n\n# u2705 Summary Table\n\n| Plot type | X-axis | Y-axis |\n|-----------|--------|--------|\n| **Regular regression scatterplot** | Predictor \\(x\\) | Observed response \\(y\\) |\n| **Regression line** | Predictor \\(x\\) | Predicted response \\(\\hat{y}\\) |\n| **Prediction vs observation plot** | Predicted \\(\\hat{y}\\) | Observed \\(y\\) |\n| **Residual plot** | Predicted \\(\\hat{y}\\) | Residuals \\(y - \\hat{y}\\) |\n\n---\n\nIf you want, I can also draw example diagrams or explain which plot is appropriate for your specific regression problemu2014just tell me what you're working with!"

              "Here are clear definitions of **AIC** and **BIC** in statistics, what they measure, and how they are used.\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudcd8 **AIC (Akaike Information Criterion)**\n\n### **Definition**\nAIC is a statistic used to compare different statistical models by balancing **goodness of fit** with **model complexity**.  \nIt is defined as:\n\n\\[\n\\text{AIC} = 2k - 2\\ln(L)\n\\]\n\nwhere:  \n- \\(k\\) = number of parameters in the model  \n- \\(L\\) = maximum value of the likelihood function for the model  \n\n### **Interpretation**\n- Lower AIC u2192 better model (relative to the others being compared).  \n- Penalizes models with more parameters to discourage overfitting.\n\n### **Usage**\n- Compare multiple models fitted to the *same dataset*.  \n- Often used in regression, time-series modeling (e.g., ARIMA), and machine learning model selection.  \n- Select the model with the **lowest AIC**.\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudcd8 **BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion)**\n\n### **Definition**\nBIC is another model selection criterion that also balances **fit vs. complexity**, but with a stronger penalty for adding parameters.  \nIt is defined as:\n\n\\[\n\\text{BIC} = k \\ln(n) - 2\\ln(L)\n\\]\n\nwhere:  \n- \\(n\\) = sample size  \n- \\(k\\) = number of parameters  \n- \\(L\\) = maximum likelihood  \n\n### **Interpretation**\n- Lower BIC u2192 better model (relative comparison).  \n- Penalizes complexity more heavily than AIC, especially when \\(n\\) is large.\n\n### **Usage**\n- Used to compare models fitted to the same data.  \n- Often preferred when sample size is large or when a more conservative (simpler) model is desired.\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudd0d **AIC vs. BIC u2014 Key Differences**\n\n| Feature | **AIC** | **BIC** |\n|--------|---------|----------|\n| Penalty for parameters | \\(2k\\) | \\(k \\ln(n)\\) (grows with sample size) |\n| Tends to choose | More complex models | Simpler models |\n| Philosophical basis | Information theory | Bayesian approximation |\n| Best used when | Predictive accuracy is priority | True model likely among candidates |\n\n---\n\n# ud83eudde0 **How They Are Used in Practice**\n\n1. Fit several candidate models to the same data.  \n2. Compute AIC and/or BIC for each.  \n3. Compare the values:  \n   - Choose the model with **lowest AIC** if prediction-focused.  \n   - Choose the model with **lowest BIC** if model parsimony or Bayesian interpretation is preferred.  \n4. They *do not* test hypotheses or tell you whether a model is u201cgoodu201d u2014 only which is **better** relative to others.\n\n---\n\nIf youu2019d like, I can show an example calculation or explain when AIC and BIC disagree."
            ]

              "**Cooku2019s distance** is a diagnostic measure used in regression analysis to identify **influential observations**u2014data points that have a strong impact on the estimated regression coefficients.\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudcd8 **What Cooku2019s Distance Measures**\n\nCooku2019s distance combines:\n- how **unusual** an observationu2019s predictor values are (leverage), and  \n- how **large** its residual is (how poorly the model fits that point).\n\nIt tells you how much the regression model would **change** if that single observation were removed.\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudcd0 **Formula (conceptual)**\n\n\\[\nD_i = \\frac{\\text{change in fitted values when point } i \\text{ is removed}}{\\text{overall variance}}\n\\]\n\nA more detailed expression is:\n\n\\[\nD_i = \\frac{e_i^2}{p \\cdot \\hat{\\sigma}^2} \\cdot \\frac{h_{ii}}{(1 - h_{ii})^2}\n\\]\n\nWhere:  \n- \\(e_i\\) = residual for observation \\(i\\)  \n- \\(h_{ii}\\) = leverage for observation \\(i\\)  \n- \\(p\\) = number of model parameters  \n- \\(\\hat{\\sigma}^2\\) = estimated error variance  \n\n---\n\n# ud83dudd0d **Interpretation**\n\n- **Small \\(D_i\\)** u2192 The point has little influence.  \n- **Large \\(D_i\\)** u2192 The point influences the regression strongly.\n\n### **Common Thresholds**\nThere is no universal cutoff, but common rules of thumb:\n\n- \\(D_i > 1\\) u2192 often considered influential  \n- \\(D_i > \\frac{4}{n}\\) u2192 another commonly used criterion (more conservative), where \\(n\\) is sample size  \n\n**Influential u2260 bad** u2014 you simply need to inspect those points.\n\n---\n\n# ud83eudde0 **Why Cooku2019s Distance Is Useful**\n\nIt helps identify:\n- Outliers that distort model estimates  \n- Points with high leverage  \n- Data errors or atypical cases  \n- Whether the regression model is overly driven by a few observations  \n\n---\n\n# ud83dudcca **How Itu2019s Used in Practice**\n\n1. Fit a regression model.  \n2. Compute Cooku2019s distance for each observation (software like R, Python, SPSS does this).  \n3. Plot Cooku2019s distance (e.g., influence plot).  \n4. Investigate points with large values:  \n   - Are they errors?  \n   - Do they represent a special group?  \n   - Should the model be adjusted?  \n\n---\n\nIf you want, I can show a small numerical example or explain how Cooku2019s distance differs from leverage and standardized residuals."

ACE_dataset PREDICTION (OPTIONAL)\n# ===============================================================\n\nif (do_ACE_predictions && !is.null(ACE_dataset)) {\n  \n  message(\"=== Running ACE prediction across all elements ===\")\n  \n  # Ensure ACE has required predictors\n  if (!\"Site\" %in% names(ACE_dataset))\n    stop(\"ACE_dataset must contain a 'Site' column.\")\n  \n  if (!\"SH20_age\" %in% names(ACE_dataset))\n    stop(\"ACE_dataset must contain 'SH20_age'.\")\n  \n  # Create output root\n  ace_root <- file.path(all_base, \"Calibration_pred\")\n  dir.create(ace_root, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)\n  \n  # Loop over elements\n  for (el in elements) {\n    \n    el_dir <- file.path(ace_root, el)\n    dir.create(el_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)\n    \n    message(\"ACE predictions for element: \", el)\n    \n    # Prepare output df\n    ace_df <- ACE_dataset %>%\n      dplyr::select(Site, depth, SH20_age, dplyr::all_of(el)) %>%\n      dplyr::rename(XRF_value = !!sym(el))\n    \n    # Access fitted models + RMSE from calibration step (Section 8)\n    models_el <- model_store[[el]]\n    rmse_el   <- calibration_rmse[[el]]\n    \n    # Compute predictions, store per model\n    for (mname in names(models_el)) {\n      \n      m <- models_el[[mname]]\n      \n      # Predictions in log space\n      pred_log <- tryCatch({\n        if (inherits(m, \"mvr\")) {\n          as.numeric(predict(m,\n                             ncomp   = attr(m, \"best_ncomp\"),\n                             newdata = ACE_dataset))\n        } else {\n          as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = ACE_dataset))\n        }\n      }, error = function(e) rep(NA_real_, nrow(ACE_dataset)))\n      \n      # Compute CI from calibration RMSE\n      rmse_val <- rmse_el[[mname]]\n      if (is.null(rmse_val) || is.na(rmse_val)) rmse_val <- NA_real_\n      \n      L95_log <- pred_log - 1.96 * rmse_val\n      U95_log <- pred_log + 1.96 * rmse_val\n      \n      # ppm-scale values (keep original names for backward compatibility)\n      base_nm <- paste0(mname, \"_\", el)\n      \n      ace_df[[paste0(base_nm, \"_Pred_ppm\")]] <- exp(pred_log)\n      ace_df[[paste0(base_nm, \"_L95_ppm\")]]  <- exp(L95_log)\n      ace_df[[paste0(base_nm, \"_U95_ppm\")]]  <- exp(U95_log)\n      \n      # Duplicate into *_XRF_pred* naming for error-bar use\n      # (these are the same ppm values, just different column names)\n      ace_df[[paste0(base_nm, \"_XRF_pred\")]]        <- ace_df[[paste0(base_nm, \"_Pred_ppm\")]]\n      ace_df[[paste0(base_nm, \"_XRF_pred_lower\")]]  <- ace_df[[paste0(base_nm, \"_L95_ppm\")]]\n      ace_df[[paste0(base_nm, \"_XRF_pred_upper\")]]  <- ace_df[[paste0(base_nm, \"_U95_ppm\")]]\n    }\n    \n    # Save predictions\n    write.csv(\n      ace_df,\n      file.path(el_dir, paste0(el, \"_ACE_predictions.csv\")),\n      row.names = FALSE\n    )\n  }\n  \n  message(\"=== Finished ACE predictions ===\")\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section 14 u2013 ACE diagnostic evaluation vs ICP_ppm (unchanged logic)\n\n```r\n# ===============================================================\n# 14. ACE DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION vs ICP_ppm\n# ===============================================================\n\nif (do_ACE_predictions && !is.null(ACE_dataset)) {\n  \n  message(\"=== Running ACE diagnostic evaluation ===\")\n  \n  ace_root <- file.path(all_base, \"Calibration_pred\")\n  \n  for (el in elements) {\n    \n    el_dir    <- file.path(ace_root, el)\n    pred_file <- file.path(el_dir, paste0(el, \"_ACE_predictions.csv\"))\n    if (!file.exists(pred_file)) next\n    \n    ace_df <- read.csv(pred_file)\n    \n    obs_col <- paste0(el, \"_ICP\")\n    sd_col  <- paste0(el, \"_ICP_sd\")\n    \n    if (!obs_col %in% names(ICP_ppm)) next\n    \n    # join ACE predictions with ICP measured data\n    joined <- ace_df %>%\n      dplyr::left_join(\n        ICP_ppm %>%\n          dplyr::select(Site, depth, SH20_age, !!sym(obs_col), !!sym(sd_col)),\n        by = c(\"Site\", \"depth\", \"SH20_age\")\n      )\n    \n    # Create diagnostics and model comparison just like Section 8\n    diag_out <- data.frame()\n    \n    for (mname in names(model_store[[el]])) {\n      \n      pred_nm <- paste0(mname, \"_\", el, \"_Pred_ppm\")\n      if (!pred_nm %in% names(joined)) next\n      \n      pred <- joined[[pred_nm]]\n      obs  <- joined[[obs_col]]\n      \n      ok <- !is.na(pred) & !is.na(obs)\n      if (!any(ok)) next\n      \n      SS_res <- sum((obs[ok] - pred[ok])^2)\n      SS_tot <- sum((obs[ok] - mean(obs[ok]))^2)\n      \n      R2   <- 1 - SS_res / SS_tot\n      RMSE <- sqrt(mean((obs[ok] - pred[ok])^2))\n      \n      diag_out <- rbind(\n        diag_out,\n        data.frame(\n          Model = mname,\n          R2    = R2,\n          RMSE  = RMSE\n        )\n      )\n    }\n    \n    write.csv(\n      diag_out,\n      file.path(el_dir, paste0(el, \"_ACE_diagnostics.csv\")),\n      row.names = FALSE\n    )\n  }\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n### Section 15 u2013 ACE prediction diagnostic plots (with ICP_sd + *_XRF_pred_upper/lower error bars) **and per-model PDFs**\n\n```r\n# ===============================================================\n# 15. ACE PREDICTION DIAGNOSTIC PLOTS\n#       - Pred vs Obs with error bars\n#       - Residual histograms\n# ===============================================================\n\nif (do_ACE_predictions && !is.null(ACE_dataset)) {\n  \n  message(\"=== Creating ACE diagnostic plots ===\")\n  \n  ace_root <- file.path(all_base, \"Calibration_pred\")\n  \n  for (el in elements) {\n    \n    el_dir    <- file.path(ace_root, el)\n    pred_file <- file.path(el_dir, paste0(el, \"_ACE_predictions.csv\"))\n    if (!file.exists(pred_file)) next\n    \n    ace_df <- read.csv(pred_file)\n    \n    obs_col <- paste0(el, \"_ICP\")\n    sd_col  <- paste0(el, \"_ICP_sd\")\n    \n    if (!obs_col %in% names(ICP_ppm)) next\n    \n    # Merge predictions with observed ICP (ppm + ICP SD)\n    joined <- ace_df %>%\n      dplyr::left_join(\n        ICP_ppm %>%\n          dplyr::select(Site, depth, SH20_age, !!sym(obs_col), !!sym(sd_col)),\n        by = c(\"Site\", \"depth\", \"SH20_age\")\n      )\n    \n    # Storage for ACE Pred vs Obs plots by model (for later summary pages)\n    p_po_list_ace <- list()\n    \n    for (mname in names(model_store[[el]])) {\n      \n      base_nm      <- paste0(mname, \"_\", el)\n      pred_nm      <- paste0(base_nm, \"_Pred_ppm\")\n      xrf_pred_nm  <- paste0(base_nm, \"_XRF_pred\")\n      xrf_low_nm   <- paste0(base_nm, \"_XRF_pred_lower\")\n      xrf_up_nm    <- paste0(base_nm, \"_XRF_pred_upper\")\n      \n      if (!pred_nm %in% names(joined))     next\n      if (!xrf_low_nm %in% names(joined))  next\n      if (!xrf_up_nm %in% names(joined))   next\n      \n      df <- joined %>%\n        dplyr::filter(\n          !is.na(.data[[pred_nm]]),\n          !is.na(.data[[obs_col]])\n        )\n      \n      if (nrow(df) == 0) next\n      \n      # Build data frame for plotting with error bars\n      df_pred <- df %>%\n        dplyr::mutate(\n          Observed  = .data[[obs_col]],\n          Predicted = .data[[pred_nm]],\n          Site      = .data[[\"Site\"]],\n          # Horizontal error bars: u00b1 ICP_sd (ppm) from ICP_ppm\n          Obs_low   = if (sd_col %in% names(df)) Observed - .data[[sd_col]] else Observed,\n          Obs_high  = if (sd_col %in% names(df)) Observed + .data[[sd_col]] else Observed,\n          # Vertical error bars from XRF prediction interval (ppm)\n          Pred_low  = .data[[xrf_low_nm]],\n          Pred_high = .data[[xrf_up_nm]]\n        )\n      \n      # Compute statistics for annotation\n      ok <- !is.na(df_pred$Observed) & !is.na(df_pred$Predicted)\n      R2   <- NA_real_\n      RMSE <- NA_real_\n      \n      if (any(ok)) {\n        obs_ok <- df_pred$Observed[ok]\n        pred_ok <- df_pred$Predicted[ok]\n        \n        SS_res <- sum((obs_ok - pred_ok)^2)\n        SS_tot <- sum((obs_ok - mean(obs_ok))^2)\n        \n        R2   <- 1 - SS_res / SS_tot\n        RMSE <- sqrt(mean((obs_ok - pred_ok)^2))\n      }\n      \n      stats_label <- paste0(\n        \"Ru00b2 = \", signif(R2, 3),\n        \"\\nRMSE = \", signif(RSE <- RMSE, 4)\n      )\n      \n      # Coordinates for annotation (top-left-ish)\n      x_left <- min(df_pred$Observed,  na.rm = TRUE)\n      x_range <- max(df_pred$Observed, na.rm = TRUE) - x_left\n      \n      y_top  <- max(df_pred$Predicted, na.rm = TRUE)\n      y_range <- y_top - min(df_pred$Predicted, na.rm = TRUE)\n      \n      x_offset <- 0.1 * x_range\n      y_offset <- 0.2 * y_range\n      \n      # Pred vs Obs with ICP & prediction-interval error bars\n      p1 <- ggplot(df_pred, aes(Observed, Predicted, colour = Site)) +\n        # Grey error bars behind points\n        geom_segment(aes(x = Obs_low, xend = Obs_high,\n                         y = Predicted, yend = Predicted),\n                     inherit.aes = FALSE,\n                     colour = \"grey80\", linewidth = 0.4) +\n        geom_segment(aes(x = Observed, xend = Observed,\n                         y = Pred_low, yend = Pred_high),\n                     inherit.aes = FALSE,\n                     colour = \"grey80\", linewidth = 0.4) +\n        geom_point(size = 1.25) +\n        ggsci::scale_color_jco(name = \"Site\") +\n        geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0) +\n        annotate(\n          \"text\",\n          x = x_left - x_offset,\n          y = y_top + y_offset,\n          hjust = 0,\n          vjust = 1,\n          label = stats_label,\n          size  = 2.7\n        ) +\n        labs(\n          x = expression(\"Observed ICP-MS (mg kg\"^{-1}*\")\"),\n          y = expression(\"Predicted (mg kg\"^{-1}*\")\"),\n          title = paste(el, mname, \"- ACE Predicted vs Observed\")\n        ) +\n        theme_bw() + theme_small +\n        coord_fixed() +\n        theme(\n          plot.title.position = \"panel\"\n        )\n      \n      # Save per-model Pred vs Obs PDF\n      ggsave(\n        file.path(el_dir, paste0(el, \"_\", mname, \"_ACE_PredVsObs.pdf\")),\n        p1, width = 12, height = 9, units = \"cm\"\n      )\n      \n      # Store for ACE summary panels\n      p_po_list_ace[[mname]] <- p1\n      \n      # Residual histogram\n      df$resid <- df[[pred_nm]] - df[[obs_col]]\n      \n      p2 <- ggplot(df, aes(resid)) +\n        geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = \"grey80\") +\n        geom_density(colour = \"red\") +\n        theme_bw() + theme_small +\n        labs(title = paste(el, mname, \"- ACE Residuals\")) +\n        theme(plot.title.position = \"panel\")\n      \n      ggsave(\n        file.path(el_dir, paste0(el, \"_\", mname, \"_ACE_Residuals.pdf\")),\n        p2, width = 12, height = 9, units = \"cm\"\n      )\n    }\n    \n    # ===========================================================\n    # 16. ACE SUMMARY PANELS (2u00d72 & 2u00d74) WITH SQUARE PANELS\n    #     u2013 same structure as Section 8.7u20138.9 but for ACE\n    # ===========================================================\n    \n    linear_models   <- c(\"OLS\", \"OLS_weighted\", \"WLS\", \"WLS_weighted\")\n    multivar_models <- c(\"Bayes\", \"RF\", \"PLS_kfold\", \"PLS_LOO\")\n    \n    get_plot_or_blank_ace <- function(model_name) {\n      if (!is.null(p_po_list_ace[[model_name]])) {\n        p_po_list_ace[[model_name]] + coord_fixed()\n      } else {\n        ggplot() + theme_void() + coord_fixed()\n      }\n    }\n    \n    ## 16.2 Single-page 2u00d74 A4 (portrait) using coord_fixed\n    \n    all_models_order <- c(\n      \"OLS\",\n      \"OLS_weighted\",\n      \"WLS\",\n      \"WLS_weighted\",\n      \"Bayes\",\n      \"RF\",\n      \"PLS_kfold\",\n      \"PLS_LOO\"\n    )\n    \n    get_plot_or_blank_ace2 <- function(model_name) {\n      if (!is.null(p_po_list_ace[[model_name]])) {\n        p_po_list_ace[[model_name]] + coord_fixed()\n      } else {\n        ggplot() + theme_void() + coord_fixed()\n      }\n    }\n    \n    all_plots_ace <- lapply(all_models_order, get_plot_or_blank_ace2)\n    \n    row1 <- all_plots_ace[[1]] | all_plots_ace[[2]]\n    row2 <- all_plots_ace[[3]] | all_plots_ace[[4]]\n    row3 <- all_plots_ace[[5]] | all_plots_ace[[6]]\n    row4 <- all_plots_ace[[7]] | all_plots_ace[[8]]\n    \n    summary_panel_all_ace <- (row1 / row2 / row3 / row4) +\n      patchwork::plot_layout(guides = \"collect\") &\n      theme(\n        legend.position  = \"bottom\",\n        legend.direction = \"horizontal\",\n        legend.box       = \"horizontal\"\n      ) &\n      guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1))\n    \n    ggsave(\n      filename = paste0(el, \"_ACE_PredObs_Model_Summary_1page_x.pdf\"),\n      path     = el_dir,\n      plot     = summary_panel_all_ace,\n      width    = 21,    # A4 portrait width (cm)\n      height   = 29.7,  # A4 portrait height (cm)\n      units    = \"cm\"\n    )\n    \n    ## Diagnostics\n    sh_W <- sh_p <- NA_real_\n    if (length(resid_vals) >= 3) {\n      sh <- tryCatch(shapiro.test(resid_vals), error = function(e) NULL)\n      if (!is.null(sh)) {\n        sh_W <- unname(sh$statistic)\n        sh_p <- sh$p.value\n      }\n    }\n    \n    bp_stat <- bp_p <- NA_real_\n    if (inherits(m, c(\"lm\",\"bayesglm\"))) {\n      bp <- tryCatch(bptest(m), error = function(e) NULL)\n      if (!is.null(bp)) {\n        bp_stat <- bp$statistic\n        bp_p    <- bp$p.value\n      }\n    }\n    \n    diag_df <- dplyr::add_row(\n      diag_df,\n      Model             = mname,\n      Shapiro_W         = sh_W,\n      Shapiro_p         = sh_p,\n      Shapiro_expl      = expl_shapiro,\n      BreuschPagan_stat = bp_stat,\n      BreuschPagan_p    = bp_p,\n      BreuschPagan_expl = expl_bp,\n      CV10_RMSE         = RMSEP_val,\n      CV10_expl         = expl_cv10,\n      AIC               = AIC_val,\n      AIC_expl          = \"Not used for ranking.\",\n      BIC               = BIC_val,\n      BIC_expl          = \"Not used for ranking.\"\n    )\n    \n    # ppm-scale values (original PI)\n      preds_df[[paste0(base_nm, \"_Pred_ppm\")]] <- exp(pred_new_log)\n      preds_df[[paste0(base_nm, \"_L95_ppm\")]]  <- exp(lower_log)\n      preds_df[[paste0(base_nm, \"_U95_ppm\")]]  <- exp(upper_log)\n      \n      #               "Great question u2014 and the answer is **because your script is intentionally following the statistical convention used in calibration modelling**.\n\nLetu2019s make this absolutely clear, because it confuses everyone at least once.\n\n---\n\n# u2705 **1. In your code: `y` = Observed ICP-MS**\nCorrect:\n\n```r\ny <- data[[y_col]]    # y_col = \"<Element>_ICP\"\n```\n\nSo:\n\n- **Observed ICP-MS (log ppm)** is stored in `y`\n- That is the *reference analytical measurement*\n\n---\n\n# u2705 **2. Why is Observed ICP on the *x-axis* and Predicted on the *y-axis*?**\nBecause this is the **standard way to present calibration validity**:\n\n### **Predicted (from model) vs Observed (true measurement)**  \nud83dudfe6 **Y-axis** = Predicted  \nud83dudfe9 **X-axis** = Observed  \n\nThis is the same arrangement used in:\n\n- Regression diagnostics  \n- Method comparison  \n- PLS calibration validation  \n- Machine learning performance plots  \n\n**Reason:**  \nYou want to visually check how close the **predicted** values are to the **true** analytical values.  \n\nIf the model is perfect, all points fall on the **1:1 line**, which is drawn as:\n\n```r\ngeom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0)\n```\n\nThat line only makes conceptual sense if:\n\n```\nY = Predicted\nX = Observed\n```\n\nNot the other way around.\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudcca **3. This is EXACTLY what your output plots show**\n\nInside Section 8:\n\n```r\naes(Observed, Predicted)\n```\n\nis equivalent to:\n\n```r\naes(x = Observed, y = Predicted)\n```\n\nMeaning:\n\n| Axis | Variable | Meaning |\n|------|----------|---------|\n| **X-axis** | Observed (ICP-MS) | true chemical measurements |\n| **Y-axis** | Predicted | model estimates from XRF |\n\n---\n\n# ud83cudfaf **4. Why not plot Observed on Y and Predicted on X?**\n\nYou *could*, but:\n\n- The 1:1 calibration line becomes visually unintuitive  \n- RMSE, RMSEP, and regression metrics are always interpreted as  \n  **predicted relative to observed**  \n- Every chemometrics textbook uses **Predicted vs Observed**, not the reverse  \n- All your summary and multi-model panel tools assume this orientation  \n- You already have vertical error bars = prediction uncertainty  \n- You already have horizontal error bars = observed ICP uncertainty  \n  u2192 so axis orientation is consistent with the meaning of each error bar\n\nSo the current implementation is **correct, expected, and statistically standard**.\n\n---\n\n# u2714 TL;DR u2014 Why predicted is on Y-axis?\n\nBecause this is a **Predicted vs Observed validation plot**, not an u201cObserved vs Predictedu201d plot.\n\nOr in words:\n\n> u201cHow well do the modelu2019s predictions (Y) match the actual observed ICP values (X)?u201d\n\nThis is the universally accepted orientation.\n\n---\n\n# If you *want* to flip axes anywayu2026\n\nI can provide a patch that flips:\n\n```r\naes(Observed, Predicted)\n```\n\nto:\n\n```r\naes(Predicted, Observed)\n```\n\nand automatically adjusts:\n\n- 1:1 line  \n- Error bars  \n- Annotation placement  \n- Summary pages  \n- ACE sections  \n\nJust say:\n\nud83dudc49 **u201cFlip axes everywhereu201d**  \nor  \nud83dudc49 **u201cFlip axes in Section 8 onlyu201d**\n\nHappy to proceed!"

happens in Section 8\n\n### In Section 8 you now do (correctly):\n\n```r\nscale_x_continuous(limits = c(x_min, x_max))\nscale_y_continuous(limits = c(y_min, y_max))\ncoord_fixed()\n```\n\nBut for present\n\n> u26a0ufe0f `coord_fixed()` enforces *data-unit ratio*, **not panel shape**\n\n---\n\n## Why this shows up for RF and not others\n\n| Model | Prediction behavior | Effect |\n|----|----|----|\n| OLS / WLS | Linear, symmetric | x/y ranges similar u2192 square |\n| PLS | Regularised | ranges similar |\n| **RF** | Nonlinear, high variance | **y-range >> x-range** |\n| RF |               "This comes down to **how ggplot treats `colour` vs `fill` for different point shapes**, and **which aesthetic your site/age plots are mapping**.\n\n### Short answer\nYour **ICP-MS age plots are using a *filled* point shape (e.g. shape 16)**, so `colour = \"blue\"` fills the point completely.  \nYour **element age plots are using a *fillable* shape (e.g. shape 21)**, so `colour` controls the outline and `fill = \"white\"` controls the interior.\n\nThey are behaving correctly u2014 theyu2019re just using **different shapes**.\n\n---\n\n## Whatu2019s actually happening\n\n### ggplot point shapes fall into two families\n\n| Shape type | Examples | Uses `colour` | Uses `fill` |\n|-----------|---------|--------------|------------|\n| **Solid shapes** | 16, 17, 18 | u2714 | u2716 |\n| **Fillable shapes** | 21u201325 | u2714 (outline) | u2714 (inside) |\n\n---\n\n### Your element age plots (correct)\nYouu2019ve likely got something like this defined globally:\n\n```r\ngeom_point(\n  shape = 21,\n  colour = \"blue\",\n  fill   = \"white\",\n  size   = 2\n)\n```\n\nu2714 Blue outline  \nu2714 White fill  \nu2714 Matches your design intent\n\n---\n\n### Your ICP-MS depth/age plots (blue filled circles)\nThey are almost certainly using either:\n\n```r\ngeom_point(colour = \"blue\")        # default shape = 16\n```\n\nor\n\n```r\ngeom_point(shape = 16, colour = \"blue\")\n```\n\nShape **16 ignores `fill`**, so the point is solid blue.\n\n---\n\n## Why this didnu2019t show up elsewhere\nBecause:\n- Element age plots explicitly set **shape = 21**\n- ICP-MS plots rely on **defaults**, which are shape = 16\n\nSo ggplot is doing exactly what itu2019s told u2014 just inconsistently.\n\n---\n\n## How to make them match (recommended fix)\n\nWherever you plot ICP-MS age/depth points, change:\n\n```r\ngeom_point(colour = \"blue\", size = 2)\n```\n\nto:\n\n```r\ngeom_point(\n  shape  = 21,\n  colour = \"blue\",\n  fill   = \"white\",\n  size   = 2\n)\n```\n\nThat will make **ICP-MS points visually identical** to your element plots.\n\n---\n\n## One-line rule to remember (worth keeping)\n\n> **If you want hollow circles, you must use shapes 21u201325 and set both `colour` and `fill`.**\n\n---\n\nIf you want, I can:\n- Audit your plotting helpers and point out exactly where shape 16 is slipping in\n- Suggest a single global helper function so this never diverges again\n- Help you encode ICP vs XRF visually (outline vs fill) consistently across all plots"

              "Yes u2014 and you can do this **cleanly, quantitatively, and comparably across models and elements** using **signal-to-noise ratios (SNR)** derived from your *existing outputs*. Below is a **practical framework + ready-to-drop R code** that fits your pipeline.\n\n---\n\n## 1ufe0fu20e3 What u201csignalu201d and u201cnoiseu201d mean in *your* context\n\nFor **XRF-calibrated model outputs downcore**, a defensible definition is:\n\n### **Signal**\nThe magnitude of the predicted concentration variability:\n- either **mean predicted ppm**\n- or **standard deviation of predicted ppm downcore**\n\n### **Noise**\nUncertainty associated with predictions:\n- **RMSE_ppm** (model calibration error)\n- or **prediction CI width** (preferred for downcore stability)\n- or **downcore roughness** (high-frequency variance)\n\nYou already compute **all three**, so we can use them.\n\n---\n\n## 2ufe0fu20e3 Three complementary SNR metrics (recommended)\n\n### **A. Model SNR (global stability)**\n> u201cWhich model is intrinsically least noisy?u201d\n\n\\[\n\\textbf{SNR}_{\\text{model}} = \\frac{\\text{mean(predicted ppm)}}{\\text{RMSE}_{ppm}}\n\\]\n\nHigher = better (strong signal, low noise)\n\n---\n\n### **B. Downcore CI-based SNR (prediction stability)**\n> u201cWhich model produces the tightest predictions downcore?u201d\n\n\\[\n\\textbf{SNR}_{\\text{CI}} = \n\\frac{\\text{sd(predicted ppm)}}{\\text{mean(CI width ppm)}}\n\\]\n\nwhere  \n\\[\n\\text{CI width} = U95_{ppm} - L95_{ppm}\n\\]\n\nThis directly answers **u201csmallest downcore errorsu201d**.\n\n---\n\n### **C. Roughness-penalised SNR (optional but powerful)**\n> u201cWhich model produces smooth, geochemically plausible profiles?u201d\n\n\\[\n\\textbf{SNR}_{\\text{smooth}} =\n\\frac{\\text{sd(predicted ppm)}}{\\text{sd(diff(predicted ppm))}}\n\\]\n\nThis penalises jitter/noise even if RMSE is low.\n\n---\n\n## 3ufe0fu20e3 Output table structure (what youu2019ll get)\n\n| Element | Model | Mean_ppm | RMSE_ppm | Mean_CI_width | SD_pred | SNR_model | SNR_CI | SNR_smooth |\n|-------|------|---------|---------|--------------|--------|----------|--------|------------|\n| Ca | PLS_kfold | 4.12 | 0.18 | 0.42 | 0.95 | **22.9** | **2.26** | **5.4** |\n| Ca | RF | 4.20 | 0.31 | 0.88 | 1.02 | 13.5 | 1.16 | 2.1 |\n\nYou can rank **per element** or **globally across all elements**.\n\n---\n\n## 4ufe0fu20e3 Drop-in R code (uses your existing files)\n\nThis assumes:\n- `preds_store[[el]]` exists\n- Columns like `MODEL_el_Pred_ppm`, `MODEL_el_L95_ppm`, `MODEL_el_U95_ppm`\n\n### **Build SNR table**\n\n```r\n# ===============================================================\n# SNR TABLE: Stability of XRF-calibrated model outputs\n# ===============================================================\n\nsnr_table <- list()\n\nfor (el in elements) {\n  \n  df <- preds_store[[el]]\n  if (is.null(df)) next\n  \n  for (mname in names(model_store[[el]])) {\n    \n    pred_col <- paste0(mname, \"_\", el, \"_Pred_ppm\")\n    l_col    <- paste0(mname, \"_\", el, \"_L95_ppm\")\n    u_col    <- paste0(mname, \"_\", el, \"_U95_ppm\")\n    \n    if (!all(c(pred_col, l_col, u_col) %in% names(df))) next\n    \n    pred <- df[[pred_col]]\n    l95  <- df[[l_col]]\n    u95  <- df[[u_col]]\n    \n    ok <- !is.na(pred) & !is.na(l95) & !is.na(u95)\n    if (sum(ok) < 5) next\n    \n    pred <- pred[ok]\n    ci_width <- u95[ok] - l95[ok]\n    \n    mean_pred <- mean(pred)\n    sd_pred   <- sd(pred)\n    mean_ci   <- mean(ci_width)\n    \n    # RMSE from calibration\n    rmse_ppm <- global_summary %>%\n      dplyr::filter(Element == el, Model == mname) %>%\n      dplyr::pull(RMSE_ppm)\n    \n    # Roughness (downcore noise)\n    roughness <- sd(diff(pred))\n    \n    snr_table[[length(snr_table) + 1]] <- data.frame(\n      Element        = el,\n      Model          = mname,\n      Mean_ppm       = mean_pred,\n      RMSE_ppm       = rmse_ppm,\n      Mean_CI_width  = mean_ci,\n      SD_pred        = sd_pred,\n      SNR_model      = mean_pred / rmse_ppm,\n      SNR_CI         = sd_pred / mean_ci,\n      SNR_smooth     = sd_pred / roughness\n    )\n  }\n}\n\nsnr_df <- do.call(rbind, snr_table)\n\nwrite.csv(\n  snr_df,\n  file.path(all_base, \"XRF_Model_SNR_Stability.csv\"),\n  row.names = FALSE\n)\n```\n\n---\n\n## 5ufe0fu20e3 How to interpret the results (important)\n\n### u2714 Best models:\n- **High SNR_model**\n- **High SNR_CI**\n- **High SNR_smooth**\n\n### u26a0 Warning signs:\n- High RMSE but smooth u2192 *biased but stable*\n- Low RMSE but low SNR_smooth u2192 *overfitting / jitter*\n- Wide CI but smooth u2192 *under-constrained model*\n\n---\n\n## 6ufe0fu20e3 One-sentence interpretation for a paper\n\n> u201cModel stability was assessed using signal-to-noise ratios derived from predicted concentration variance relative to calibration error, prediction interval width, and downcore roughness, allowing identification of models producing the most robust and least noisy geochemical profiles.u201d\n\n---\n\n## 7ufe0fu20e3 Short README version\n\n> u201cModel stability was quantified using signal-to-noise ratios based on predicted variance relative to calibration RMSE, prediction interval width, and downcore smoothness.               "Yes u2014 you can make this **collapse cleanly with only a title visible** by wrapping the code in **Markdown `<details>` blocks**.  \nThis works in GitHub, many Markdown viewers, and most RMarkdown / Quarto HTML outputs.\n\nBelow is your **Section 11 extension reformatted** so it collapses to a single clickable title.\n\n---\n\n<details>\n<summary><strong>ud83dudd27 Section 11 Extension u2014 XRF_pred SNR, Robustness & Production Model Selection</strong></summary>\n\n```r\n# ===============================================================\n# SECTION 11 EXTENSION:\n# XRF_pred SNR, robustness, stability flags, production model\n# ===============================================================\n\nscale01 <- function(x) {\n  rng <- range(x, na.rm = TRUE)\n  if (!is.finite(diff(rng)) || diff(rng) == 0)\n    return(rep(NA_real_, length(x)))\n  (x - rng[1]) / diff(rng)\n}\n\nsnr_rows <- list()\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------\n# 1. Compute SNR + stability metrics (XRF_pred ONLY)\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------\nfor (el in elements) {\n  \n  df <- preds_store[[el]]\n  if (is.null(df)) next\n  \n  for (mname in names(model_store[[el]])) {\n    \n    pred_col <- paste0(mname, \"_\", el, \"_Pred_ppm\")\n    l_col    <- paste0(mname, \"_\", el, \"_L95_ppm\")\n    u_col    <- paste0(mname, \"_\", el, \"_U95_ppm\")\n    \n    if (!all(c(pred_col, l_col, u_col) %in% names(df))) next\n    \n    pred <- df[[pred_col]]\n    l95  <- df[[l_col]]\n    u95  <- df[[u_col]]\n    \n    ok <- !is.na(pred) & !is.na(l95) & !is.na(u95)\n    if (sum(ok) < 6) next\n    \n    pred <- pred[ok]\n    ci_w <- u95[ok] - l95[ok]\n    \n    rmse_ppm <- global_summary %>%\n      dplyr::filter(Element == el, Model == mname) %>%\n      dplyr::pull(RMSE_ppm)\n    \n    roughness <- sd(diff(pred), na.rm = TRUE)\n    \n    snr_rows[[length(snr_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(\n      Element        = el,\n      Model          = mname,\n      Mean_ppm       = mean(pred, na.rm = TRUE),\n      RMSE_ppm       = rmse_ppm,\n      Mean_CI_width  = mean(ci_w, na.rm = TRUE),\n      SD_pred        = sd(pred, na.rm = TRUE),\n      Roughness      = roughness,\n      SNR_model      = mean(pred, na.rm = TRUE) / rmse_ppm,\n      SNR_CI         = sd(pred, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(ci_w, na.rm = TRUE),\n      SNR_smooth     = sd(pred, na.rm = TRUE) / roughness\n    )\n  }\n}\n\nsnr_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(snr_rows)\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------\n# 2. Merge SNR metrics into global_summary\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------\nglobal_summary <- global_summary %>%\n  dplyr::left_join(\n    snr_df %>%\n      dplyr::select(\n        Element, Model,\n        Mean_ppm, Mean_CI_width,\n        SNR_model, SNR_CI, SNR_smooth,\n        Roughness\n      ),\n    by = c(\"Element\", \"Model\")\n  )\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------\n# 3. Robustness class (for colour-coding)\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------\nglobal_summary <- global_summary %>%\n  dplyr::mutate(\n    Robustness_Class = dplyr::case_when(\n      Robust_Rank == 1 & !Unstable_flag ~ \"Preferred\",\n      Robust_Rank <= 2 & !Unstable_flag ~ \"Acceptable\",\n      TRUE                              ~ \"Unstable\"\n    )\n  )\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------\n# 7.               "Below is a **clear methodological explanation** followed by **practical visualisation code** you can drop into your workflow.\n\n---\n\n## 1ufe0fu20e3 How robustness is used to classify models\n\n### Conceptual logic\n\nRobustness is designed to answer:\n\n> *Which calibrated XRF model gives predictions that are accurate, stable downcore, and minimally noisy?*\n\nIt combines **model accuracy** with **signal stability**.\n\n---\n\n### Metrics used\n\nFor each **element u00d7 model**, robustness is derived from:\n\n1. **Accuracy**\n   - **Ru00b2** (calibration or validation performance)\n\n2. **Noise / uncertainty**\n   - **SNR\\_CI**  \n     Signal-to-noise ratio based on prediction uncertainty  \n     (signal variability u00f7 mean CI width)\n\n3. **Downcore stability**\n   - **SNR\\_smooth**  \n     Penalises high point-to-point roughness (spiky profiles)\n\n---\n\n### Robustness score\n\nEach metric is **scaled 0u20131 within each element**, then combined:\n\n```text\nRobustness Score =\n  0.4 u00d7 SNR_CI_scaled\n+ 0.3 u00d7 SNR_smooth_scaled\n+ 0.3 u00d7 Ru00b2_scaled\n```\n\nThis ensures:\n- Models with **narrow CIs**,  \n- **smooth downcore behaviour**, and  \n- **high explanatory power**  \nare favoured.\n\n---\n\n### Classification rules\n\n| Class        | Definition |\n|-------------|-----------|\n| **Preferred** | Highest robustness score **and** not flagged unstable |\n| **Acceptable** | Rank 2u20133 robustness, stable but slightly noisier |\n| **Unstable** | High roughness or poor SNR despite reasonable Ru00b2 |\n\nUnstable models are **never selected** as production models, even if Ru00b2 is high.\n\n---\n\n### Automatic production model selection\n\nFor each element:\n- The **highest-ranked stable model** is automatically selected\n- Stored as `Production_Model`\n- Used consistently for:\n  - Downcore plots\n  - ACE predictions\n  - Reporting\n\nThis prevents subjective model picking.\n\n---\n\n## 2ufe0fu20e3 Visualising SNR and robustness\n\n### A.               "A **radar plot** (also called a spider plot) is a way to show **multiple performance dimensions at once** for each model, on the **same scale**, so you can judge *overall robustness* rather than a single metric.\n\nBelow is how to interpret the **specific radar plots youu2019re generating**.\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudd0d What each axis means (in your plots)\n\nEach **spoke** of the radar corresponds to a *scaled* metric (0u20131):\n\n1. **Ru00b2u209b (Predictive skill)**\n   - How well the model reproduces ICP-MS values\n   - 1 = near-perfect prediction\n   - 0 = poor predictive skill\n\n2. **SNR_CIu209b (Prediction stability / uncertainty)**\n   - Signal-to-noise ratio based on CI width\n   - High values = narrow confidence intervals relative to signal\n   - Low values = noisy / unstable predictions\n\n3. **SNR_smoothu209b (Downcore smoothness)**\n   - Measures how smooth the depth profile is\n   - Penalises oscillatory / over-fitted models\n   - High values = geochemically plausible trends\n\nAll axes are **scaled to [0,1]**, so **distance from centre is comparable**.\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudd78 How to read the shape\n\n### 1ufe0fu20e3 Area = overall robustness\n- **Large, filled polygons** u2192 strong models\n- **Small or spiky shapes** u2192 weak or unstable models\n\nA model that performs well in *only one* metric will look **lopsided**.\n\n---\n\n### 2ufe0fu20e3 Balance matters more than peaks\nExample:\n\n| Shape | Interpretation |\n|-----|---------------|\n| ud83dudd3a Tall spike on Ru00b2 only | Good fit but unstable / noisy |\n| ud83dudfe6 Wide, rounded shape | Robust and trustworthy |\n| ud83eude93 One collapsed axis | Critical failure mode |\n\nA model with:\n```\nRu00b2 = 0.95\nSNR = 0.25\nSmoothness = 0.30\n```\nis **worse** than one with:\n```\nRu00b2 = 0.85\nSNR = 0.80\nSmoothness = 0.85\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudd01 Comparing models on the same radar\n\nEach coloured polygon is **one model**:\n\n- If one polygon **encloses** another u2192 it dominates it\n- If polygons cross u2192 trade-offs exist\n- Overlapping shapes u2192 similar performance\n\nud83dudc49 **The preferred model** is usually the one with:\n- Largest area\n- No axis close to zero\n- Smooth, rounded shape\n\n---\n\n## u26a0 Common warning patterns\n\n### u274c Overfitting\n- High Ru00b2\n- Low smoothness\n- Spiky shape\n\n### u274c Noisy prediction\n- High Ru00b2\n- Very low SNR_CI\n- Narrow spike near centre on uncertainty axis\n\n### u274c Underfit\n- Moderate values everywhere\n- Small overall polygon\n\n---\n\n## u2705 How you should *use* the radar plot\n\n### u2714 Decision rule (what reviewers expect)\n\n> *u201cModels were selected based on joint performance across predictive skill, uncertainty, and downcore smoothness. Preference was given to models with consistently high scores across all metrics rather than maximising Ru00b2 alone.u201d*\n\n### u2714 Practical workflow\n1. Use **heatmap** u2192 screen models\n2. Use **radar plots** u2192 final per-element decision\n3. Flag:\n   - Preferred\n   - Acceptable\n   - Unstable\n\n---\n\n## ud83euddea What the radar plot is NOT\n\n- u274c Not a statistical test\n- u274c Not an optimisation surface\n- u274c Not meant for absolute thresholds\n\nItu2019s a **decision-support visualisation**.\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudcdd One-line caption for figures\n\n> *Radar plots summarise model robustness across predictive skill (Ru00b2), uncertainty (SNR), and downcore smoothness. Larger, more balanced shapes indicate more stable and geochemically plausible models.*\n\n---\n\nIf you want, I can:\n- Add **model ranking numbers inside radar plots**\n- Automatically **select the dominant polygon**\n- Generate **per-element recommendation text** from radar geometry"

              "Short answer: **no u2014 u201cunstableu201d is *not* defined as Robustness < 0.75 by default** in your current pipeline.\n\nHere is the precise, code-faithful definition based on what youu2019ve implemented.\n\n---\n\n## How *unstable* is actually defined in your robustness framework\n\n### 1. **Robustness_score (0u20131)**\nYou compute robustness as a **continuous score**, e.g.:\n\n```r\nRobustness_score =\n  0.6 * SNR_CI_s +\n  0.4 * SNR_smooth_s\n```\n\n(or variants including Ru00b2 in Section 11A).\n\nu27a1ufe0f **This score itself does *not* define instability.**  \nIt is only used for **ranking** and comparison.\n\n---\n\n### 2. **What u201cunstableu201d actually means (key point)**\n\nInstability is determined by **downcore behaviour**, *not* the robustness score threshold.\n\nSpecifically, instability is flagged using **roughness / smoothness**, e.g.:\n\n```r\nRoughness_norm = scale01(Roughness)\n\nUnstable_flag =\n  Roughness_norm > 0.7\n```\n\nor equivalently in later logic:\n\n- **High short-scale variance**\n- **Low SNR_smooth**\n- **Large point-to-point fluctuations relative to signal**\n\nSo:\n\n> u2705 A model can have **high robustness_score** but still be **unstable**  \n> u274c A low robustness_score does *not automatically* mean unstable\n\n---\n\n### 3. How models are classified in practice\n\nFrom your Section 11A logic:\n\n```r\nRobustness_Class =\n  case_when(\n    Robust_Rank == 1 & !Unstable_flag ~ \"Preferred\",\n    Robust_Rank <= 2 & !Unstable_flag ~ \"Acceptable\",\n    TRUE                              ~ \"Unstable\"\n  )\n```\n\nThis means:\n\n| Condition | Classification |\n|---------|---------------|\n| Best-ranked **and** stable | **Preferred** |\n| Next-best **and** stable | **Acceptable** |\n| Any unstable model | **Unstable** |\n\nu27a1ufe0f **Instability overrides robustness score.**\n\n---\n\n## Why you *might* be thinking u201c< 0.75u201d\n\nThat threshold is **reasonable**, but it is **not currently implemented**.\n\nSome users expect logic like:\n\n```r\nRobustness_score < 0.75 u2192 unstable\n```\n\nBut your code does **not** do this u2014 and thatu2019s actually good science, because:\n\n- Robustness is *relative* across models\n- Stability is a *physical / stratigraphic* property\n\n---\n\n## If you *want* a numeric robustness threshold (optional)\n\nYou could add an **explicit rule**, e.g.:\n\n```r\nUnstable_flag =\n  Roughness_norm > 0.7 |\n  Robustness_score < 0.5\n```\n\nor classify:\n\n| Robustness_score | Interpretation |\n|------------------|----------------|\n| u2265 0.8 | Very robust |\n| 0.6u20130.8 | Moderate |\n| < 0.6 | Weak |\n\nBut **this would be a design choice**, not what your current pipeline does.\n\n---\n\n## One-line definition you can put in methods / README\n\n> *A model is classified as unstable if it exhibits high downcore roughness (low smoothness SNR), irrespective of its overall robustness score.*\n\n---\n\nIf you want, I can:\n- add an **explicit robustness threshold option**\n- visualise **instability flags directly on depth profiles**\n- or help you justify this definition in a **methods paragraph for reviewers**"

              "Here is a **clear, reviewer-facing justification** explaining **why this robustness-based, element-specific approach is necessary in palaeoclimate reconstructions**, written to align *exactly* with your Section 11 terminology and logic.\n\n---\n\n## **Why an element-specific robustness framework is necessary**\n\n### **Primary manuscript / Methods justification**\n\n> Palaeoclimate reconstructions derived from geochemical proxies are inherently element-specific, reflecting differences in geochemical behaviour, measurement uncertainty, and proxy sensitivity to environmental processes. Consequently, a single regression model cannot be assumed to perform consistently across all elements.  \n>  \n> To address this, we evaluate model performance using a composite **Robustness_score**, integrating signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and uncertainty dominance through model-derived confidence intervals and downcore smoothness. This framework explicitly accounts for both predictive skill and stability of the reconstructed signal, which are critical requirements for palaeoclimate interpretation.\n\n---\n\n### **Why traditional u201cbest-fitu201d metrics are insufficient**\n\n> Conventional model selection based solely on goodness-of-fit metrics (e.g. Ru00b2 or RMSE) may favour models that reproduce calibration data but yield unstable or uncertainty-dominated downcore reconstructions.
