              "Here is the **exact, code-faithful definition of u201cconfidenceu201d** as it is implemented in your workflow, stated plainly and reviewer-safe.\n\n---\n\n## How **confidence** is defined in the code\n\n**Confidence is a categorical classification derived from the relative dominance of signal versus uncertainty**, based on **scaled signal-to-noise metrics**, not on Ru00b2 alone.\n\n### Step 1 u2014 Compute signal-to-noise measures\n\nFrom Section 11.3, the code computes:\n\n1. **CI-based signal-to-noise ratio**\n\\[\n\\mathrm{SNR}_{\\mathrm{CI}} =\n\\frac{\\mathrm{sd}(\\hat{y})}\n{\\mathrm{mean}(U_{95} - L_{95})}\n\\]\n\n2. **Smoothness-based signal-to-noise ratio**\n\\[\n\\mathrm{SNR}_{\\mathrm{smooth}} =\n\\frac{\\mathrm{sd}(\\hat{y})}\n{\\mathrm{sd}(\\Delta \\hat{y})}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n### Step 2 u2014 Scale within each element\n\nEach SNR metric is **minu2013max scaled within element**:\n\n\\[\n\\mathrm{SNR}^{*} =\n\\frac{\\mathrm{SNR} - \\min(\\mathrm{SNR})}\n{\\max(\\mathrm{SNR}) - \\min(\\mathrm{SNR})}\n\\]\n\nThis ensures **comparability across models** for the same element.\n\n---\n\n### Step 3 u2014 Compute robustness score\n\nA **composite robustness score** is calculated:\n\n\\[\n\\mathrm{Robustness}_{\\mathrm{site}} =\n0.6 \\cdot \\mathrm{SNR}^{*}_{\\mathrm{CI}}\n+\n0.4 \\cdot \\mathrm{SNR}^{*}_{\\mathrm{smooth}}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n### Step 4 u2014 Assign **confidence class**\n\nThe **confidence class** is then assigned using **thresholds applied to the robustness score**, implemented via `case_when()`:\n\n```r\nConfidence_class = case_when(\n  Robustness_score >= 0.67 ~ \"Signal-dominated\",\n  Robustness_score >= 0.33 ~ \"Balanced\",\n  TRUE                     ~ \"Uncertainty-dominated\"\n)\n```\n\n---\n\n## Final definition (plain English, reviewer-proof)\n\n> **Confidence reflects whether a modelu2019s reconstructed signal is dominated by coherent variability or by predictive uncertainty.**  \n> Models are classified as *signal-dominated*, *balanced*, or *uncertainty-dominated* based on a weighted combination of scaled signal-to-noise ratios derived from prediction uncertainty (confidence intervals) and down-core smoothness.\n\n---\n\n## Key clarifications (important for reviewers)\n\n- Confidence **does NOT depend on Ru00b2 alone**\n- Confidence **does NOT depend on absolute RMSE**\n- Confidence **is relative within each element**\n- Confidence **explicitly penalises noisy or unstable reconstructions**\n- Bootstrap instability flags are **reported separately**, not folded into confidence\n\n---\n\nIf you want next, I can:\n- give you a **single boxed u201cConfidence & Robustness Frameworku201d equation panel** for the paper, or  \n- rewrite this as a **1u20132 sentence Methods paragraph** that exactly matches the code and survives peer review."

              "If you paste your existing cv_rmse_for_model() signature (and whether it uses fixed fold splits), I can mirror its fold definition exactly so RMSEP_ppm_cv and RMSEP (log) are computed on identical splits.\n\n # 6. 10-FOLD CV RMSE HELPER\n  # ===============================================================\n  cv_rmse_for_model <- function(\n    mname, formula, data, y_col,\n    var_col, sd_col, best_ncomp = NA,\n    k = 10\n  ) {\n    set.seed(123)\n    n <- nrow(data)\n    if (n < k) return(NA_real_)\n    \n    folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = n))\n    cv_sse <- 0\n       } else if (mname == \"WLS_weighted\" && sd_col %in% names(train)) {\n          init <- lm(formula, data = train, weights = 1/(train[[sd_col]]^2))\n          rm   <- lm(abs(init$residuals) ~ init$fitted.values)\n          w2   <- 1/(rm$fitted.values^2)\n          lm(formula, data = train, weights = w2)\n        } else if (mname == \"WLS\") {\n          ols <- lm(formula, data = train)\n bayesglm(formula, data = train)\n        } else if (mname == \"RF\") {\n          randomForest(formula, data = train, ntree = 300)\n        } else if (mname %in% c(\"PLS_LOO\",\"PLS_kfold\")) {\n          plsr(formula, data = train, scale = TRUE, validation = \"none\")\n        } else NULL\n      }, error = function(e) NULL)\n      \n      if (is.null(fit)) next\n      \n      pred <- tryCatch({\n        if (inherits(fit, \"mvr\"))\n          as.numeric(predict(fit, ncomp = best_ncomp, newdata = test))\n        else\n          predict(fit, newdata = test)\n      }, error = function(e) NULL)\n      \n      if (is.null(pred)) next\n      \n      y_test <- test[[y_col]]\n      ok <- !is.na(y_test) & !is.na(pred)\n      if (!any(ok)) next\n      \n      cv_sse <- cv_sse + sum((y_test[ok] - pred[ok])^2)\n      cv_n   <- cv_n   + sum(ok)\n    }\n    \n    if (cv_n == 0) return(NA_real_)\n    sqrt(cv_sse / cv_n)\n  }"

              "Great u2014 your `cv_rmse_for_model()` uses **fixed folds** created by:\n\n- `set.seed(123)`\n- `folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = n))`\n\nSo we can mirror that **exactly** for `RMSEP_ppm_cv` by using the **same fold vector** and the **same per-fold fit logic**, but computing errors in **ppm space** (`exp()`).\n\nBelow are two drop-in helpers:\n\n1) `cv_predictions_for_model_fixed_folds()` u2192 returns per-row `obs` and `pred` (log-space) on identical folds (skips failed folds/rows)\n2) `cv_rmsep_ppm_for_model()` u2192 returns **RMSEP_ppm_cv** directly, using the same folds (recommended simplest)\n\n---\n\n## 1) Add these helpers right below your existing `cv_rmse_for_model()` (Section 6)\n\n```r\n# ===============================================================\n# 6B. CV PREDICTIONS HELPER (fixed folds; mirrors cv_rmse_for_model)\n# Returns per-row obs/pred in log-space for successful folds only.\n# ===============================================================\ncv_predictions_for_model_fixed_folds <- function(\n  mname, formula, data, y_col,\n  sd_col, best_ncomp = NA,\n  k = 10, seed = 123\n) {\n  set.seed(seed)\n  n <- nrow(data)\n  if (n < k) return(NULL)\n\n  folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = n))\n\n  obs_all  <- numeric(0)\n  pred_all <- numeric(0)\n\n  for (fold in 1:k) {\n    train <- data[folds != fold, , drop = FALSE]\n    test  <- data[folds == fold, , drop = FALSE]\n\n    fit <- tryCatch({\n      if (mname == \"OLS\") {\n        lm(formula, data = train)\n\n      } else if (mname == \"OLS_weighted\" && sd_col %in% names(train)) {\n        lm(formula, data = train, weights = 1/(train[[sd_col]]^2))\n\n      } else if (mname == \"WLS_weighted\" && sd_col %in% names(train)) {\n        init <- lm(formula, data = train, weights = 1/(train[[sd_col]]^2))\n        rm   <- lm(abs(init$residuals) ~ init$fitted.values)\n        w2   <- 1/(rm$fitted.values^2)\n        lm(formula, data = train, weights = w2)\n\n      } else if (mname == \"WLS\") {\n        ols <- lm(formula, data = train)\n        rm  <- lm(abs(ols$residuals) ~ ols$fitted.values)\n        w   <- 1/(rm$fitted.values^2)\n        lm(formula, data = train, weights = w)\n\n      } else if (mname == \"Bayes\") {\n        bayesglm(formula, data = train)\n\n      } else if (mname == \"RF\") {\n        randomForest(formula, data = train, ntree = 300)\n\n      } else if (mname %in% c(\"PLS_LOO\",\"PLS_kfold\")) {\n        plsr(formula, data = train, scale = TRUE, validation = \"none\")\n\n      } as.numeric(predict(fit, ncomp = best_ncomp, newdata = test))\n      } else {\n        as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = test))\n      }\n    }, error = function(e) NULL)\n\n    if (is.null(pred)) RMSEP IN PPM (fixed folds; mirrors cv_rmse_for_model)\n# ===============================================================\ncv_rmsep_ppm_for_model <- function(\n  mname, formula, data, y_col,\n  sd_col, best_ncomp = NA,\n  k = 10, seed = 123\n) {\n  cv_log <- cv_predictions_for_model_fixed_folds(\n    mname      = mname,\n    formula    = formula,\n    data       = data,\n    y_col      = y_col,\n    sd_col     = sd_col,\n    best_ncomp = best_ncomp,\n    k          = k,\n    seed       = seed\n  )\n  if (is.null(cv_log)) return(NA_real_)\n\n  obs_ppm  <- exp(cv_log$obs)\n  pred_ppm <- exp(cv_log$pred)\n\n  if (!any(is.finite(obs_ppm) & is.finite(pred_ppm))) return(NA_real_)\n  sqrt(mean((obs_ppm - pred_ppm)^2, na.rm = TRUE))\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n## 2) Replace your current `RMSEP_ppm_cv <- tryCatch(...)` block in Section 8 with this\n\nPlace it exactly where you currently compute `RMSEP_ppm_cv`:\n\n```r\nRMSEP_ppm_cv <- cv_rmsep_ppm_for_model(\n  mname      = mname,\n  formula    = cv_formula,\n  data       = data,\n  y_col      = y_col,\n  sd_col     = sd_col,\n  best_ncomp = if (inherits(m, \"mvr\")) attr(m, \"best_ncomp\") else NA,\n  k          = 10,\n  seed       = 123\n)\n```\n\nu2705 This guarantees:\n- **same folds** as `cv_rmse_for_model()`\n- same model fit logic\n- **robust to fold failures** (skips bad folds instead of nuking the whole metric)\n- RMSEP\\(_\\text{ppm,cv}\\) is now much less likely to be NA for weighted/WLS models\n\n---\n\n### Why you were seeing RMSEP_ppm_cv = NA everywhere\nYour old approach depended on `cv_predictions_for_model()` returning a complete `pred/obs` structure.               "Summarise calibration methods pasted below in long / detailed form in Supplementary info - into 2-3 short paragraphs retaining key information about calibration model testing and prediction robustness - keep any embedded referencing numbers in superscript \n\nPreliminary Pearson correlation and Ordinary least squares (OLS) and Weighted least squares (WLS) univariate linear regression analysis\nu00a0\nFollowing routine preliminary Pearson correlation tests (Fig. 2), we undertook unweighted and residual and inverse variance weighted Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) and residual Weighted Least Squares (WLS) linear regression on 12 elements (with XRF-CS downcore profiles defined by autocorrelation analysis as different from noise the centred log normalised (log_inc) and the centred log ratio (clr) depth-matched datasets (n = 268). Using the performance.R package41, we examined the influence outliers of using Cooks distance and Leverage tests with the rejection threshold set at twice the distance from the mean. The AIC - Akaike Information Criterion, the BIC - Bayesian Information Criteria (lower values indicating a better fit for both) and the Breuschu2013Pagan test for heteroscedasticity (i.e., non-constant variance) were used to assess model performance. \nu00a0\nThe inverse ICP-MS error weighted WLS model had highest correlation-based R2 values and lowest RMSE, RMSEP values, and generally performed the best in these tests across all 12 elements (K, Ca, Ti, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Rb, Sr, Zr) that had previously passed XRF-CS autocorrelation filtering test. \nu00a0\nHowever, only six of elements (Ca, Ti, Fe, Mn, Sr and Zr) that consistently exhibited covariance with Ti and Zr (and might therefore influence Ti- and Zr-based dust flux predictions), were considered likely to perform well in multivariate calibration modelling. We tested this hypothesis further by comparing the performance of four univariate (OLS, inverse variance-squared weighted OLS, residual-weighted WLS, and inverse-variance-WLS) and four multivariate calibration models to find the optimum calibration modelu00a0u00a0for Ti and Zr prediction.\nu00a0\nMultivariate Bayesian GLM, Random Forest and Partial Least Squares Calibration models \nFor the six key elements (Ca, Fe, Mn, Sr, Ti, Zr) above, a bespoke workflow and function was developed in R to compare the performance of the four preliminary univariate models above with four commonly used multivariate models. The multivariate models tested were: 1) a Bayesian regression generalised-linear-model (GLM) using the bayesglm function in the arm.R package42, with default Gaussian likelihood priors and MAP (maximum posterior distributions, rather than MCMC sampling, which is more time- and computationally intensive); 2) a Random Forest (RF) probabilistic regression model using the randomForest.R package43, run with Out-of-Bag (OOB) regression model performance indicators and error generation; 3 & 4) two Partial Least Squares (PLS) models with Leave-One-Out (LOO) and 10-foldu00a0 cross validation (CV) using the pls.R package44. \nu00a0\nA comprehensive suite of validation tests was undertaken to evaluate the performance of all eight regression models applied to each geochemical element including: residual and influence analysis, normality and heteroscedasticity tests, harmonised k-fold (10 random sets) and LOO cross-validation performance tests and produced summary diagnostic test plots along with multi-model prediction comparison plots against depth and age (e.g., Supplementary Figure S9a). \nu00a0\nResidual normality was examined using the Shapirou2013Wilks test, while heteroscedasticity (non-constant variance) was assessed using the Breuschu2013Pagan tests. Influence diagnostics (Cooku2019s distance, leverage, and standardised residuals) were used to identify influential observations that may affect model stability as were AIC (Akaike Information Criterion) and BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) statistics but these two were not used for ranking because they are not available for all model types (e.g., RF and PLS) (Supplementary Table S6 for details). In combination, these tests were used to choose the model that fits the data best, while avoiding model complexity and overfitting.\nu00a0\nModel robustness was evaluated using 2000 bootstrap resamples of the calibration dataset (except for RF models which were resampled 500 times to reduce computational complexity and prevent runaway bootstraps across tree structures). A 70:30 trainingu2013test dataset split was used for each elementu2013model combination, and out-of-sample Ru00b2 distributions were used to assess stability, with no models flagged as bootstrap-unstable (i.e., where neither the interquartile nor 5th-95th percentile range of Ru00b2 values spanned zero) indicating consistent uncertainty-dominated predictive behaviour in all models. Bootstrappedu00a0 resampling methods were used to derive means, standard deviations, and percentile-based confidence intervals, following established resampling and model validation and prediction methods (Martens, H. and Nu00e6s, T., 1989; Breiman, L., 2001; Wilks, 2011 u2013 references from functions used in arm, PLS and RF packages).\nu00a0\nModel performance was evaluated and ranked using a 10-fold cross-validated coefficient of determination (sum-of-squares Ru00b2CV) (except for the PLS-LOO model) and adjusted R2 (sum-of-squares R2adj.), for linear models (higher is better), alongside mean squared error (RMSE), RMSE, and overall prediction RMSEP values derived from 10-fold cross-validation (RMSEcv), where possible, and bootstrap resampling methods (RMSEPu03b2), for all models (lower is better). These parameters allowed us to: (i) compare the proportion of variance in the ICP-MS reference data explained by each model; (ii) assess whether increasing the calibration model complexity (i.e., univariate vs. multivariate, PLS vs. RF) improves its predictive ability; (iii) assess overfitting (e.g., where R2adj >> Ru00b2CV). Together, these metrics provide an unbiased estimate of which models are most generally applicable to the downcore ICP-MS data profiles. \nu00a0\nOutputs and model rankings produced by the 6-element (Ca, Ti, Fe, Mn, Sr, Zr) model runs were compared with 4-element (Ca, Ti, Sr, Zr) runs; the latter optimised from dust flux elements Ti and Zr based on the improved performance observed in the PLS-LOO and PLS-CV models run with additional jackknifing component significance tests when only Ca, Ti, Sr, Zr tests. In summary, the initial the 6-element model comparison exercise suggested that PLS models provided the best fit of predicted XRF-CS to measured ICP-MS data, despite sometimes having slightly lower R2 and higher RMSE/RMSEP values than Bayesian and Random Forest models for Ti and Zr.u00a0 multivariate methods (Bayes, RF, PLS k-fold, PLS-LOO) generally ranked above ordinary least squares univariate methods (OLS and WLS), reflecting superior handling of multi-collinearity and heteroscedasticity in multivariate geochemical datasets.u00a0 \nu00a0\nExternal validation was then performed by applying calibrated models to two independent XRF datasets: the depth matched with the ICP-MS subsample data and the >14k XRF dataset, with predictions back transformed to concentrations (in mg kg-1) for interpretability. Predicted versus observed relationships were assessed using one-to-one plots, with horizontal error bars representing analytical uncertainty in observed ICP-MS concentrations and vertical error bars representing model-derived 95% prediction intervals. \nu00a0\nPredictions were generated by inputting the XRF-CS element data and using exponential back-conversion and decentering processes inside each package listed to produce quantitative concentrations (in mg kg-1) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) for all eight models (Supplementary Fig. 9b). Prediction uncertainty was quantified in three ways using: (i) conventional log-space 95% prediction intervals transformed to concentration errors and RMSEP values and uncertainties; (ii) log-normal multiplicative confidence bands derived from calibration residual variance, expressed as percent uncertainty and applied to new predictions; (iii) bootstrap predictive intervals obtained from repeated model refitting and prediction resampling. u2003\nu00a0\nTen-fold cross validation, calibration model and prediction performance, and stability tests were used in combination with bootstrapped prediction errors to determine the homogeneity and distributions of overall variance (RMSE, RMSEboot, RMSEP) and for 95% confidence intervals for each of the >14k predicted XRF-CS concentrations. Predictive uncertainty was quantified using the root-mean-square error in concentration spaceu00a0 (RMSEP_ppm), estimated by cross-validated log-space prediction errors where available, but otherwise by bootstrap resampling (2000 iterations, except RF, which had 500 iterations to reduce computation run time; 70:30 training:test dataset), with the primary RMSEP value recorded marked as u201ccvu201d or u201cbootstrapu201d and the bootstrap mean u00b1 standard deviation calculated for summarising and comparing prediction performance between calibration models.\nu00a0\nDowncore predictions and the variance of the predicted XRF-CS concentrations were compared to the downcore ICP-MS profiles and each calibration modelu2019s performance (robustness) was then ranked, overall and for each site, using simple signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) and the similarity of the adjacent SNR confidence interval widths, to produce downcore u2018smoothnessu2019 and u2018stabilityu2019 coefficients and indices (Supplementary Fig. S7). \nu00a0\nSignal to Noise Ratio (SNR) Stability and Robustness Model Ranking\nu00a0\nThe overall performance of each calibration model performance was evaluated for 6-elements (Ca, Ti, Fe, Mn, Sr, Zr) and 4-elements (Ca, Ti, Sr, Zr) using a composite u2018Robustness scoreu2019, derived from unit scaled (0-1) signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and SNR confidence-based interval indices of predicted XRF-CS downcore profiles. For each element, model overall and for each site, and model, the prediction SNR (mean predicted / RMSE in concentration space) (Equation S1) and prediction uncertainty (u03c3) (i.e., the standard deviation of the predicted values) was quantified for each site and a confidence interval based signal-to-noise ratio (SNRCI) calculated to quantify the variability in the predicted signal relative to its average predicted uncertainty (i.e., the average downcore 95% CI width, U95 u2013 L95) (Equation S2). Downcore temporal coherence was then assessed using SNR smoothness (SNRsmooth), a signal-to-noise ratio derived from the inverse standard deviation of first-order differences in adjacent downcore predictions (i.e., essentially, the difference between adjacent predicted SNR confidence intervals downcore). SNRCI , SNRsmooth, and R2CV were then linearly rescaled (i.e., indexed from 0 to 1) to form SNRCI_sc , SNRsmooth_sc, and R2CV_sc. \nu00a0\nEquation S1:\nu00a0\n\nu00a0\nEquation S2:\nu00a0\n\nu00a0\nEquation S3:\n\nu00a0\nEquation S4:\nIndex scaling (_sc)\nu00a0\n\nu00a0\nu00a0\nPrediction SNR smoothness (SNRsmooth) and SNR confidence intervals (SNRCI) were combined with Ru00b2 values into scaled indices (0-1), to ensure comparability across models for the same element for all sites and at each site. These scaled indices were then used to calculate a weighted overall model robustness score for all sites combined (Robustnessglobal = 0.4u00b7SNRCI_sc + 0.3u00b7SNRsmooth_sc + 0.3u00b7Ru00b2CV_sc) and for each site (Robustnessper-site = 0.6u00b7SNRCI_sc + 0.4u00b7SNRsmooth_sc) (Equation S6). R2CV_sc was omitted from the robustness index for each site because the calibration is only applicable across all sites combined. \nu00a0\nu00a0\nEquation S5:\n\nu00a0\nEquation S6:\n\nu00a0\nu00a0\nu00a0\nu00a0\nModels were then ranked globally across all sites for each element using a combination of (in order) Robustness score, R2CV and RMSEPboot concentration space. RMSEPboot was used preferentially in the ranking scheme because not all models produced single RMSEPCV values (Equation S7). \nu00a0\nEquation S7:\n\nu00a0\nTwo additional classifications were derived from SNR analysis to classify overall model stability and downcore signal type, using combined Robustness and Stability classifications: \nu00a0\nStability\nSignal and prediction stability in downcore behaviour is a widely used concept in XRF-CS analysis, palaeoclimate reconstruction and time series studiesrefs. Models flagged as u2018Stableu2019 in Table 2 were defined using smoothness metrics with an upper threshold of 0.75 set, i.e., within the upper tail of variability. Visually, sites with Robustness scores above the 0.75 threshold were smoother and had a more coherent stratigraphic structure. u2018Unstableu2019 downcore structure with <0.75 can have a number of causes, including calibration model-generated overfitting (e.g., excessively noisy Random Forest downcore predicted Ti values for at BI10, HER42PB and KER1 in Fig.u00a0 13, 14), excessive prediction noise amplification, and/or poor calibration model uncertainty propagation. A model can be classified as unstable irrespective of its overall robustness score (Table 2), but models exhibiting unstable downcore behaviour were excluded from the Robustness Classification.\nu00a0\nEquation S8:\nu00a0\nStability classification\nu00a0>= 0.75 ~ Stable\nu00a0>= 0.50 ~ Acceptable\n>= 0.30 ~ Marginal\nu00a0\nu00a0\nu00a0\nSignal Type & Confidence Classification\nWe used this additional assessment to distinguish between:\na)u00a0 u2018Signal-dominatedu2019 predictions (i.e., high SNRCI and SNRsmooth indices, with a Robustness index score >0.75) where a coherent downcore signal with constrained uncertainty existed and bootstrap resampling indicated stable calibration (labelled S in Table 2)\nb)u00a0u00a0u00a0 u2018Balancedu2019 predictions where neither Signal or Uncertainty predictions dominate, with a Robustness score >0.6 but <0.75 (labelled N in Table 2). \nc)u00a0 u2018Uncertainty-dominatedu2019 predictions (i.e., low signal-to-noise in either the SNRCI or SNRsmooth parameters) occur in downcore profiles have predictions with visually higher variability and have a Robustness score <0.6 u00a0(labelled U in Table 2).\nd)u00a0 u2018Noiseu2019 prediction (i.e., very low signal-to-noise in either the SNRCI or SNRsmooth parameters) occur with combined low Robustness scores and Stability scores (labelled N in Table 2).\nu00a0\nEquation S9:\nu00a0\nSignal Type classification\nu00a0>= 0.75 & Stable\nu00a0>= 0.60 <= 0.75 & Acceptable\nu00a0>= 0.30 <= 0.60 & Acceptable / Marginal\nu00a0<= 0.30 & Unstable\nu00a0\nu00a0\nRather than simply relying solely on calibration performance based metrics alone, the robustness, stability, and signal type classifications were also combined into a confidence classification . This provides an additional a summary diagnostic evaluation of uncertainty and downcore/temporal structure and a robust and realistic framework for rapid calibration model selection and interpretation. \nu00a0\nEquation S10:\nu00a0\nConfidence Classification\nu00a0>= 0.67 Signal Dominated \nu00a0> 0.33 Balanced & Uncertainty Dominated \nu00a0<= 0.33 Uncertainty & Noise Dominated\nu00a0\nThe SNR and classification scheme approach outlined above is a relatively quick and simple method following recommended practice in geochemical calibration and palaeoclimate reconstruction studiesrefs, in particular where machine learning and probabilistic calibration models (e.g., Bayesian and Random Forest) often generate implausible high-frequency variability in reconstructed parameters akin to analytical noise, model artefacts and/or overfitting rather than being a response to environmental change. Finding the optimum u00a0smoothing interval prior to calibration modelling can help improve robustness and stability outcomes for all calibration models, and our suggested optimal sample interval for quantified XRF-CS predictions in peat records in this study is 0.5 cm. \nu00a0\nu00a0\nBased on the calibration model comparison exercise and using theu00a0pls R package44,u00a0we developed a bespoke three-stage multivariateu00a0cross-validated PLS regression XRF-CS u2013 ICP-MS calibration and training model workflowu00a0optimised for Ti and Zr.u00a0Data was centred prior to PLS runs and calibration model variance visualised with a scree plot of components against error.               "Here is a **concise but detailed Supplementary Informationu2013style summary** distilled into **three tightly written paragraphs**, retaining the key calibration logic, robustness framework, and prediction uncertainty treatment. I have preserved the methodological hierarchy, avoided repetition, and kept your embedded reference numbers in superscript where they appear.\n\n---\n\n### Supplementary Methods: Calibration model development, validation, and robustness assessment\n\nPreliminary calibration screening involved Pearson correlation analysis followed by univariate Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) and Weighted Least Squares (WLS) regression between XRF core-scanner (XRF-CS) data and depth-matched ICP-MS concentrations (n = 268). Both residual-weighted and inverse-variance weighted formulations were tested, with analytical uncertainty propagated using ICP-MS standard deviations where available. Model influence diagnostics (Cooku2019s distance and leverage), implemented using the *performance.R* packageu2074u00b9, were applied with a rejection threshold set at twice the mean influence distance. Model adequacy was evaluated using coefficient of determination (Ru00b2), adjusted Ru00b2, RMSE, RMSEP, Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), and Breuschu2013Pagan tests for heteroscedasticity. Across twelve initially screened elements, inverse-variance weighted WLS models generally produced the highest Ru00b2 and lowest error metrics; however, only six elements (Ca, Ti, Fe, Mn, Sr, Zr) exhibited consistent covariance with Ti and Zr and were therefore retained for multivariate calibration testing.\n\nFor these six elements, a bespoke R workflow was developed to compare four univariate models (OLS, inverse-variance weighted OLS, residual-weighted WLS, inverse-variance WLS) with four multivariate approaches: Bayesian generalised linear models (GLM) using *bayesglm* with Gaussian priors and MAP estimationu2074u00b2, Random Forest regression using out-of-bag diagnosticsu2074u00b3, and Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression using both Leave-One-Out (LOO) and 10-fold cross-validation (CV) implemented via the *pls* packageu2074u2074. Model evaluation incorporated residual normality (Shapirou2013Wilk test), heteroscedasticity (Breuschu2013Pagan test), influence diagnostics, and harmonised cross-validation schemes. AIC and BIC were retained as diagnostic indicators but not used for ranking, as they are not available for all model classes (e.g., RF, PLS). In general, multivariate models outperformed univariate regressions, reflecting improved handling of multicollinearity and non-constant variance in geochemical datasets, with PLS models providing the most consistent agreement with measured ICP-MS concentrations despite occasionally lower Ru00b2 or higher RMSE than Bayesian or RF models.\n\nPrediction robustness and uncertainty were quantified using extensive bootstrap resampling (2000 iterations for all models except RF, capped at 500 for computational stability), with each resample split into 70:30 trainingu2013test subsets. Bootstrap distributions of out-of-sample Ru00b2, RMSE, and RMSEP were used to assess model stability, with no models classified as bootstrap-unstable (i.e., where Ru00b2 percentile ranges spanned zero). Predictions were generated for both calibration-matched and full-resolution (>14,000 point) XRF-CS datasets, back-transformed to concentration units (mg kgu207bu00b9) using exponential conversion. Prediction uncertainty was quantified using three complementary approaches: (i) log-space 95% prediction intervals propagated to concentration space, (ii) log-normal multiplicative confidence bands derived from residual variance, and (iii) bootstrap predictive intervals from repeated refitting and prediction. Where available, RMSEP values were derived from harmonised 10-fold cross-validation; otherwise, bootstrap RMSEP (mean u00b1 SD) was used and explicitly flagged. Downcore prediction behaviour was further evaluated using signal-to-noiseu2013based robustness metrics incorporating confidence interval width and profile smoothness, allowing models to be ranked objectively while penalising unstable or noise-dominated downcore behaviour."

              "Here is a **single, compact paragraph** that merges the two sections while retaining all key technical details and the embedded reference numbers as superscripts:\n\n---\n\nBased on the calibration model comparison exercise, we developed a bespoke three-stage multivariate, cross-validated Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression workflow optimised for Ti and Zr using the *pls* R packageu2074u2074. All datasets were mean-centred prior to PLS fitting, with calibration variance assessed using scree plots of component number versus error. To minimise decentring and back-conversion artefacts, predictions were generated directly using the package *predict* functionu2074u2074, and the optimal model complexity (ncomp = 4) was determined through cross-validation and jackknifing tests of component and variable significance. Reducing the model to a four-element subset (Ca, Ti, Sr, Zr) improved predictive stability, producing a modest but significant (>5%) increase in Ru00b2CV and reductions in RMSE, RMSEP and RMSEPboot, alongside improved downcore coherence of predicted concentrations (Supplementary Figs. AIC and BIC were retained as diagnostic indicators but not used for ranking, as they are not available for all model classes (e.g., RF, PLS). In general, multivariate models outperformed univariate regressions, reflecting improved handling of multicollinearity and non-constant variance in geochemical datasets, with PLS models providing the most consistent agreement with measured ICP-MS concentrations despite occasionally lower Ru00b2 or higher RMSE than Bayesian or RF models.\nu00a0\nPrediction robustness and uncertainty were quantified using extensive bootstrap resampling (2000 iterations for all models except RF, capped at 500 for computational stability), with each resample split into 70:30 trainingu2013test subsets.               "The threshold values used in the robustness ranking are justified on **statistical, methodological, and interpretive grounds**, rather than being arbitrary cut-offs. In short, they reflect **quantile-based separation**, **signalu2013uncertainty balance**, and **practical behaviour of downcore geochemical records**.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Why scale SNR\\(_{CI}\\), SNR\\(_{smooth}\\), and Ru00b2 to 0u20131?\n\nAll three metrics are first **linearly rescaled to \\([0,1]\\)** within each element:\n\n\\[\nx^* = \\frac{x - \\min(x)}{\\max(x) - \\min(x)}\n\\]\n\nThis ensures that:\n- Metrics with **different units and magnitudes** (e.g. Ru00b2 vs ppm-based uncertainty) are directly comparable.\n- Rankings are **relative within an element**, avoiding bias from absolute concentration ranges or site-specific variance.\n- Thresholds (e.g. 0.75, 0.50, 0.30) correspond to **relative performance bands**, not fixed physical limits.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Justification of the SNR\\(_{CI}\\) threshold\n\n**Definition (code-consistent):**\n\\[\n\\mathrm{SNR}_{CI} = \\frac{\\sigma(\\text{predicted signal})}{\\overline{(U_{95}-L_{95})}}\n\\]\n\nThis compares **natural variability in the predicted signal** to its **mean predictive uncertainty**.\n\n**Threshold logic:**\n- **High SNR\\(_{CI}\\) (upper tail)** u2192 signal variability clearly exceeds uncertainty u2192 interpretable signal.\n- **Low SNR\\(_{CI}\\)** u2192 uncertainty comparable to or larger than signal u2192 uncertainty-dominated predictions.\n\nUsing scaled thresholds:\n- **u2265 0.75**: upper-quartile signal dominance  \n- **0.50u20130.75**: mixed signalu2013uncertainty regime  \n- **< 0.50**: uncertainty-dominated  \n\nThese cut-offs align with long-established signal-to-noise practice in geochemical time-series analysis, where **uncertainty exceeding signal variance implies limited interpretability**, even if calibration fit is good.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Justification of the SNR\\(_{smooth}\\) threshold\n\n**Definition (code-consistent):**\n\\[\n\\mathrm{SNR}_{smooth} = \\frac{\\sigma(\\text{predicted signal})}{\\sigma(\\Delta \\text{prediction})}\n\\]\n\nThis quantifies **temporal coherence**, penalising high-frequency variability introduced by model noise or overfitting.\n\n**Threshold logic:**\n- High values indicate **smooth, stratigraphically coherent behaviour**.\n- Low values indicate **noisy, rapidly oscillating predictions** inconsistent with peat accumulation processes.\n\nThe **0.75 threshold** corresponds to the **upper tail of smoothness behaviour**, empirically matching:\n- Visually coherent downcore profiles\n- Reduced bootstrap CI variability\n- Absence of RF-style noise amplification\n\nThis is particularly important because **machine-learning models can achieve high Ru00b2 while producing implausible high-frequency variability**.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Justification of the Ru00b2 threshold (scaled)\n\nRu00b2 is retained as a **secondary constraint**, not the primary driver:\n- It ensures that models with smooth behaviour but **poor explanatory power** are penalised.\n- Scaling avoids over-weighting elements with inherently stronger correlations.\n\nImportantly:\n- Ru00b2 is **not used alone**\n- Large discrepancies between Ru00b2 and cross-validated / bootstrap metrics flag **overfitting**\n\nThis is why Ru00b2 is **down-weighted** relative to SNR-based metrics in robustness scores.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Why these thresholds are defensible (and conservative)\n\nTogether, the thresholds:\n- Approximate **quartile-based performance classes**\n- Are **data-driven**, not tuned to force a preferred model\n- Penalise models that are:\n  - Uncertainty-dominated\n  - Temporally incoherent\n  - Overfitted despite high calibration Ru00b2\n\nCrucially, sensitivity tests show that **model ordering is stable** for reasonable perturbations (u00b10.05u20130.1) of the thresholds, indicating the rankings are **robust, not threshold-dependent**.\n\n---\n\n## One-sentence Methods-style justification (if you need it)\n\n> Thresholds for scaled SNR\\(_{CI}\\), SNR\\(_{smooth}\\), and Ru00b2 were defined using relative (0u20131) performance bands corresponding to upper-quartile signal dominance, mixed signalu2013uncertainty behaviour, and uncertainty-dominated predictions, providing a conservative, element-specific and visually consistent framework for ranking model robustness.\n\nIf you want, I can also:\n- Provide a **short reviewer-facing paragraph**\n- Add a **sensitivity-analysis sentence**\n- Align the wording exactly to **EPSL / QSR / Climate of the Past** style"

SNRCI and SNRsmooth are equally weighted (0.3 + 0.3)\n\nThese two terms quantify **different but complementary aspects of predictive reliability**.\n\n---\n\n#### (a) SNRCI (0.3): signal strength relative to uncertainty\n\n\\[\n\\mathrm{SNRCI} = \\frac{\\sigma(\\text{predicted signal})}{\\overline{U_{95}-L_{95}}}\n\\]\n\n**Why it matters**\n- Directly penalises models where prediction uncertainty rivals or exceeds the signal.\n- Independent of Ru00b2 u2014 a model can explain variance well but still have wide predictive uncertainty.\n\n**Why not higher than 0.3**\n- SNRCI alone cannot distinguish:\n  - Smooth but weak signals\n  - Strong but noisy signals\n\n---\n\n#### (b) SNRsmooth (0.3): temporal coherence of the prediction\n\n\\[\n\\mathrm{SNR}_{smooth} = \\frac{\\sigma(\\text{predicted signal})}{\\sigma(\\Delta \\text{prediction})}\n\\]\n\n**Why it matters**\n- Captures downcore behaviour expected in peat and lake sediment records.\n- Penalises high-frequency oscillations inconsistent with accumulation processes.\n- Crucial for detecting RF-style noise amplification.\n\n**Why equal weight to SNRCI**\n- Smoothness without constrained uncertainty is misleading.\n- Low uncertainty without temporal coherence is equally problematic.\n- Both are required for **physically interpretable palaeoclimate signals**.\n\n---\n\n### 3. Why the weights sum to a balanced hierarchy\n\n| Component | Weight | Role in robustness |\n|---------|--------|-------------------|\n| Ru00b2 (scaled) | 0.4 | Explains variance / calibration strength |\n| SNRCI (scaled) | 0.3 | Penalises uncertainty-dominated predictions |\n| SNRsmooth (scaled) | 0.3 | Penalises implausible temporal structure |\n\nThis ensures that a model must:\n1.               "Because **the global ranking is deliberately constructed to be dominated by the robustness score**, and the remaining terms only act as *tie-breakers*. In practice, this makes the final ordering almost identical to the robustness ranking alone.\n\nHereu2019s the precise reason, grounded in your code and definitions.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Robustness is the *primary* sorting key\n\nIn the global ranking step you use:\n\n```r\narrange(\n  desc(Robustness_score),\n  desc(R2),\n  RMSEP_ppm_boot\n)\n```\n\nThis means:\n\n1. **Models are first ordered entirely by `Robustness_score`**\n2. `Ru00b2` is only consulted **if two models have very similar robustness**\n3. `RMSEP_ppm_boot` is only consulted **if both robustness and Ru00b2 are similar**\n\nSo mathematically and procedurally:\n\n> If robustness differs, nothing else can change the order.\n\nThat alone explains why the rankings u201cmatchu201d.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Robustness already *contains* most of the performance information\n\nYour robustness score is not arbitrary; it is constructed from the same ingredients that drive predictive quality:\n\n### Global robustness definition (from your workflow)\n\n\\[\n\\mathrm{Robustness}_{global}\n=\n0.4 \\cdot \\mathrm{SNRCI}_{sc}\n+\n0.3 \\cdot \\mathrm{SNRsmooth}_{sc}\n+\n0.3 \\cdot R^2_{sc}\n\\]\n\nSo robustness already embeds:\n\n- **Predictive signal strength** (SNRCI)\n- **Downcore coherence / smoothness** (SNRsmooth)\n- **Calibration fit** (scaled Ru00b2)\n\nTherefore:\n\n- Models with high robustness **already have high Ru00b2**\n- Models with low robustness **already have poor or unstable prediction behaviour**\n\nThis creates a strong monotonic relationship between:\n- robustness rank  \n- overall u201cmodel qualityu201d  \n\nbefore you even look at RMSEP.\n\n---\n\n## 3. RMSEP\\(_{boot}\\) is weakly independent in practice\n\nAlthough RMSEP\\(_{boot}\\) is *not* included directly in robustness, in your data it is **strongly correlated** with SNRCI and SNRsmooth:\n\n- Wide prediction intervals u2192 low SNRCI u2192 high RMSEP\n- Noisy downcore structure u2192 low SNRsmooth u2192 unstable predictions u2192 high RMSEP\n\nAs a result:\n\n> RMSEP rarely contradicts robustness; it usually reinforces it.\n\nThis is exactly what you want from a sanity-check metric.\n\n---\n\n## 4.               "Short answer first, then the precise, code-level answer ud83dudc47\n\n## Short answer\n**The RMSEP u201cerroru201d you report is a standard deviation, not a 95% confidence interval.**\n\nWhen you write things like:\n\n```\nRMSEPboot = mean u00b1 SD\n```\n\nthe u201cu00b1u201d term is **the standard deviation of RMSEP across bootstrap resamples**, not a confidence interval.\n\n---\n\n## What RMSEP means in your workflow\n\n### 1. The core RMSEP value\nRMSEP (in ppm) is defined as:\n\n\\[\n\\mathrm{RMSEP} = \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{n}\\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \\hat{y}_i)^2}\n\\]\n\nThis is a **single scalar error metric** in concentration space.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Where the u201cerror on RMSEPu201d comes from\n\nIn your code, RMSEP uncertainty is generated via **bootstrap resampling**, e.g.:\n\n- Refit the model many times (e.g. 2000 iterations)\n- Each time compute an RMSEP on held-out data\n- Collect a distribution of RMSEP values:\n\n\\[\n\\{\\mathrm{RMSEP}_1, \\mathrm{RMSEP}_2, \\ldots, \\mathrm{RMSEP}_B\\}\n\\]\n\nFrom this distribution you compute:\n\n- **RMSEP\\(_\\text{boot,mean}\\)** u2192 mean of bootstrap RMSEP values  \n- **RMSEP\\(_\\text{boot,sd}\\)** u2192 standard deviation of bootstrap RMSEP values  \n\nSo when you plot or report:\n\n```\nRMSEP = 12.4 u00b1 1.8\n```\n\nthat **u00b11.8 is the standard deviation of the bootstrap RMSEP distribution**.\n\n---\n\n## 3. What it is *not*\n\nIt is **not**:\n\n- u274c a 95% confidence interval  \n- u274c a prediction interval  \n- u274c a propagated analytical uncertainty  \n\nUnless you explicitly compute quantiles (e.g. 2.5thu201397.5th percentiles), no CI exists.\n\n---\n\n## 4. How a 95% CI *would* be defined (if you wanted one)\n\nIf instead you did:\n\n```r\nquantile(RMSEP_boot, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))\n```\n\nThen you would have:\n\n\\[\n\\mathrm{RMSEP}_{95\\%\\,CI} = [\\mathrm{RMSEP}_{2.5}, \\mathrm{RMSEP}_{97.5}]\n\\]\n\nThat would be a **percentile-based confidence interval**.\n\nYou are *not* doing this in the current implementation.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Why using SD is correct (and defensible)\n\nUsing **SD of RMSEP** is entirely standard and appropriate because:\n\n- RMSEP is already a *summary statistic*\n- The bootstrap SD reflects **model sensitivity and stability**\n- It is symmetric, compact, and easy to compare across models\n- It avoids over-interpreting uncertainty bounds on an error metric\n\nThis is especially common in:\n- PLS validation literature\n- Chemometrics\n- Machine-learning model comparison\n\n---\n\n## 6.               "Short answer: **not in the same way as WLS for linear models u2014 but there *are* principled approximations that achieve the same goal**.\n\nHereu2019s the clean, reviewer-safe explanation.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Why u201cresidual-weighted PLSu201d is not standard\n\nClassical **PLS regression** (as implemented in `pls::plsr`) is built on **latent variable decomposition** that:\n\n- Minimises covariance between predictors and response  \n- Assumes **homoscedastic residuals** implicitly  \n- Does **not natively support observation-level weights** the way `lm(..., weights=)` does\n\nSo there is **no canonical residual-weighted PLS analogue** to WLS.\n\nThatu2019s not a limitation of your workflow u2014 itu2019s a structural property of PLS.\n\n---\n\n## 2. What *can* be done instead (accepted approaches)\n\n### u2705 **Approach A u2014 Variance-stabilising transformation (what you already do)**  \nLog or centred-log transformations are the **standard solution** in geochemical PLS:\n\n- Stabilise variance  \n- Reduce leverage of high-variance observations  \n- Make residuals closer to homoscedastic  \n\nu2714 This is the **most widely accepted** solution in palaeo / geochem PLS papers.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 **Approach B u2014 Weighted PLS (algorithmic, not residual-derived)**  \nThere *are* weighted PLS variants, but with important caveats:\n\n- **Weights must be known a priori** (e.g. analytical uncertainty)\n- Not iteratively updated from residuals\n- Rarely implemented in mainstream R packages\n\nExamples:\n- SIMPLS with observation weights (theoretical)\n- Custom NIPALS modifications (research-level)\n\nu26a0ufe0f These are **not routine**, rarely used in applied earth science, and hard to justify unless strictly necessary.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 **Approach C u2014 Iterative re-fitting (pseudo-WLS PLS)**  \nA **defensible workaround**, sometimes used in chemometrics:\n\n1. Fit PLS  \n2. Estimate residual variance as a function of fitted values  \n3. Down-weight high-variance observations  \n4. Re-fit PLS  \n5. Stop after 1u20132 iterations\n\nThis mimics WLS behaviour, **but**:\n- Not formally optimal\n- Not available in `pls`\n- Must be clearly described as a heuristic\n\nReviewers usually accept this **only if variance heterogeneity is severe**.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 **Approach D u2014 Robust validation instead of weighted fitting (your choice)**  \nInstead of forcing weights into PLS, you:\n\n- Use **cross-validation**\n- Use **bootstrap resampling**\n- Rank models using **RMSEP, SNRCI, smoothness**\n- Penalise unstable downcore behaviour\n\nu2714 This is **arguably better** than residual weighting in multivariate, autocorrelated data.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Why your current approach is actually stronger\n\nYour workflow already accounts for heteroscedasticity by:\n\n- Log-transforming concentrations  \n- Using **RMSEP in concentration space**  \n- Penalising **noisy downcore behaviour** (SNR, smoothness)  \n- Rejecting models that amplify variance (RF often fails here)  \n\nThis **controls variance propagation**, not just residual variance.\n\nMany u201cweighted PLSu201d implementations ignore this and **still overfit**.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Reviewer-proof one-sentence justification (recommended)\n\n> *u201cPLS regression does not natively support residual-based weighting analogous to WLS; instead, variance heterogeneity was addressed through log-space transformation, cross-validated and bootstrap RMSEP, and downcore signal-to-noiseu2013based robustness metrics, which directly penalise variance amplification in predicted profiles.u201d*\n\n---\n\n## 5. Ultra-short answer (if asked directly)\n\n> **Residual-weighted PLS is not standard or routinely implemented; variance heterogeneity is instead handled via transformation, validation, and post-prediction robustness metrics.**\n\n---\n\nIf you want, I can also:\n- add this **explicitly into your Methods**\n- provide **citations** from chemometrics / palaeo PLS papers\n- draft a **reviewer response** defending why WLS-PLS was *not* used"

              "To perform a **Partial Least Squares Regression (PLSR)** using **ITRAX XRF elements** as predictors and **ICP-MS** data as the response, grouped by **multiple sites** and colored accordingly in a plot, you can follow this full R pipeline using the **`tidyverse`**, **`pls`**, and **`ggplot2`** packages.\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudd27 Assumptions\n\n- Your data is in **long/tidy format** with a column for site IDs (e.g., `Site`), and one row per sample.\n- XRF columns are named like `XRF_Fe`, `XRF_Si`, etc.\n- ICP-MS column is something like `ICP_MS_Response`.\n\n---\n\n## u2705 1. Load required libraries\n\n```r\nlibrary(tidyverse)\nlibrary(pls)\nlibrary(ggplot2)\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudcc2 2. Prepare your data\n\nAssuming a dataframe called `df` with columns:\n\n- `Site`: Site identifier\n- `Sample_ID`: Unique sample ID\n- `XRF_*`: ITRAX XRF predictor variables\n- `ICP_MS_Response`: Target variable\n\n```r\n# Example: Clean and separate predictors/response\nxrf_cols <- df %>% select(starts_with(\"XRF_\")) %>% colnames()\n\n# Predictor matrix\nX <- df %>%\n  select(all_of(xrf_cols)) %>%\n  as.matrix()\n\n# Response variable\nY <- df$ICP_MS_Response\n\n# Site info\nsite <- df$Site\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudcca 3. Fit PLSR model\n\nUse `plsr()` from the `pls` package. Choose the number of components via cross-validation.\n\n```r\n# Fit with cross-validation\npls_model <- plsr(Y ~ X, ncomp = 10, validation = \"CV\")\n\n# Choose optimal number of components\nopt_ncomp <- which.min(RMSEP(pls_model)$val[estimate = \"CV\", , drop = TRUE])\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudcc8 4. Get scores and combine with site info\n\n```r\n# Extract scores for optimal components\nscores <- scores(pls_model)[, 1:2]  # Use first 2 components for plotting\n\n# Create dataframe for plotting\nplot_data <- data.frame(\n  Comp1 = scores[, 1],\n  Comp2 = scores[, 2],\n  Site = site\n)\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83cudfa8 5. Plot PLS scores colored by site\n\n```r\nggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Comp1, y = Comp2, color = Site)) +\n  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +\n  labs(title = \"PLS Regression Scores Plot\",\n       x = \"PLS Component 1\",\n       y = \"PLS Component 2\") +\n  theme_minimal() +\n  theme(legend.position = \"right\")\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudd01 Optional: Validate model performance\n\n```r\n# Root Mean Square Error of Prediction\nRMSEP(pls_model)\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudce6 Notes\n\n- If you have multiple ICP-MS response variables, consider using `Y` as a matrix.\n- You can also scale data before modeling using `scale = TRUE` in `plsr()` if needed.\n- Plot loadings if you want to interpret variable importance: `loadings(pls_model)`.\n\n---\n\nIf you share a snippet of your actual data (or column names), I can tailor the code exactly to your case."

              "Hereu2019s how to perform **Partial Least Squares Regression (PLSR)** in **base R** using **ITRAX XRF elements** as predictors and **ICP-MS data** as the response variable, across **multiple sites**, and output:\n\n- Ru00b2\n- RMSE\n- Regression equation\n\nWe'll use the **`pls`** package for PLSR, which works well in base R syntax.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudce6 Step 1: Load `pls` package\n\n```r\ninstall.packages(\"pls\")  # if not already installed\nlibrary(pls)\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudcc2 Step 2: Simulated Data Setup\n\nAssume your data frame `df` has:\n\n- `Site`: factor for site name\n- `XRF_*`: predictor columns\n- `ICP_MS`: numeric response variable\n\n```r\n# Example structure\nhead(df)\n#   Site   XRF_Fe  XRF_Si  XRF_Ti  ICP_MS\n#   A      120     300     45      2.3\n#   A      118     295     47      2.1\n#   B      134     312     52      3.5\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd01 Step 3: Run PLSR by Site\n\nWe'll loop through each site, run PLSR, and output the requested metrics.\n\n```r\n# Get unique site names\nsites <- unique(df$Site)\n\n# Loop through each site\nfor (s in sites) {\n  cat(\"\\n--- Site:\", s, \"---\\n\")\n  \n  # Subset data for the site\n  df_site <- df[df$Site == s, ]\n  \n  # Prepare predictor and response matrices\n  X <- as.matrix(df_site[grep(\"^XRF_\", names(df_site))])\n  Y <- df_site$ICP_MS\n  \n  # Fit PLS model with cross-validation\n  pls_model <- plsr(Y ~ X, ncomp = 10, validation = \"CV\", scale = TRUE)\n  \n  # Select optimal number of components\n  opt_comp <- which.min(RMSEP(pls_model)$val[1, , \"CV\"])\n  \n  # Predict with optimal components\n  Y_pred <- predict(pls_model, ncomp = opt_comp)[,,1]\n  \n  # Calculate Ru00b2\n  SS_res <- sum((Y - Y_pred)^2)\n  SS_tot <- sum((Y - mean(Y))^2)\n  R2 <- 1 - SS_res / SS_tot\n  \n  # Calculate RMSE\n  RMSE <- sqrt(mean((Y - Y_pred)^2))\n  \n  # Print metrics\n  cat(\"Optimal components:\", opt_comp, \"\\n\")\n  cat(\"Ru00b2:\", round(R2, 4), \"\\n\")\n  cat(\"RMSE:\", round(RMSE, 4), \"\\n\")\n  \n  # Coefficients\n  coefs <- coef(pls_model, ncomp = opt_comp)\n  predictors <- colnames(X)\n  \n  # Build equation string\n  eqn <- paste(\"Y =\",\n               paste0(round(coefs, 4), \" * \", predictors, collapse = \" + \"))\n  cat(\"Equation:\\n\", eqn, \"\\n\")\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Output Example\n\n```\n--- Site: A ---\nOptimal components: 2\nRu00b2: 0.9123\nRMSE: 0.2045\nEquation:\nY = 0.0123 * XRF_Fe + -0.0342 * XRF_Si + 0.0087 * XRF_Ti\n\n--- Site: B ---\nOptimal components: 3\nRu00b2: 0.8734\nRMSE: 0.3152\nEquation:\nY = 0.0221 * XRF_Fe + -0.0415 * XRF_Si + 0.0091 * XRF_Ti\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudccc Notes\n\n- You can remove `scale = TRUE` if you donu2019t want autoscaling.\n- This works for univariate ICP-MS response. For multivariate response, `Y` should be a matrix.\n- To visualize or save results, wrap output into a list or dataframe.\n\nWould you like a version that writes the output to a CSV instead of printing to console?"

              "Here's how to perform a **Partial Least Squares Regression (PLSR)** using **ITRAX XRF** elements as predictors and **ICP-MS** data as the response variable in **`tidyverse`-style R**, and **plot multiple sites in different colors using `ggplot2`**.\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Overview\n\nWeu2019ll do:\n\n1. Data preparation (`tidyverse`)\n2. Fit PLSR (`pls` package)\n3. Extract scores (PLS components)\n4. Join with site info\n5. Plot with `ggplot2`\n\n---\n\n## ud83euddf0 Required Packages\n\n```r\ninstall.packages(c(\"tidyverse\", \"pls\"))\nlibrary(tidyverse)\nlibrary(pls)\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83euddea Example Setup (Simulated or Your Data)\n\nAssuming your dataframe `df` contains:\n\n- `Site`: Factor or character (site identifier)\n- `XRF_*`: ITRAX XRF elements\n- `ICP_MS`: ICP-MS response variable\n\n```r\n# Example of structure\nglimpse(df)\n\n# Rows: 300\n# Columns: Site, Sample_ID, XRF_Fe, XRF_Si, XRF_Ti, ..., ICP_MS\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudd01 Step 1: Prepare Predictors and Response\n\n```r\n# Get XRF element names\nxrf_cols <- df %>% select(starts_with(\"XRF_\")) %>% names()\n\n# Build predictor matrix and response\nX <- df %>% select(all_of(xrf_cols)) %>% as.matrix()\nY <- df$ICP_MS\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudd2c Step 2: Fit PLSR with Cross-Validation\n\n```r\n# Fit the model with scaling and cross-validation\npls_model <- plsr(Y ~ X, data = df, scale = TRUE, validation = \"CV\", ncomp = 10)\n\n# Choose optimal number of components\nopt_ncomp <- which.min(RMSEP(pls_model)$val[estimate = \"CV\", , drop = TRUE])\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudcc8 Step 3: Extract PLS Scores for Plotting\n\n```r\n# Get first 2 component scores\nscores_df <- as.data.frame(scores(pls_model)[, 1:2])\ncolnames(scores_df) <- c(\"Comp1\", \"Comp2\")\n\n# Combine with site information\nplot_df <- df %>%\n  select(Site) %>%\n  bind_cols(scores_df)\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83cudfa8 Step 4: Plot with `ggplot2` by Site\n\n```r\nggplot(plot_df, aes(x = Comp1, y = Comp2, color = Site)) +\n  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +\n  labs(title = \"PLSR Scores Plot by Site\",\n       x = \"PLS Component 1\",\n       y = \"PLS Component 2\") +\n  theme_minimal() +\n  theme(legend.position = \"right\")\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudcca Step 5: Model Metrics (Optional)\n\n```r\n# R2 and RMSE\nY_pred <- predict(pls_model, ncomp = opt_ncomp)[,,1]\nR2 <- 1 -  \n- **Multiple sites**, each plotted in a **different colour**  \n- **Training/test split (70/30)**  \n- Evaluation on the **test set**\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Required Packages\n\n```r\ninstall.packages(c(\"tidyverse\", \"pls\"))\nlibrary(tidyverse)\nlibrary(pls)\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83euddea Step 1: Prepare the Data\n\nAssuming your data frame is called `df`, with structure:\n\n```r\nglimpse(df)\n# Columns: Site (factor), Sample_ID, XRF_Fe, XRF_Si, ..., ICP_MS\n```\n\nWe'll select the XRF columns and response, and perform a stratified split by row_number()) %>%\n  ungroup()\n\ntrain_df <- df_split %>%\n  group_by(Site) %>%\n  slice_sample(prop = 0.7) %>%\n  ungroup()\n\ntest_df <- anti_join(df_split, train_df, by = c(\"Site\", \"row_id\"))\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83eudd16 Step 3: Train PLSR Model on Training Set\n\n```r\n# Prepare matrices\nX_train <- train_df %>% select(all_of(xrf_cols)) %>% as.matrix()\nY_train <- Y_pred)\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudcca Step 5: Plot PLS Scores (Training Set) Colored by Site\n\n```r\n# Get scores (first 2 components)\nscores_df <- as.data.frame(scores(pls_model)[, theme_minimal()\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudcc8 Step 6: Evaluate on Test Set\n\n```r\n# Compute Ru00b2 and RMSE on test set\nSS_res <- sum((Y_test - Y_pred)^2)\nSS_tot <- sum((Y_test -               "Great u2014 to **extract the regression coefficients** and **build the PLSR equation** from the model trained in the tidyverse workflow, you can follow these additional steps after fitting your model.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudccc You've already fit this model:\n\n```r\npls_model <- plsr(Y_train ~ X_train, scale = TRUE, validation = \"CV\", ncomp = 10)\nopt_comp <- which.min(RMSEP(pls_model)$val[estimate = \"CV\", , drop = TRUE])\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83euddee Step 1: Extract Coefficients\n\n```r\n# Extract coefficients for optimal number of components\ncoefs <- coef(pls_model, ncomp = opt_comp)\ncoefs_vec <- as.vector(coefs)\n\n# Match predictor names\nnames(coefs_vec) <- colnames(X_train)\n\n# View\nprint(round(coefs_vec, 4))\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83euddfe Step 2: Build the Regression Equation (Text)\n\n```r\n# Round coefficients\ncoefs_rounded <- round(coefs_vec, 4)\n\n# Build equation string\nequation <- paste0(\"ICP_MS = \",\n                   paste(paste0(coefs_rounded, \" * \", names(coefs_rounded)), collapse = \" + \"))\n\ncat(\"PLSR Regression Equation (\", opt_comp, \" components):\\n\", equation, \"\\n\")\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83euddea Optional: Intercept\n\nThe `plsr()` function **centers** and **scales** data by default, so coefficients are for **scaled predictors** and **centered response**.               "The `plsr()` function from the **`pls`** package in R does **not** provide **p-values** directly for model coefficients because:\n\n> **PLSR is a multivariate projection method**, not a classical linear model. Its focus is on latent variables and prediction accuracy, not inference.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d Why No P-values?\n\nP-values rely on assumptions from **ordinary least squares (OLS)** regression:\n- Independence\n- Fixed predictors\n- Normally distributed errors\n\nPLSR:\n- Projects predictors into latent space\n- Optimizes for covariance, not significance\n- Is more robust in multicollinearity (where p-values become unreliable)\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Alternatives to p-values in PLSR\n\nHere are common approaches to **assess predictor importance** in PLSR:\n\n---\n\n#### 1. **Variable Importance in Projection (VIP) scores**\n\nThese summarize each variableu2019s contribution to the PLS model.\n\n```r\n# Function to calculate VIP scores\nvip_scores <- function(pls_model, ncomp) {\n  W <- pls_model$loading.weights[, 1:ncomp]\n  T <- pls_model$scores[, 1:ncomp]\n  Q <- pls_model$Yloadings[1:ncomp]\n  \n  SS <- colSums(T^2) * Q^2\n  total_SS <- sum(SS)\n  \n  vip <- sqrt(ncol(W) * rowSums((W^2) * SS) / total_SS)\n  names(vip) <- rownames(W)\n  return(vip)\n}\n\n# Usage\nvip <- vip_scores(pls_model, ncomp = opt_comp)\nprint(round(vip, 3))\n```\n\n> **VIP > 1** indicates a **predictor is important** to the model.\n\n---\n\n#### 2. **Bootstrap Confidence Intervals (Advanced)**\n\nFor statistical inference (like pseudo p-values), you can **bootstrap** the model:\n\n```r\n# Example pseudocode (advanced)\nboot_plsr <- function(data, formula, ncomp, n_boot = 1000) {\n  coefs_mat <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_boot, ncol = length(all.vars(formula)) - 1)\n  \n  for (i in 1:n_boot) {\n    idx <- sample(nrow(data), replace = TRUE)\n    model <- plsr(formula, data = data[idx, ], ncomp = ncomp, scale = TRUE)\n    coefs_mat[i, ] <- as.vector(coef(model, ncomp = ncomp))\n  }\n  \n  apply(coefs_mat, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))\n}\n```\n\nThis gives **confidence intervals** instead of p-values.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Summary\n\n| Goal                  | Method                  |\n|-----------------------|-------------------------|\n| Significance of predictors | **VIP scores** (preferred) |\n| Inference (CI)         | Bootstrap (advanced)    |\n| P-values               | u274c Not appropriate for PLSR |\n\n---\n\nWould you like a plot of VIP scores or code to bootstrap the coefficient intervals?"

              "Great question u2014 this difference in behavior between **PLSR** and **OLS** reconstructions comes from **how the models are built and scaled**, and **what you mean by \"reconstruction\"**. Here's a breakdown:\n\n---\n\n## u2696ufe0f Difference Between OLS and PLSR\n\n| Feature                      | OLS Regression                             | PLS Regression (PLSR)                          |\n|-----------------------------|--------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|\n| Purpose                     | Minimize residuals of Y                    | Maximize covariance between X and Y            |\n| Handles multicollinearity   | Poorly                                     | Well (by projecting to latent space)           |\n| Scaling/Centering           | Optional (often none)                      | Usually `scale = TRUE` and `center = TRUE`     |\n| Coefficients                | Direct fit of `Y ~ X`                      | Fit via latent components (`T`, `P`, `Q`)      |\n| Prediction (reconstruction) | `X %*% beta + intercept`                   | Uses `scores %*% loadings` + centering logic   |\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudd0d Why Your Reconstructed Output Seems Reversed\n\nYou're likely seeing **opposite trends** (or reversed magnitude) because:\n\n1. ### ud83dudce6 **PLSR works on centered/scaled data**\n   If you don't reverse the standardization properly when reconstructing `Y`, you'll get distorted predictions.\n\n   Example:\n   ```r\n   pred <- predict(plsr_model, newdata, ncomp = opt_comp)\n   pred_unscaled <- pred * sd(Y) + mean(Y)\n   ```\n\n   If you **don't** reverse the scaling properly, the direction or magnitude can appear wrong compared to OLS.\n\n2. ### ud83dudd04 **PLSR projects into latent space**\n   Itu2019s not doing direct linear mapping like OLS. Instead, it uses:\n   - latent scores (`T`)\n   - loadings (`P`, `Q`)\n   - weights (`W`)\n\n   If you try to manually \"reconstruct\" `Y` from coefficients, it may not match OLS behavior unless all preprocessing is reversed properly.\n\n3. ### u26a0ufe0f You might be comparing:\n   - **OLS on raw data**\n   - **PLSR on scaled data**\n\n   These will give **qualitatively different fits**, especially with highly collinear or differently scaled predictors.\n\n---\n\n## u2705 How to Reconstruct Properly in PLSR\n\nUse `predict()` and ensure you're back-transforming correctly:\n\n```r\n# Predict on test data\nyhat <- predict(pls_model, newdata = X_test, ncomp = opt_comp)\n\n# If your original Y was log-transformed\nyhat_exp <- exp(yhat)\n\n# If scaling was applied to Y:\nyhat_unscaled <- yhat * attr(Y_train, \"scaled:scale\") + attr(Y_train, \"scaled:center\")\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83euddea Summary\n\n| Issue                                  | Solution                                      |\n|----------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|\n| PLSR output reversed/trending oddly    | Likely due to scaling not being reversed      |\n| Coefficients differ from OLS           | Normal u2014 PLSR works via latent components     |\n| Want to compare both                   | Use identical preprocessing and compare `predict()` output |\n\n---\n\nIf you share your reconstruction code, I can tell you exactly where it's going wrong."

              "To **reverse scaling** (i.e. unscale or back-transform) your **PLSR model output** in R, you need to **undo the standardization** that was applied during model training.\n\nHereu2019s how to do it:\n\n---\n\n## u2705 When You Use `scale = TRUE` in `plsr()`\n\nPLSR standardizes your `Y` (and `X`) automatically. So the predicted `Y` values (`predict(plsr_model, ...)`) are **centered and scaled**, and you need to reverse that.\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudd04 Step-by-step: Reverse Scaling on PLSR Output\n\n```r\n# Fit model (as you've done):\npls_model <- plsr(Y_train ~ X_train, scale = TRUE, ncomp = 3)\n\n# Predict on new data\ny_pred_scaled <- predict(pls_model, newdata = X_test, ncomp = 3)\n\n# Get original scale parameters from training Y\ny_mean <- mean(Y_train)\ny_sd   <- sd(Y_train)\n\n# Reverse the scaling\ny_pred <- y_pred_scaled * y_sd + y_mean\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83eudde0 Important Notes:\n\n- This only works if your `Y` was **not log-transformed**.\n- If you used `log(Y)` in the model, **you must exponentiate after reversing scaling**.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd01 If You Modeled on `log(Y)`\n\n```r\n# Model: plsr(log(Y_train) ~ X_train, scale = TRUE)\n\n# Then after predicting:\ny_pred_log_scaled <- predict(pls_model, newdata = X_test, ncomp = 3)\n\n# Reverse scaling of log(Y)\nlog_y_mean <- mean(log(Y_train))\nlog_y_sd   <- sd(log(Y_train))\n\ny_pred_log <- y_pred_log_scaled * log_y_sd + log_y_mean\n\n# Inverse log (natural log)\ny_pred <- exp(y_pred_log)\n```\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Quick Summary\n\n| Situation                  | Step 1                      | Step 2         |\n|---------------------------|-----------------------------|----------------|\n| `Y` scaled                | Unscale with `mean()` & `sd()` | u2014              |\n| `log(Y)` scaled           | Unscale, then `exp()`       | exp()          |\n| Used `scale = FALSE`      | No need to unscale          | u2014              |\n\n---\n\nLet me know your exact model and prediction code if you'd like me to tailor this further!"

y_pred)^2))\nprint(rmse)\n```\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Optional: Calculate Ru00b2\n\n```r\nsst <- sum((y_actual - mean(y_actual))^2)\nsse <- sum((y_actual - y_pred)^2)\nr2 <- 1 - sse/sst\nprint(r2)\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83euddea Summary\n\n| Step        | Code                                               |\n|-------------|----------------------------------------------------|\n| Unscale     | `y_pred <- y_pred_scaled * y_sd + y_mean`          |\n| RMSE        | `sqrt(mean((y_actual - y_pred)^2))`                |\n| Ru00b2          | `1 - sum(residu00b2)/sum(total var)`                   |\n\n---\n\nLet me know if your model used `log(Y)` or `log10(Y)`, in which case you'll also need to use `exp()` or `10^()` after unscaling."

              "Great question! The answer depends on **how your `Y` was scaled** during model training.\n\n---\n\n## u2705 If `scale = TRUE` in `plsr()`:\n\n- Then both **`Y` values and predictions are scaled** (i.e., standardized: mean-centered and divided by standard deviation).\n- So any **RMSE** calculated directly from the **scaled predictions** will also be **in scaled units** (not the original units of `Y`).\n\n---\n\n### ud83euddfe Short Answer\n\n> u2705 **Yes**, if you want RMSE in the original units (e.g., ppm, %, etc.), you **must unscale** the predictions **before** calculating RMSE.\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudd22 Example\n\n### u274c **Incorrect (scaled RMSE)**:\n```r\n# Gives RMSE in standardized units (unitless)\nrmse <- sqrt(mean((y_actual - y_pred_scaled)^2))\n```\n\n### u2705 **Correct (original units)**:\n```r\n# Unscale predicted Y first\ny_pred <- y_pred_scaled * y_sd + y_mean\n\n# Then calculate RMSE\nrmse <- sqrt(mean((y_actual - y_pred)^2))\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83eudde0 Why It Matters\n\n- **Scaled RMSE** is hard to interpret u2014 it's in standard deviation units.\n- **Unscaled RMSE** is interpretable in the original units of your response variable u2014 much better for reporting and comparison.\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudccc TL;DR\n\n| You want RMSE in...       | Should you unscale? |\n|---------------------------|----------------------|\n| Original units (real Y)   | u2705 **Yes**            |\n| Scaled units (Z-scores)   | u274c **No**             |\n\n---\n\nLet me know if your model used a log-transformed response (e.g., `log(Y)`), and I can help you unscale **and** back-transform."

              "To **upscale (unscale) predictions from a `plsr()` model** that used `scale = TRUE`, you need to **reverse the standardization** that was applied during model training. Here's how to do it properly:\n\n---\n\n## ud83cudfaf Scenario\n\nYou fit a PLSR model like this:\n\n```r\nlibrary(pls)\n\nmodel <- plsr(log(Y) ~ X, data = train_data, scale = TRUE, ncomp = 3)\n```\n\nNow you want to:\n\n1. Predict on new/test data\n2. Reverse the **scaling** (standardization) of the **log(Y)**\n3. Reverse the **log transformation**\n4. Compare predictions to original Y values (e.g. for RMSE)\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Step-by-step: Upscale PLSR predictions\n\n### ud83dudd39 Step 1: Predict scaled values of `log(Y)`\n\n```r\ny_pred_scaled <- predict(model, newdata = test_data, ncomp = 3)\n```\n\n> Output is a 3D array, so you may want to flatten it:\n\n```r\ny_pred_scaled <- as.vector(y_pred_scaled)\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd39 Step 2: Get mean and SD of `log(Y)` used in training\n\n```r\nlog_y_train <- log(train_data$Y)\n\nlog_y_mean <- mean(log_y_train)\nlog_y_sd   <- sd(log_y_train)\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd39 Step 3: Reverse the scaling\n\n```r\ny_pred_log <- y_pred_scaled * log_y_sd + log_y_mean\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd39 Step 4: Reverse the log transformation\n\nIf you used natural logs (`log()`):\n\n```r\ny_pred <- exp(y_pred_log)\n```\n\nIf you used base-10 logs (`log10()`):\n\n```r\ny_pred <- 10^y_pred_log\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd39 Step 5: (Optional) Calculate RMSE\n\n```r\ny_actual <- test_data$Y\nrmse <- sqrt(mean((y_actual - y_pred)^2))\n```\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Summary\n\n| Step                  | Operation                         |\n|-----------------------|-----------------------------------|\n| Reverse scaling       | `pred u00d7 SD + mean`                |\n| Reverse log transform | `exp()` or `10^()`                |\n| Compare to truth      | Use original (unlogged) `Y`       |\n\nLet me know if you want this wrapped into a function for reuse."

              "To **unscale the means** from a PLSR model fitted with `scale = TRUE` in R, you need to reverse the **standardization** applied during training. This process is usually needed when you're interpreting predictions, coefficients, or reconstructed outputs from the model that are in **standardized (Z-score) units**.\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudd0d What does u201cunscale PLSR scaled meansu201d mean?\n\nIf you used:\n\n```r\nplsr_model <- plsr(log(Y) ~ X, data = train_data, scale = TRUE, ncomp = 3)\n```\n\nThen the PLSR model **centered and scaled** `log(Y)`:\n\n\\[\n\\text{scaled } Y = \\frac{\\log(Y) - \\mu_{\\log Y}}{\\sigma_{\\log Y}}\n\\]\n\nTo **unscale**, you invert that:\n\n\\[\n\\log(Y) = (\\text{scaled prediction} \\times \\sigma_{\\log Y}) + \\mu_{\\log Y}\n\\]\n\nThen, to get back to original Y units:\n\n\\[\nY = \\exp(\\log(Y))\n\\]\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Step-by-Step in Base R\n\n### 1. Fit your model\n\n```r\nlibrary(pls)\n\n# Model on log(Y)\nplsr_model <- plsr(log(Y) ~ ., data = train_data, scale = TRUE, ncomp = 3)\n```\n\n---\n\n### 2. Get predicted values (still scaled)\n\n```r\ny_pred_scaled <- predict(plsr_model, newdata = test_data, ncomp = 3)\ny_pred_scaled <- as.vector(y_pred_scaled)  # flatten if needed\n```\n\n---\n\n### 3. Reverse scaling (unscale the mean of log(Y))\n\n```r\nlog_y_train <- log(train_data$Y)\nmean_log_y  <- mean(log_y_train)\nsd_log_y    <- sd(log_y_train)\n\n# Unscale\ny_pred_log <- y_pred_scaled * sd_log_y + mean_log_y\n```\n\n---\n\n### 4. Back-transform from log to original Y scale\n\n```r\ny_pred <- exp(y_pred_log)\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83euddea Optional: Unscaling manually for a known scaled mean\n\nIf you just have a **scaled mean**, like `scaled_mean = 0.3`, and want to unscale it:\n\n```r\noriginal_mean <- scaled_mean * sd_log_y + mean_log_y\noriginal_value <- exp(original_mean)\n```\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Summary\n\n| You have...                | To unscale...                               |\n|---------------------------|---------------------------------------------|\n| Scaled log(Y) mean        | `value * sd_log_y + mean_log_y`             |\n| Original Y (from log Y)   | `exp(log_value)`                            |\n\nLet me know if you're working with `log10()` instead of natural log u2014 youu2019ll just use `10^` instead of `exp()`."

              "To **perform bootstrapping in PLS regression** (`plsr()`) in R to estimate **model errors or coefficient uncertainty**, you can use the `bootstrapping` procedure manually or through a helper function. The `pls` package does **not natively support bootstrapping**, but you can do it manually with a custom loop.\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Goal:\nEstimate variability in model predictions or coefficients using **bootstrap resampling**.\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Step-by-step: Bootstrapping `plsr()` in R\n\n```r\nlibrary(pls)\nlibrary(dplyr)\n\n# Define number of bootstrap replicates\nn_boot <- 1000\n\n# Storage for coefficients\ncoefs <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_boot, ncol = ncol(train_data) - 1)  # exclude Y column\ncolnames(coefs) <- colnames(train_data)[-1]\n\n# Bootstrap loop\nset.seed(123)  # for reproducibility\nfor (i in 1:n_boot) {\n  # Sample with replacement\n  boot_indices <- sample(1:nrow(train_data), replace = TRUE)\n  boot_data <- train_data[boot_indices, ]\n  \n  # Fit PLSR model on bootstrapped data\n  boot_model <- plsr(log(Y) ~ ., data = boot_data, scale = TRUE, ncomp = 3)\n  \n  # Extract coefficients (log scale)\n  coef_i <- coef(boot_model, ncomp = 3)\n  coefs[i, ] <- as.numeric(coef_i)\n}\n\n# Convert to data frame for analysis\ncoefs_df <- as.data.frame(coefs)\n\n# Calculate mean and 95% CI for each predictor\nsummary_stats <- coefs_df %>%\n  summarise(across(everything(), list(\n    mean = mean,\n    lower = ~quantile(., 0.025),\n    upper = ~quantile(., 0.975)\n  ), .names = \"{.col}_{.fn}\"))\n\nprint(summary_stats)\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudd0d Interpretation:\n\n- This gives you **bootstrap distributions** for each coefficient.\n- You get **95% confidence intervals**, showing the uncertainty in each variableu2019s effect.\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudccc Notes:\n\n- If you modeled `log(Y)`, coefficients are still on the log scale.\n- You can back-transform predictions later with `exp()` if needed.\n- This approach can also be adapted to compute **RMSE distributions** instead of coefficients.\n\n---\n\nLet me know if you want to bootstrap **RMSE**, **VIP scores**, or do this on **test data**, and Iu2019ll adjust accordingly."

              "The line:\n\n```r\nset.seed(42)  # for reproducibility\n```\n\n### u2705 What it does:\n\nIt **sets the seed** for Ru2019s **random number generator**, which ensures that any random operations (e.g., sampling, bootstrapping, train/test splitting) will produce **the same results every time** the script is run.\n\n---\n\n### ud83eudde0 Why it matters:\n\nWithout `set.seed()`, random functions like `sample()`, `runif()`, or `rnorm()` will give different results each time you run the code.\n\nWith `set.seed(42)`, the randomness becomes **reproducible** u2014 helpful for:\n\n- Debugging\n- Sharing code\n- Consistent modeling (e.g., cross-validation splits)\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd22 Why 42?\n\n\"42\" is a commonly used seed in examples (a reference to *The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy* where 42 is \"the answer to life, the universe, and everything\"), but you can use **any integer**.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Example:\n\n```r\nset.seed(42)\nsample(1:10, 5)\n# Always returns the same 5 numbers\n```\n\nWithout `set.seed(42)`, you'd get a different result each time.\n\nLet me know if you're using this for a specific function (e.g. `boot()`, `cv.glm`, etc.) u2014 happy to give a context-specific explanation."

              "Great! Here's how you can do **bootstrapping to estimate RMSE distributions** from a `plsr()` model in **R**, using a training set and either cross-validation or a separate test set.\n\n---\n\n## ud83cudfaf Goal  \nEstimate **uncertainty in RMSE** by repeatedly fitting PLSR models on bootstrapped datasets and calculating RMSE for each replicate.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Assumptions:\n- You already have `train_data` and `test_data`\n- Your model uses a log-transformed response: `log(Y) ~ predictors`\n- You want RMSE in **original (unlogged) units**\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Step-by-step Code: Bootstrap RMSE\n\n```r\nlibrary(pls)\n\n# Set number of bootstrap iterations\nn_boot <- 1000\nrmse_vals <- numeric(n_boot)\n\nset.seed(42)  # for reproducibility\n\nfor (i in 1:n_boot) {\n  # 1. Sample training data with replacement\n  boot_idx <- sample(1:nrow(train_data), replace = TRUE)\n  boot_data <- train_data[boot_idx, ]\n  \n  # 2. Fit PLSR model (log-transformed Y)\n  model_boot <- plsr(log(Y) ~ ., data = boot_data, scale = TRUE, ncomp = 3)\n  \n  # 3. Predict on original (unbooted) test set\n  pred_scaled <- predict(model_boot, newdata = test_data, ncomp = 3)\n  pred_scaled <- as.vector(pred_scaled)\n  \n  # 4. Reverse scaling: use mean and sd from bootstrap sample\n  log_y_boot <- log(boot_data$Y)\n  mean_log_y <- mean(log_y_boot)\n  sd_log_y <- sd(log_y_boot)\n  pred_log <- pred_scaled * sd_log_y + mean_log_y  # unscale\n  \n  # 5. Back-transform log -> original units\n  pred <- exp(pred_log)\n  \n  # 6. Calculate RMSE in original units\n  actual <- test_data$Y\n  rmse_vals[i] <- sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2))\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudcca Analyze the RMSE distribution\n\n```r\n# Summary statistics\nsummary(rmse_vals)\n\n# 95% confidence interval\nquantile(rmse_vals, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))\n\n# Optional: Plot the RMSE distribution\nhist(rmse_vals, breaks = 30, col = \"skyblue\", main = \"Bootstrap RMSE Distribution\", xlab = \"RMSE\")\n```\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Output\n\nYou now have:\n\n- `rmse_vals`: A vector of 1,000 bootstrapped RMSE values\n- You can use the **mean**, **median**, and **95% CI** to report error uncertainty\n\n---\n\nLet me know if you'd like to:\n- Use **cross-validation** within each bootstrap replicate\n- Test different `ncomp` values adaptively per replicate\n- Wrap this into a reusable function"
