              "To **back-predict (inverse transform) a CLR (centered log-ratio) transformed ICP-MS dataset** and reconstruct it in **ppm**, you need to apply the **inverse CLR transformation** followed by **rescaling to the original total (e.g., 1,000,000 ppm for major elements or 100% for proportions)**.\n\n---\n\n## ud83euddea Assumptions:\n- You applied a CLR transformation:  \n  `clr(x) = log(x / gmean(x))`, where `gmean` is the geometric mean\n- You now have **CLR-predicted values** (from a model like PLSR)\n- You want to convert them back to **original ppm concentrations**\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Step-by-Step: Inverse CLR Transformation in R\n\nLetu2019s assume your predicted data is in a matrix or data frame called `clr_pred`.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd39 Step 1: Inverse CLR (back-transform from log-ratios)\n\n```r\n# clr_pred: a data frame or matrix of CLR values (rows = samples, cols = elements)\n\n# Exponentiate each element\nexp_data <- exp(clr_pred)\n\n# Normalize each row to sum to 1\ncomposition <- exp_data / rowSums(exp_data)\n```\n\nAt this point, each row is a composition (parts per one). To recover **ppm**:\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd39 Step 2: Rescale to Total (e.g. 1,000,000 ppm or 100%)\n\n```r\n# If your original data was scaled to total 1,000,000 ppm (e.g. compositional closure)\ncomposition_ppm <- composition * 1e6  # or use original row sums if you preserved them\n```\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Full Example\n\n```r\n# Example: Inverse CLR back to ppm\nclr_to_ppm <- function(clr_matrix, total = 1e6) {\n  exp_matrix <- exp(clr_matrix)\n  comp_matrix <- exp_matrix / rowSums(exp_matrix)\n  comp_matrix * total\n}\n```\n\n```r\n# Apply to predicted CLR output\nppm_reconstructed <- clr_to_ppm(clr_pred)\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83eudde0 Notes:\n\n- This assumes you used **centered log-ratio** transformation.\n- All outputs will be **positive and compositional**, summing to your chosen `total`.\n- The reconstruction won't match original **absolute values** unless you reverse any further scaling or transformations (e.g., closure, normalization).\n\n---\n\nLet me know if:\n- You need to reverse an **ILR or ALR** instead\n- Your data had **zero values** (requiring imputation)\n- You want to compute **error metrics** (e.g., RMSE between ICP-MS and reconstructed ppm)"

Predict `Ti_ICP` from CLR inputs  \n2.               "Great question.\n\nThe expression:\n\n```r\npred_clr <- predict(plsr_model, ncomp = 3, type = \"response\", validation = \"CV\")[,,1]\n```\n\nis extracting a **specific slice** from a **3-dimensional array** that the `predict()` function returns when used with `plsr()` and `validation = \"CV\"`.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d What does `[,,1]` mean?\n\nIt is **array indexing**:  \n- `[,,1]` means:\n  - Keep **all rows** (`:`),\n  - Keep **all columns** (`:`),\n  - Select only the **first \"slice\" along the third dimension** (which often corresponds to the response variable or component).\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudce6 Why is `predict()` returning a 3D array?\n\nWhen you do cross-validation (`validation = \"CV\"`), the output of `predict()` is:\n\n```r\n[ n_samples , n_responses , n_components ]\n```\n\nFor example, if:\n- you have 100 samples\n- 3 compositional components (e.g., `Ti`, `Ca`, `Sr`)\n- and used up to 5 components\n\nThen:\n```r\ndim(predict(...))  # u2192 100 x 3 x 5\n```\n\n---\n\n### u2705 So, `[,,1]` means:\n\n\"Give me the predictions from the **1st component** across all samples and response variables.\"\n\nIn your case, since you're using `ncomp = 3`, you might want:\n\n```r\npred_clr <- predict(plsr_model, ncomp = 3, type = \"response\", validation = \"CV\")[,,3]\n```\n\nTo extract predictions from the **3-component model**.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd01 Final Tip:\n\nIf you're not doing cross-validation, and `validation = \"none\"` (or not specified), `predict()` will return a **2D matrix** instead, and no `[,,n]` slicing is needed.\n\nLet me know if you'd like help selecting the optimal number of components using RMSEP."

              "Great question!\n\nThe function `sweep()` in R is used to **apply an operation across rows or columns** of a matrix or data frame, by \"sweeping out\" a summary statistic or vector.\n\n---\n\n### ud83eudde0 Your line:\n\n```r\npred_ppm <- sweep(pred_acomp, 1, total_icp, `*`)\n```\n\n### ud83dudd0d Breakdown:\n\n- `pred_acomp`: matrix of predicted **compositional proportions** (e.g., for Ti, Ca, Sr), from `clrInv()`\n- `total_icp`: numeric vector of **total concentrations (ppm)** for each sample (e.g., rowSums of original ICPMS data)\n- `1`: apply the operation **across rows** (i.e., row-wise)\n- `` `*` ``: multiply each row by the corresponding value in `total_icp`\n\n---\n\n### u2705 What this line does:\n\nIt **converts predicted compositions back to ppm**, by multiplying each row (which sums to 1) by the original total ICPMS concentration:\n\n#### Example:\n\n| Proportion (pred_acomp row) | Total ICP (ppm) | Resulting PPM (pred_ppm row) |\n|-----------------------------|------------------|-------------------------------|\n| Ti = 0.6, Ca = 0.3, Sr = 0.1 | 1000             | Ti = 600, Ca = 300, Sr = 100  |\n\nSo `sweep()` handles this row-by-row multiplication efficiently.\n\n---\n\n### ud83euddea Mini example:\n\n```r\nmat <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.5,\n                0.6, 0.4), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)\n\ntotals <- c(1000, 2000)\n\nsweep(mat, 1, totals, `*`)\n#      [,1] [,2]\n# [1,]  500  500\n# [2,] 1200  800\n```\n\n---\n\nLet me know if youu2019d like to reverse this or normalize ppm back to proportions!"

              "In the **tidyverse**, we generally avoid using `sweep()` and instead use `dplyr` with `mutate()` and `rowwise()` (or `across()`) to do row-wise operations.\n\nIf you're trying to **multiply each row of predicted proportions (`pred_acomp`) by the corresponding value in `total_icp`**, here's how to do that in **tidyverse style**.\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Example: Tidyverse version of `sweep(pred_acomp, 1, total_icp, '*')`\n\nAssuming:\n\n- `pred_acomp` is a **data frame or tibble** with predicted proportions (e.g., Ti, Ca, Sr)\n- `total_icp` is a **numeric vector** of the same length as the number of rows\n\n```r\nlibrary(dplyr)\n\n# Add total_icp as a column\npred_ppm <- pred_acomp %>%\n  mutate(total_icp = total_icp) %>%\n  rowwise() %>%\n  mutate(across(-total_icp, ~ .x * total_icp)) %>%\n  ungroup() %>%\n  select(-total_icp)  # Remove helper column if not needed\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83eudde0 Whatu2019s happening:\n\n- `mutate(total_icp = total_icp)`: temporarily add `total_icp` to align with each row\n- `rowwise()`: ensures the multiplication happens per row\n- `across(-total_icp, ~ .x * total_icp)`: multiply each component (Ti, Ca, Sr) by the rowu2019s `total_icp`\n- `ungroup()`: return to regular data frame\n- `select(-total_icp)`: optional cleanup\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Output\n\nYouu2019ll get a tibble of predicted **ppm** values, row-wise reconstructed from the proportions.\n\nLet me know if you want to keep `total_icp` in the output or combine this with actual values for comparison (e.g., for RMSE)."

              "Great question u2014 when your **original ICP data** (used in training) and your **new XRF data** (used for prediction) are **different lengths**, you **cannot reuse the training total ICP values** directly. Instead, you must create or estimate **total ICP values for the new data**, based on how you want to interpret or apply the predicted CLR outputs.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd01 Here's why:\nThe inverse CLR (`clrInv()`) returns **relative proportions**, not absolute concentrations. To convert those to **ppm**, you must **multiply by a total** (like `sum(Ti_ICP + Ca_ICP + Sr_ICP)` per sample).\n\n---\n\n## u2705 3 Options to Handle `total_icp_new`\n\n### **Option 1: If you have ICP totals for new samples**\nIf your new data has actual ICP measurements for those same components (`Ti_ICP`, `Ca_ICP`, `Sr_ICP`), then you can calculate:\n\n```r\ntotal_icp_new <- rowSums(df_icp_new[, c(\"Ti_ICP\", \"Ca_ICP\", \"Sr_ICP\")])\n```\n\nThen use:\n\n```r\npred_ppm <- sweep(pred_acomp, 1, total_icp_new, `*`)\n```\n\n---\n\n### **Option 2: Use average total ICP from training data (approximation)**\nIf you **donu2019t** have new ICP values but want to scale predictions into ppm anyway, you can **assume** the same total ICP as the **mean total** from training:\n\n```r\n# From training ICP data\ntotal_icp_train_mean <- mean(rowSums(df_icp_train[, c(\"Ti_ICP\", \"Ca_ICP\", \"Sr_ICP\")]))\n\n# Apply same total to all predictions\ntotal_icp_new <- rep(total_icp_train_mean, nrow(pred_acomp))\n\n# Scale predictions\npred_ppm <- sweep(pred_acomp, 1, total_icp_new, `*`)\n```\n\nThis assumes your new samples are from a similar compositional system and differ mainly in proportions.\n\n---\n\n### **Option 3: Leave as proportions**\nIf your goal is **relative comparison** only (e.g. looking at Ti vs Sr dominance), you can skip ppm scaling and use the inverse CLR proportions (`pred_acomp`) directly.\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Summary\n\n| Situation                              | What to do                                  |\n|----------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|\n| You have ICP data for new samples      | Use `rowSums()` on the new ICP dataset      |\n| No ICP data for new samples            | Use `mean(rowSums(...))` from training set  |\n| Only want relative info (no ppm)       | Just use `clrInv()` outputs (proportions)   |\n\n---\n\nLet me know which of these youu2019re using and I can give you exact code!"

              "To **convert PLSR coefficients from clr space back to ppm**, you need to **undo the centered log-ratio (clr) transformation**, which operates on compositional data in the log-ratio space. \n\n### u26a0ufe0f Important:\n- CLR-transformed coefficients are not directly interpretable in ppm.\n- To **approximate** ppm-like interpretation, you typically need to:\n  1. Back-transform the clr prediction using the **inverse CLR**.\n  2. Multiply by the total sum (e.g., total ICP in ppm).\n  3. The coefficients themselves donu2019t directly \"convert\" back to ppm unless applied to a specific inverse-transformed sample.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Step-by-step workaround:\n\nIf you're looking to **use these clr coefficients to get ppm predictions**, the typical process is:\n\n1. **Make predictions in clr space:**\n\n```r\npred_clr <- predict(plsr_model, newdata = xrf_clr_new, ncomp = 3)[,,1]\n```\n\n2. **Convert clr prediction to composition (proportions):**\n\nYou need the `compositions` package:\n\n```r\nlibrary(compositions)\n\n# Turn into acomp object and back-transform clr to proportions\npred_acomp <- clrInv(pred_clr)  # Inverse clr transformation\n```\n\n3. **Multiply by row sums (total ICP) to convert proportions into ppm:**\n\n```r\n# Suppose total_icp is the row sum (ppm total) for each sample\npred_ppm <- sweep(pred_acomp, 1, total_icp, `*`)\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83eudde0 Why you can't directly convert clr coefficients to ppm:\n- CLR coefficients are in **log-ratio space**, meaning they describe **relative** relationships.\n- There's no single set of ppm-scale coefficients unless you also specify a sample context (e.g., the geometric mean of all variables).\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Summary:\nYou **donu2019t convert clr coefficients into ppm directly**. Instead:\n- Apply the model to get predictions in clr,\n- Back-transform predictions to composition (with `clrInv()`),\n- Multiply by total ICP to get back to ppm.\n\nLet me know if you want help wrapping this into a function or computing the ppm equation for a given sample!"

              "Great question u2014 and an important one when applying a PLSR model trained on **clr-transformed compositional data** to **new XRF data**, where you want to recover **predicted values in ppm**, but donu2019t have the full ICP dataset (i.e., you donu2019t know the total ICP row sums).\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d Problem Recap:\n\nYour **PLSR model** was trained with:\n\n- `Y` (response): `clr(acomp(Ti_ICP, Ca_ICP, Sr_ICP))`\n- `X`: `clr(acomp(Ti, Ca, Sr))`\n\nYou can predict **clr-transformed** values (e.g., `Ti_ICP_clr`) on new data, but to get **ppm**, you typically need the **total ICP sum** for each row. Without it, you canu2019t multiply your predicted clr compositions to rescale to ppm.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Solution Options:\n\n#### **Option 1: Assume a fixed total ICP (e.g., 100 or 1,000,000 ppm)**\n\nYou can **normalize the composition** to an arbitrary total. For example, if you assume the total sum is 1,000,000 ppm:\n\n```r\nlibrary(compositions)\n\n# Step 1: Get predicted clr values from model\npred_clr <- predict(plsr_model, newdata = xrf_clr_new, ncomp = 3)[,,1]\n\n# Step 2: Convert from clr to proportions\npred_acomp <- clrInv(pred_clr)  # returns proportions summing to 1\n\n# Step 3: Multiply by arbitrary total to express in ppm\n# (e.g., 1,000,000 ppm total u2014 typical for weight-based concentrations)\npred_ppm <- sweep(pred_acomp, 1, 1e6, `*`)\n```\n\n> This will give you **relative concentrations in ppm scale**, assuming the total equals 1,000,000 ppm. While the absolute values may not be exact, the **relative differences between samples and components** will be meaningful.\n\n---\n\n#### **Option 2: Estimate total ICP from training data**\n\nIf your training ICP data has known total row sums, you can estimate a representative total (e.g., the **mean row sum**) and apply that to the new predictions:\n\n```r\n# Calculate average total from training ICP\nmean_total_icp <- mean(rowSums(training_icp_df))\n\n# Multiply predicted proportions by average total\npred_ppm <- sweep(pred_acomp, 1, mean_total_icp, `*`)\n```\n\nThis assumes new samples have similar overall concentrations to the training data u2014 reasonable in many environmental geochemistry contexts.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd01 Optional: Extract predicted Ti_ICP from this\n\n```r\nTi_ICP_pred_ppm <- pred_ppm[, \"Ti_ICP\"]\n```\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Summary\n\nIf you donu2019t have total ICP values for new data:\n\n- **You must assume** a total composition (e.g., 1,000,000 ppm),\n- Or **estimate** it from the training data.\n\nYou **cannot recover ppm directly from clr predictions without a total**, because clr only gives **ratios**, not absolute magnitudes.\n\n---\n\nLet me know if you'd like to wrap this into a reusable prediction function or make per-site predictions!"

              "Yes, you **can perform bootstrapping on a new test dataset** to **reconstruct uncertainty (e.g., RMSE, confidence intervals)** for predictions in **ppm**, even when your model was trained using **clr-transformed compositional data**.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 What you *can* do:\n\nIf you have:\n- A trained `plsr_model` (e.g. on clr(Ti_ICP, Ca_ICP, Sr_ICP) ~ clr(Ti, Ca, Sr))\n- A **new XRF dataset**\n- **Predictions** from the model in ppm (via inverse clr and scaling)\n  \nThen you can:\n1. Bootstrap the new dataset (resampling rows with replacement)\n2. Predict clr values from each resample\n3. Invert the clr to get back to ppm\n4. Compute statistics like **mean**, **standard deviation**, and **confidence intervals** across bootstrap replicates.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd01 Workflow Example (R Code)\n\n```r\nlibrary(pls)\nlibrary(compositions)\nlibrary(dplyr)\nlibrary(tibble)\n\n# Inputs\nxrf_clr_new <- clr(acomp(new_xrf_df))  # new data already in clr\nn_boot <- 1000                         # number of bootstrap samples\ntotal_assumption <- 1e6               # assumed total ppm\n\n# Storage\npred_boot_list <- vector(\"list\", n_boot)\n\nset.seed(123)  # reproducibility\nfor (i in 1:n_boot) {\n  # Step 1: Bootstrap rows\n  idx <- sample(nrow(xrf_clr_new), replace = TRUE)\n  xrf_boot <- xrf_clr_new[idx, ]\n  \n  # Step 2: Predict in clr space\n  pred_clr <- predict(plsr_model, newdata = xrf_boot, ncomp = 3)[,,1]\n  \n  # Step 3: Inverse clr -> proportions\n  pred_acomp <- clrInv(pred_clr)\n  \n  # Step 4: Convert to ppm\n  pred_ppm <- sweep(pred_acomp, 1, total_assumption, `*`)\n  \n  # Step 5: Store results\n  pred_boot_list[[i]] <- pred_ppm\n}\n\n# Combine results into 3D array\npred_array <- array(unlist(pred_boot_list), \n                    dim = c(nrow(xrf_clr_new), ncol(pred_ppm), n_boot),\n                    dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(pred_ppm), NULL))\n\n# Step 6: Compute summary statistics\n# Example: Ti_ICP predictions\nTi_preds <- pred_array[, \"Ti_ICP\", ]\nTi_mean  <- rowMeans(Ti_preds)\nTi_sd    <- apply(Ti_preds, 1, sd)\n\n# Optional: 95% confidence intervals\nTi_ci_lower <- apply(Ti_preds, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025)\nTi_ci_upper <- apply(Ti_preds, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975)\n\n# Combine into tibble\nTi_summary <- tibble(\n  Ti_pred_mean = Ti_mean,\n  Ti_pred_sd   = Ti_sd,\n  Ti_ci_lower  = Ti_ci_lower,\n  Ti_ci_upper  = Ti_ci_upper\n)\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83eudde0 Notes:\n- This gives **uncertainty bounds** on predicted ppm values without needing true `Ti_ICP` values.\n- You're bootstrapping **the test data**, not retraining the model u2014 so this is **model-based prediction error**, not model variability.\n- If you want **model uncertainty**, you'd need to bootstrap the training data and **refit the model each time**.\n\n---\n\nLet me know if you'd like to include RMSE or visualizations (like error bars or ribbon plots)!"

              "To compute **RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error)** for multiple components like **Ti**, **Ca**, and **Sr**, you compare the predicted vs actual values for each component. Hereu2019s how to do it in **R**, for both base R and `tidyverse` approaches:\n\n---\n\n### u2705 **Assumptions**\nYou have:\n\n- Actual values (in ppm or CLR space):  \n  `actual <- data.frame(Ti = ..., Ca = ..., Sr = ...)`\n\n- Predicted values:  \n  `predicted <- data.frame(Ti = ..., Ca = ..., Sr = ...)`\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudcd8 METHOD 1: Base R\n\n```r\nrmse_vec <- function(actual, predicted) {\n  sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))\n}\n\n# Compute RMSE for each column\nrmse_Ti <- rmse_vec(actual$Ti, predicted$Ti)\nrmse_Ca <- rmse_vec(actual$Ca, predicted$Ca)\nrmse_Sr <- rmse_vec(actual$Sr, predicted$Sr)\n\n# Combine into a named vector\nrmse_all <- c(Ti = rmse_Ti, Ca = rmse_Ca, Sr = rmse_Sr)\nprint(rmse_all)\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudcd8 METHOD 2: `tidyverse` (dplyr + purrr)\n\n```r\nlibrary(dplyr)\nlibrary(purrr)\n\nrmse_all <- map2_dbl(actual, predicted, ~ sqrt(mean((.x - .y)^2)))\nrmse_all\n```\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Output:\n\nYou'll get something like:\n\n```\n     Ti       Ca       Sr \n12.53     34.82    5.76 \n```\n\n(Units depend on your data u2014 usually ppm or CLR units.)\n\n---\n\n### ud83eudde0 Tip:\n\nIf you're working with **CLR-transformed values**, the RMSE will be in CLR space.  \nTo express it in **ppm**, you need to:\n\n1.               "Great question u2014 and it goes to the heart of **compositional data analysis**.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d **Why lower CLR values can translate into higher ppm values**\n\nThis seemingly counterintuitive effect is due to the **log-ratio nature of CLR (Centered Log-Ratio)** transformation.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd2c Here's why it happens:\n\nThe **CLR** of a composition (like Ti, Ca, Sr) transforms the data using:\n\n\\[\n\\text{clr}(x_i) = \\log\\left(\\frac{x_i}{g(x)}\\right)\n\\]\n\nWhere:\n\n- \\( x_i \\) = the proportion of component *i* (e.g., Ti),\n- \\( g(x) \\) = the **geometric mean** of all components.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudea8 So what does a lower CLR value mean?\n\nIt **doesn't** mean that the raw value \\( x_i \\) is low.  \nIt means **\\( x_i \\) is lower *relative* to the geometric mean of the other components**.\n\nNow imagine this:\n\n- If **other components (Ca, Sr)** are very small,\n- Then **\\( g(x) \\)** becomes small,\n- So even a **moderate \\( x_i \\)** gives a **high CLR**,\n- Conversely, a low CLR could mean a **large ppm** if the rest are larger still.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudcc8 Inverse CLR is not linear\n\nWhen you inverse the CLR, the **exponentiation + renormalization** can lead to **nonlinear recovery** of the ppm values.\n\n\\[\nx_i = \\frac{\\exp(\\text{clr}_i)}{\\sum \\exp(\\text{clr}_j)} \\times \\text{Total}\n\\]\n\nSo:\n\n- Even a **small increase** in one componentu2019s CLR value can **decrease the proportions** of others.\n- The final **ppm** depends on **all components together**, not just one.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudccc Example:\n\nLetu2019s say your inverse CLR output is this (log-space):\n\n| Component | CLR |\n|-----------|-----|\n| Ti        | -1  |\n| Ca        | -2  |\n| Sr        | -2  |\n\nExponentiating:\n\n| Component | exp(CLR) |\n|-----------|----------|\n| Ti        | 0.3679   |\n| Ca        | 0.1353   |\n| Sr        | 0.1353   |\n\nSum: 0.6385  \nSo Ti proportion = 0.3679 / 0.6385 u2248 57.6%\n\nNow change Ti's CLR to `-2`:\n\n| Ti        | -2 u2192 exp(-2) = 0.1353  \n| Sum       | 0.4059  \n| Ti prop   | 0.1353 / 0.4059 u2248 33.3%\n\nud83dudc49 Even though the CLR dropped by only 1 unit, the ppm dropped from **57.6% to 33.3%** u2014 a nonlinear effect!\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Summary\n\n- CLR is a **relative log transformation**, not absolute.\n- A **lower CLR value** doesnu2019t always mean **lower concentration in ppm**.\n- Due to **renormalization**, the **ppm scale is nonlinear** with respect to CLR.\n\nLet me know if you'd like an R code demo or a plot to illustrate this!"

              "Great! Here's an R code demo to **illustrate how small changes in CLR values can cause nonlinear effects in ppm** due to the inverse CLR transformation.\n\nWeu2019ll:\n1. Simulate a few sets of CLR values for three components: Ti, Ca, Sr.\n2. Apply inverse CLR (via `acomp()` from `compositions` package).\n3. Plot how CLR values map back to ppm for Ti.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 **R Code Example**\n\n```r\n# Load required package\nlibrary(compositions)\nlibrary(tibble)\nlibrary(ggplot2)\nlibrary(dplyr)\n\n# Step 1: Create a sequence of CLR values for Ti, holding Ca and Sr constant\nclr_demo <- tibble(\n  Ti_clr = seq(-4, 2, by = 0.1),   # vary Ti CLR value\n  Ca_clr = -1,                    # fixed CLR value\n  Sr_clr = -1                     # fixed CLR value\n)\n\n# Step 2: Convert from CLR to composition (proportions)\n# Ensure clr_demo is a matrix and convert to acomp\nclr_matrix <- as.matrix(clr_demo)\nacomp_result <- clrInv(clr_matrix)  # inverse CLR back to proportions\n\n# Step 3: Convert proportions to ppm by multiplying by total (e.g., 100000 ppm = 100%)\ntotal_ppm <- 100000\nppm <- sweep(acomp_result, 1, total_ppm, `*`) %>% as_tibble()\n\n# Step 4: Combine CLR and PPM for plotting\nplot_data <- bind_cols(clr_demo, ppm)\nnames(plot_data)[4:6] <- c(\"Ti_ppm\", \"Ca_ppm\", \"Sr_ppm\")\n\n# Step 5: Plot CLR(Ti) vs PPM(Ti)\nggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Ti_clr, y = Ti_ppm)) +\n  geom_line(color = \"#0072B2\", size = 1.2) +\n  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = \"dashed\", color = \"gray\") +\n  geom_hline(yintercept = total_ppm / 3, linetype = \"dotted\", color = \"gray40\") +\n  labs(\n    title = \"Inverse CLR: How Ti_clr Translates to Ti_ppm\",\n    x = \"CLR(Ti)\",\n    y = \"Predicted Ti (ppm)\"\n  ) +\n  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudccc What You'll See\n\n- As **CLR(Ti)** increases, **Ti_ppm** increases u2014 but **not linearly**.\n- Around `CLR = 0`, Ti is approximately 1/3 of total (since log ratio to geometric mean is zero).\n- The curve steepens rapidly, showing how even small shifts in CLR can drastically change ppm.\n\n---\n\nLet me know if youu2019d like to:\n- Overlay points from a real dataset,\n- Add Ca/Sr variability,\n- Export the plot,\n- Or simulate bootstrapped confidence bands!"

              "Great! Let's simulate **bootstrapped confidence bands** for **Ti_ppm** predicted from varying CLR(Ti), while keeping Ca_clr and Sr_clr constant. This will help visualize the variability due to model uncertainty.\n\nWe'll:\n1. Vary `Ti_clr` across a range.\n2. Bootstrap multiple inverse CLR samples by adding noise.\n3. Convert to ppm.\n4. Plot median u00b1 confidence intervals (ribbon).\n\n---\n\n### u2705 **R Code: Simulate Bootstrapped Confidence Bands**\n\n```r\n# Load required packages\nlibrary(compositions)\nlibrary(tibble)\nlibrary(dplyr)\nlibrary(ggplot2)\n\nset.seed(123)\n\n# Parameters\nn_boot <- 1000\nTi_clr_vals <- seq(-4, 2, by = 0.1)\n\n# Step 1: Generate base matrix (fixed Ca_clr, Sr_clr)\nbase_clr <- tibble(\n  Ti_clr = Ti_clr_vals,\n  Ca_clr = -1,\n  Sr_clr = -1\n)\n\n# Step 2: Bootstrap - add small normal noise to simulate uncertainty\nboot_results <- lapply(1:n_boot, function(i) {\n  noisy_clr <- base_clr + matrix(rnorm(n = nrow(base_clr) * 3, mean = 0, sd = 0.1), ncol = 3)\n  colnames(noisy_clr) <- colnames(base_clr)\n  noisy_acomp <- clrInv(as.matrix(noisy_clr))  # inverse clr to proportions\n  noisy_ppm <- sweep(noisy_acomp, 1, 100000, `*`)  # scale to ppm\n  tibble(Ti_ppm = noisy_ppm[, \"Ti\"])\n})\n\n# Step 3: Combine and summarize\nboot_matrix <- do.call(cbind, boot_results)\nsummary_df <- tibble(\n  Ti_clr = Ti_clr_vals,\n  Ti_ppm_median = apply(boot_matrix, 1, median),\n  Ti_ppm_lower = apply(boot_matrix, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025),\n  Ti_ppm_upper = apply(boot_matrix, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975)\n)\n\n# Step 4: Plot with ribbon\nggplot(summary_df, aes(x = Ti_clr, y = Ti_ppm_median)) +\n  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Ti_ppm_lower, ymax = Ti_ppm_upper), fill = \"#0072B2\", alpha = 0.3) +\n  geom_line(color = \"#0072B2\", size = 1.2) +\n  labs(\n    title = \"Bootstrapped Confidence Bands for Ti_ppm from CLR(Ti)\",\n    x = \"CLR(Ti)\",\n    y = \"Predicted Ti (ppm)\"\n  ) +\n  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudccc Explanation\n\n- This simulates **1,000 noisy CLR vectors** at each Ti_clr level.\n- The noise mimics uncertainty in model prediction or CLR estimation.\n- We plot:\n  - **Median prediction (line)**\n  - **95% confidence interval (ribbon)**\n\n---\n\nLet me know if you'd like to:\n- Use real model RMSE values instead of noise,\n- Include **Ca** or **Sr** predictions too,\n- Or export this to PDF/CSV."

              "That warning:\n\n```\nWarning message:\nIn acomp(pred_clr_upper) :\n  Negative values in composition are used as detection limits\n```\n\nis triggered when you try to convert data with **negative values** into a **compositional object** using `acomp()` from the `compositions` package. Compositions (like clr or alr) assume **strictly positive values**, as they represent parts of a whole (e.g., ppm, proportions).\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d Why This Happens\n\nWhen you compute:\n\n```r\npred_clr_upper <- sweep(pred_xrf_clr, 2, RMSE_clr, `+`)\n```\n\nYouu2019re adding RMSE (which might be large) to clr-transformed values. This can:\n- Distort the log-ratio structure\n- Lead to exponentiated (inverse clr) values that are **zero or negative**, which is mathematically invalid\n\n---\n\n### u2705 How to Handle It Properly\n\nHere are **best-practice options** to resolve or avoid this:\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Option 1: Use `clrInv()` directly instead of `acomp()`\n\n```r\npred_acomp_upper <- clrInv(pred_clr_upper)\n```\n\nThis avoids calling `acomp()` on possibly invalid log-ratios. However, **check the result** for any NaNs or negative values if your RMSE is too large.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Option 2: Clip large errors (e.g., u00b12 * RMSE)\n\nEnsure that `pred_clr_upper` remains within a reasonable range:\n\n```r\nmax_rmse <- 2 * RMSE_clr  # e.g., cap RMSE to u00b12u03c3\n\npred_clr_upper <- sweep(pred_xrf_clr, 2, pmin(RMSE_clr, max_rmse), `+`)\n```\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Option 3: Replace negative values before applying `acomp()` (not ideal, but works)\n\nIf you must use `acomp()`, replace negatives with a small detection limit:\n\n```r\npred_clr_upper[pred_clr_upper < -10] <- -10  # limit how negative values go\npred_acomp_upper <- acomp(pred_clr_upper)\n```\n\nBut **be cautious**: this alters the geometry and may bias results.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Option 4: Work directly in CLR space for intervals\n\nIf the prediction intervals are for **visualization only**, and you later convert them to ppm via `clrInv()` and then multiply by total ICP:\n\n```r\npred_ppm_upper <- sweep(clrInv(pred_clr_upper), 1, total_icp, `*`)\n```\n\nThen you **donu2019t need to use `acomp()`** at all.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudeab Avoid This:\n\n```r\nacomp(pred_clr_upper)  # causes the warning if values are too negative\n```\n\n---\n\n### Summary\n\n| Action | Recommendation |\n|--------|----------------|\n| Use `clrInv()` directly | u2705 Preferred |\n| Clip excessive RMSE | u2705 Safe & common |\n| Avoid negative CLR inputs | u2705 Required |\n| Replace with detection limits | u26a0ufe0f Acceptable with caution |\n| Use `acomp()` on negatives | u274c Avoid |\n\n---\n\nWould you like help implementing any of these options for your current dataset or plotting prediction intervals correctly in ppm space?"

              "To **bootstrap predictions on a new dataset** using a trained **PLSR model** (e.g., predicting `Ti_ICP` from XRF data) and then compute **RMSE**, **5th and 95th percentile confidence intervals**, here's a complete example in R:\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Assumptions:\n- Your model is trained (`pls_final`)\n- You have a new dataset: `xrf_new` (same variables as in training)\n- You want to get:\n  - Predicted `Ti_ICP` values (or more if multivariate)\n  - RMSE from bootstrap replicates\n  - 5th and 95th percentiles (CI bands)\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Step-by-step R Code:\n\n```r\nlibrary(pls)\nlibrary(dplyr)\n\n# Set bootstrap parameters\nn_boot <- 1000\nset.seed(42)\n\n# Placeholder to store predictions\nboot_preds <- matrix(NA, nrow = nrow(xrf_new), ncol = n_boot)\n\n# Bootstrap loop\nfor (i in 1:n_boot) {\n  # Sample with replacement from training data\n  boot_idx <- sample(1:nrow(df_xrf), replace = TRUE)\n  \n  # Fit PLSR model on bootstrap sample\n  boot_model <- plsr(df_icp[boot_idx, \"Ti_ICP\"] ~ df_xrf[boot_idx, ],\n                     ncomp = opt_comp_final, scale = TRUE)\n  \n  # Predict on new XRF dataset\n  boot_preds[, i] <- predict(boot_model, newdata = xrf_new, ncomp = opt_comp_final)[, , 1]\n}\n\n# --- Compute summary statistics ---\n# Mean prediction\npred_mean <- rowMeans(boot_preds)\n\n# RMSE per prediction\npred_rmse <- apply(boot_preds, 1, sd)\n\n# Confidence intervals (5th and 95th percentiles)\npred_lower <- apply(boot_preds, 1, quantile, probs = 0.05)\npred_upper <- apply(boot_preds, 1, quantile, probs = 0.95)\n\n# --- Combine into a final results dataframe ---\nresults_df <- xrf_new %>%\n  mutate(\n    Ti_pred_mean = pred_mean,\n    Ti_RMSE = pred_rmse,\n    Ti_CI_lower = pred_lower,\n    Ti_CI_upper = pred_upper\n  )\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudcc8 Optional: Plot with Confidence Ribbon\n\n```r\nlibrary(ggplot2)\n\nggplot(results_df, aes(x = 1:nrow(results_df), y = Ti_pred_mean)) +\n  geom_line(color = \"blue\") +\n  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Ti_CI_lower, ymax = Ti_CI_upper), alpha = 0.2, fill = \"blue\") +\n  labs(title = \"Bootstrapped Ti_ICP Prediction with 90% Confidence Interval\",\n       x = \"Sample Index\", y = \"Ti_ICP Predicted (ppm)\") +\n  theme_minimal()\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudca1 Export as CSV:\n```r\nwrite.csv(results_df, \"bootstrapped_Ti_predictions.csv\", row.names = FALSE)\n```\n\n---\n\nLet me know if you're predicting multiple ICP elements or need to do this for `clr`-transformed data!"

              "To compute **upper and lower confidence intervals** from new PLSR model predictions (e.g., after applying a trained model to new XRF data), you can follow this step-by-step approach in **R**.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Assumptions:\n- You have a **trained PLSR model** using `plsr()` from the `pls` package.\n- You've predicted **clr-transformed values** (`pred_clr`) from **new XRF data**.\n- You have RMSEs (or bootstrapped standard errors) for each predicted component.\n\n---\n\n### u2699ufe0f Step-by-step Workflow:\n\n#### **1. Make predictions on new data**\n```r\n# Predict from new data\npred_clr <- predict(plsr_model, newdata = xrf_clr_new, ncomp = opt_comp_final)[,,1]  # Matrix output\npred_clr <- as.data.frame(pred_clr)  # Optional: convert to df for easier manipulation\n```\n\n---\n\n#### **2. Compute RMSE (or standard error) for each component**\nIf you already have `RMSE_clr` from validation:\n```r\n# Named vector like: c(Ti_ICP = 0.12, Ca_ICP = 0.09, Sr_ICP = 0.08)\nRMSE_clr\n```\n\nIf not, compute it:\n```r\nRMSE_clr <- apply((actual_clr - pred_clr_train)^2, 2, sqrt)\n```\n\n---\n\n#### **3. Calculate confidence intervals in clr space**\n```r\n# Upper and lower bounds (u00b1 RMSE)\npred_clr_upper <- sweep(pred_clr, 2, RMSE_clr, `+`)\npred_clr_lower <- sweep(pred_clr, 2, RMSE_clr, `-`)\n```\n\n---\n\n#### **4. Convert back from clr u2192 ppm**\nYou'll need the **total ICP (row sums)** of the training data to reproject to ppm:\n\n```r\nlibrary(compositions)\n\n# Convert back from clr (centered log-ratio) to proportions\npred_acomp        <- clrInv(pred_clr)\npred_acomp_upper  <- clrInv(pred_clr_upper)\npred_acomp_lower  <- clrInv(pred_clr_lower)\n\n# Multiply by total ICP (row sums) if available\ntotal_icp_train <- rowSums(df_icp)  # or mean total if test data has no ICP\n\n# Option 1: Multiply by row-wise total from training set (estimate)\npred_ppm        <- sweep(pred_acomp,        1, total_icp_train, `*`)\npred_ppm_upper  <- sweep(pred_acomp_upper,  1, total_icp_train, `*`)\npred_ppm_lower  <- sweep(pred_acomp_lower,  1, total_icp_train, `*`)\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudce6 Optional: Combine into a tidy tibble\n```r\nlibrary(dplyr)\n\nresults_ppm <- bind_cols(\n  pred_ppm        %>% rename_with(~ paste0(.x, \"_pred\")),\n  pred_ppm_lower  %>% rename_with(~ paste0(.x, \"_lower\")),\n  pred_ppm_upper  %>% rename_with(~ paste0(.x, \"_upper\"))\n)\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudcca Optional: Plot with confidence ribbon\n```r\nlibrary(ggplot2)\n\nggplot(results_ppm, aes(x = Ti_ICP_pred)) +\n  geom_point(aes(y = Ti_ICP_pred)) +\n  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Ti_ICP_lower, ymax = Ti_ICP_upper), alpha = 0.3) +\n  labs(title = \"PLSR Predictions with Confidence Interval (Ti)\",\n       x = \"Prediction\", y = \"Ti_ICP (ppm)\") +\n  theme_minimal()\n```\n\n---\n\n### Would you like the above exported as CSV or PDF for each element?"

              "To **overlay a plot using data from a different tibble** on top of an existing `ggplot` and ensure both datasets use the **same x and y scale**, you can simply add a second `geom_` layer and specify a new `data = other_tibble` inside that layer.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Example\n\nAssume you have:\n\n- `df1`: your **main tibble**  \n- `df2`: your **secondary tibble**  \n- You want to **overlay a line or points from `df2`** onto a plot of `df1`.\n\n```r\nggplot(df1, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var)) +\n  geom_point(color = \"blue\") +\n  # Overlay second dataset\n  geom_line(data = df2, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var), color = \"red\") +\n  # Optional: fix scales to be consistent\n  scale_x_continuous(limits = range(c(df1$x_var, df2$x_var))) +\n  scale_y_continuous(limits = range(c(df1$y_var, df2$y_var))) +\n  theme_minimal()\n```\n\n---\n\n### u2705 If Axis Ranges Must Be Fixed\n\nIf the x and y ranges need to be locked to both datasets (e.g., so both data sets fully show up), use:\n\n```r\nx_all <- range(c(df1$x_var, df2$x_var), na.rm = TRUE)\ny_all <- range(c(df1$y_var, df2$y_var), na.rm = TRUE)\n\nggplot(df1, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var)) +\n  geom_point(color = \"blue\") +\n  geom_line(data = df2, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var), color = \"red\") +\n  scale_x_continuous(limits = x_all) +\n  scale_y_continuous(limits = y_all) +\n  theme_minimal()\n```\n\n---\n\nLet me know if your tibbles have **different column names** or you want to **map different aesthetics** (like color or shape per dataset)."

              "No, **RMSE** (Root Mean Square Error) and the **95% Confidence Interval (CI)** are **not the same thing**, although they are both used to assess model performance and uncertainty.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd39 What is RMSE?\n\n- **RMSE** measures the **average magnitude of the error** between predicted and actual values.\n- It is calculated as:\n\n  \\[\n  \\text{RMSE} = \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{n} \\sum_{i=1}^n (\\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2}\n  \\]\n\n- RMSE is a **single number** summarizing error and does **not provide a distribution** or confidence range.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd39 What is a 95% Confidence Interval?\n\n- A **95% Confidence Interval** gives a **range** of values that you can be 95% confident contains the true mean (or prediction).\n- CI is based on **sampling variation** and helps quantify **uncertainty** around a point estimate.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d Key Differences\n\n| Feature              | RMSE                             | 95% Confidence Interval              |\n|----------------------|----------------------------------|--------------------------------------|\n| Type                 | Point estimate of average error | Range of plausible values            |\n| Uncertainty included | u274c No                           | u2705 Yes                               |\n| Derived from         | Model residuals                 | Sampling distribution                |\n| Units                | Same as response variable       | Same as response variable            |\n| Format               | Single value                    | Lower and upper bounds (e.g., [a, b])|\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Use Together\nYou can use **RMSE** to report overall prediction accuracy and **95% CIs** to communicate **uncertainty** around individual predictions or coefficients.\n\n---\n\nLet me know if you'd like to visualize RMSE *and* 95% CIs on a plot, or compute both for your PLSR model!"
            ]

              "Great! Here's how you can **compute and visualize both RMSE and 95% confidence intervals (CIs)** for a **PLSR model** in R using `ggplot2` and `pls`. Iu2019ll break it into clear steps:\n\n---\n\n## u2705 **1. Compute PLSR Model & Predict**\nAssuming you already have your training dataset (`df_xrf`, `df_icp`) and a fitted model:\n\n```r\nlibrary(pls)\nlibrary(tidyverse)\n\n# Fit model (with cross-validation)\npls_model <- plsr(df_icp ~ df_xrf, ncomp = 3, validation = \"CV\")\n\n# Predict (with CV)\npred_array <- predict(pls_model, ncomp = 3, type = \"response\", validation = \"CV\")\npred_df <- as.data.frame(pred_array[,,1])\nnames(pred_df) <- paste0(names(pred_df), \"_pred\")\n\n# Actual values\nactual_df <- as.data.frame(df_icp)\n```\n\n---\n\n## u2705 **2. Compute RMSE per component**\n```r\nrmse_vals <- sqrt(colMeans((pred_df - actual_df)^2))\nrmse_df <- tibble(Variable = names(rmse_vals), RMSE = rmse_vals)\nprint(rmse_df)\n```\n\n---\n\n## u2705 **3. Bootstrap 95% Confidence Intervals (optional but recommended)**\n\nHereu2019s a simple bootstrap to estimate 95% prediction intervals:\n\n```r\nset.seed(123)\nlibrary(boot)\n\n# Function for bootstrapping\nboot_pred <- function(data, indices) {\n  d <- data[indices, ]\n  mod <- plsr(df_icp ~ df_xrf, data = d, ncomp = 3)\n  preds <- predict(mod, newdata = df_xrf, ncomp = 3)[,,1]\n  return(as.vector(preds[, \"Ti_ICP\"]))  # change for other elements\n}\n\nboot_obj <- boot(data = df, statistic = boot_pred, R = 100)\nboot_ci <- boot.ci(boot_obj, type = \"perc\")\n```\n\nOr you can simulate CIs by calculating prediction bounds using RMSE:\n\n```r\n# Example: Ti_ICP\nplot_df <- tibble(\n  actual = df_icp$Ti_ICP,\n  pred = pred_df$Ti_ICP_pred,\n  upper = pred_df$Ti_ICP_pred + rmse_vals[\"Ti_ICP\"],\n  lower = pred_df$Ti_ICP_pred - rmse_vals[\"Ti_ICP\"]\n)\n```\n\n---\n\n## u2705 **4. Visualize with `ggplot2`**\n\n```r\nggplot(plot_df, aes(x = actual, y = pred)) +\n  geom_point(size = 2, color = \"#0072B2\") +\n  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = \"dashed\", color = \"gray\") +\n  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) +\n  labs(title = \"PLSR Predicted vs Measured (Ti)\",\n       x = \"Measured Ti_ICP (ppm)\",\n       y = \"Predicted Ti_ICP (ppm)\") +\n  theme_minimal()\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudcdd **Exporting CSV with Residuals, RMSE, and CIs**\n\n```r\nplot_df <- plot_df %>%\n  mutate(residual = actual - pred)\n\nwrite_csv(plot_df, \"PLSR_Ti_predictions_with_CI.csv\")\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd01 Repeat for Ca, Sr, Zr?\nYou can wrap the process in a loop or use `map()` to apply it across all elements (`Ti_ICP`, `Ca_ICP`, etc.).\n\nWould you like me to provide a full generalized function that handles all components with plots and exports?"

              "Great question u2014 how to properly represent **RMSE values** from **CLR or log-transformed PLSR models** when quoting them in reconstructed **ppm (original units)** is important for accurate and interpretable reporting.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd01 **Understanding the Problem**\nWhen using **log-transformed** or **CLR-transformed** data in models (like PLSR), the **RMSE** is naturally computed in **transformed space**, not original units (ppm). However, end-users/readers usually interpret results in ppm. So:\n\n- You **train** the model in transformed space (log or CLR).\n- You want to **report errors (e.g., RMSE) in ppm**.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Best Practices\n\n#### u2705 **Option 1: Back-transform Predictions and Compute RMSE in ppm**\nThis is the most interpretable and recommended method:\n\n```r\n# After back-transforming predictions and actual values into ppm:\npred_ppm <- ...  # inverse CLR or exp(log_pred)\nactual_ppm <- ...\n\nrmse_ppm <- sqrt(mean((pred_ppm - actual_ppm)^2))\n```\n\nThis gives you the **RMSE in ppm**, which is directly comparable to the measurement scale.\n\n---\n\n#### u2705 **Option 2: Quote RMSE in Transformed Space, But Convert Representative Examples to ppm**\nIf you **must** quote RMSE in log or CLR space:\n\n- Indicate the transformation in your reporting (e.g., \"RMSE = 0.32 (log ppm)\").\n- Provide examples showing what this means in real ppm units:\n\n```r\n# Example: for log space\nexample_ppm <- exp(log(predicted_ppm) u00b1 RMSE_log)\n```\n\n- For CLR space, use inverse CLR (`unclr()` with `acomp::clrinv()` or `compositions::unclr`) and multiply by total composition.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudca1 Tip for CLR Space\n\nWhen back-transforming CLR:\n```r\nlibrary(compositions)\n\n# pred_clr: your CLR-space predicted values\n# total_mass: total ppm (e.g., rowSums from original ICP dataset)\n\npred_acomp <- clrInv(pred_clr)\npred_ppm <- sweep(pred_acomp, 1, total_mass, `*`)\n```\n\nThen compute RMSE:\n```r\nrmse_ppm <- sqrt(rowMeans((pred_ppm -               "The error:\n\n```\n\"All values of t are equal to  0.105565885269126 \nCannot calculate confidence intervals\"\n```\n\nmeans that during **bootstrapping**, the RMSE value was **the same across all resamples** u2014 so there's **no variability** to compute a percentile-based confidence interval.\n\n---\n\n### ud83eudde0 Why this happens:\n- Your predicted values (`pred`) and actual values (`actual`) might be **identical in every bootstrap sample**, producing the same RMSE each time.\n- This is common when:\n  - The dataset is **very small**.\n  - The model is **overfit**, giving near-identical predictions for each observation.\n  - You're using a **static model prediction** on repeated data (e.g., not updating the model during each bootstrap).\n  - `actual` and `pred` might be **constant vectors**, or contain little to no variation.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Fixes / Workarounds:\n\n#### **1. Check your input vectors**\nEnsure `actual` and `pred` are both numeric, have some variance, and are not perfectly aligned:\n\n```r\nsummary(actual)\nsummary(pred)\ntable(actual == pred)\n```\n\n#### **2. Add a small amount of noise (only if appropriate)**\nAs a workaround for purely illustrative purposes:\n\n```r\npred_jittered <- pred + rnorm(length(pred), mean = 0, sd = 1e-4)\n```\n\n> u26a0ufe0f Use this only if the lack of variation is an artifact and you're just trying to estimate error ranges illustratively u2014 **not recommended for reporting real uncertainty.**\n\n#### **3. Switch to a different bootstrap CI type**\nUse the **basic** or **normal** method instead of `\"perc\"`:\n\n```r\nboot.ci(boot_obj, type = \"basic\")  # or type = \"norm\"\n```\n\nThese methods are more robust when `t` has low variation.\n\n#### **4.               "The error message:\n\n```\n\"All values of t are equal to 0.105565885269126 \\n Cannot calculate confidence intervals\"\n```\n\nmeans that **the bootstrapped RMSE values do not vary across iterations**, i.e., all 500 boot samples returned the **exact same RMSE**. This causes `boot.ci()` to fail because it needs variability to compute percentiles or confidence intervals.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Why This Happens\n\nThere are a few common causes:\n\n1. **Input vectors `.x` and `.y` are identical or extremely close** u2192 residuals are all the same.\n2. **Too little variability in the data** (e.g., constant values).\n3. **Bootstrap resampling doesn't change results** u2192 maybe the dataset is too small or not randomized enough.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Fixes and Recommendations\n\n#### u2705 1. Use `boot.ci()` only when `t` varies\n\nYou can check before computing CI:\n\n```r\nboot_rmse_safe <- function(actual, pred, R = 1000) {\n  data <- tibble(actual = actual, pred = pred)\n  rmse_stat <- function(data, indices) {\n    d <- data[indices, ]\n    sqrt(mean((d$actual - d$pred)^2))\n  }\n  boot_obj <- boot(data = data, statistic = rmse_stat, R = R)\n  \n  if (sd(boot_obj$t, na.rm = TRUE) == 0) {\n    return(tibble(CI_lower = NA_real_, CI_upper = NA_real_, RMSE = boot_obj$t0))\n  } else {\n    ci <- boot.ci(boot_obj, type = \"perc\")\n    return(tibble(CI_lower = ci$percent[4], CI_upper = ci$percent[5], RMSE = boot_obj$t0))\n  }\n}\n```\n\nThen safely map:\n\n```r\nci_list <- map2(actual, pred, ~ boot_rmse_safe(.x, .y, R = 500))\n```\n\n---\n\n#### u2705 2. Add randomness via jitter (if appropriate for your data)\n\nIf values are too stable, you can add jitter:\n\n```r\npred_jittered <- pred + rnorm(length(pred), mean = 0, sd = 0.01)\n```\n\nBut **only do this if you're comfortable adding noise** for approximation.\n\n---\n\n#### u2705 3. Alternative: Quantile-based CI without bootstrapping\n\nIf speed and variability are more important than exact CIs:\n\n```r\nci_list <- map2(actual, pred, ~ {\n  residuals <- .x - .y\n  rmse_val <- sqrt(mean(residuals^2))\n  tibble(\n    RMSE = rmse_val,\n    CI_lower = quantile(residuals, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),\n    CI_upper = quantile(residuals, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)\n  )\n})\n```\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Summary\n\n| Problem | Fix |\n|--------|-----|\n| All bootstrap RMSEs are the same | Use fallback if `sd(t) == 0` |\n| Need variability | Try jittering predictions or use quantile method |\n| Want stability | Use `possibly()` or `tryCatch()` in `map2()` |\n\nLet me know if you want a working plot version of this or to apply it across columns like `Ti`, `Ca`, `Sr`."

              "The reason this line **doesn't work** is because you're incorrectly using the **pipe (`%>%`)** with `annotate()`, which is not designed to work with piping in that context.\n\n### ud83dudccc Problem\n```r\nannotate(\"text\", ...) %>% \n  annotate(\"text\", ...)\n```\n\nThis pipes the **output of the first `annotate()` call** (which is a `layer`, not a `ggplot` object) into the second `annotate()`, which will fail because `annotate()` expects a `ggplot` object, not a layer.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Correct Approach\n\nYou need to add both `annotate()` layers to a **ggplot object**, using `+`, like this:\n\n```r\nggplot(data, aes(x, y)) +\n  geom_point() +\n  annotate(\"text\", x = -1, y = 1.8, label = RMSE_text_Ti, parse = TRUE, hjust = 0) +\n  annotate(\"text\", x = -1, y = 2, label = R2_text_Ti, parse = TRUE, hjust = 0)\n```\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Or if you're using piping (`%>%`), wrap the full plot\n\n```r\nlibrary(ggplot2)\nlibrary(dplyr)\n\nyour_plot <- ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) +\n  geom_point()\n\nyour_plot +\n  annotate(\"text\", x = -1, y = 1.8, label = RMSE_text_Ti, parse = TRUE, hjust = 0) +\n  annotate(\"text\", x = -1, y = 2, label = R2_text_Ti, parse = TRUE, hjust = 0)\n```\n\nLet me know if you want it auto-positioned based on axis range or facets."

              "To get **confidence interval (CI) values for each row** (i.e., per observation) in a dataset like `_ICP_actual_ppm`, youu2019ll need a **resampling or prediction-based method**, such as **bootstrapping** or using the **prediction intervals from a model** (e.g., PLSR, linear model, etc.).\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Method 1: Bootstrapping Confidence Intervals per Row\n\nIf you have actual and predicted values, you can compute **bootstrap-based CIs of the prediction errors per row** like this:\n\n#### ud83dudce6 Assumes:\n- You have:\n  - `actual` u2013 a vector of true values (e.g., from `_ICP_actual_ppm$Ti`)\n  - `pred` u2013 a vector of predicted values (same length)\n\n#### ud83dudd01 Bootstrapping CI per row:\n\n```r\nlibrary(boot)\nlibrary(dplyr)\nlibrary(purrr)\n\n# Function to get bootstrap distribution of residuals per row\nbootstrap_ci_row <- function(a, p, R = 1000) {\n  resid <- a - p\n  boot_fn <- function(data, indices) {\n    resampled <- data[indices]\n    mean(resampled)\n  }\n  boot_obj <- boot(data = resid, statistic = boot_fn, R = R)\n  ci <- boot.ci(boot_obj, type = \"perc\")\n  \n  tibble(\n    CI_lower = if (!is.null(ci$percent)) ci$percent[4] else NA,\n    CI_upper = if (!is.null(ci$percent)) ci$percent[5] else NA\n  )\n}\n\n# Apply to each row\nci_df <- pmap_dfr(\n  list(actual = _ICP_actual_ppm$Ti, pred = predicted_ppm$Ti),\n  ~ bootstrap_ci_row(..1, ..2, R = 500)\n)\n\n# Combine with your original data\nfinal_df <- bind_cols(_ICP_actual_ppm, ci_df)\n```\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Method 2: Using Prediction Intervals from a Model (e.g., `pls::predict` + `predict.lm`)\n\nIf you have a fitted model and want prediction intervals per row, for example with `lm()` or `pls`:\n\n```r\n# Assuming `pls_model` and newdata exists:\npreds <- predict(pls_model, newdata = xrf_clr_new, se.fit = TRUE)  # if supported\n\n# If not supported directly by `pls::predict`, youu2019ll need to bootstrap manually\n```\n\n---\n\n### u26a0ufe0f Important Notes:\n- Bootstrapping per row is **expensive** (CPU-wise), especially for 1000+ rows and R = 1000.\n- CI width will vary per row due to prediction uncertainty and local residual variance.\n- If using bootstrapping on residuals, it's **not the same** as model-based prediction intervals (but can approximate them).\n\n---\n\nWould you like a version that handles **multiple elements (e.g., Ti, Ca, Sr)** or computes **RMSE + CI per row** and **visualizes ribbons**?"

Create output directory if needed\n  dir.create(output_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)\n\n  # Storage object for summary results\n  results_summary <- data.frame(\n    Element_ICP = character(),\n    Element_XRF = character(),\n    Optimal_ncomp_LOO = integer(),\n    Min_RMSEP = numeric(),\n    stringsAsFactors = FALSE\n  )\n\n  # ------------------------------------------------------------------\n  # Loop over elements\n  # ------------------------------------------------------------------\n  for (i in seq_along(key_elements_icp)) {\n\n    icp_el <- key_elements_icp[i]\n    xrf_el <- key_elements_xrf[i]\n\n    message(\"Running LOO-PLSR for: \", icp_el)\n\n    # Define X and Y\n    X_test <- df[, key_elements_xrf, drop = FALSE]\n    Y_test <- df[[icp_el]]\n\n    pls_df <- data.frame(X_test, Y_test = Y_test)\n\n    # --------------------------------------------------------------\n    # Fit LOO-PLSR model\n    # --------------------------------------------------------------\n    pls_train_model_LOO <- plsr(\n      Y_test ~ .,\n      data = pls_df,\n      validation = \"LOO\",\n      jackknife = TRUE,\n      scale = scale,\n      center = center\n    )\n\n    rmsep_obj <- RMSEP(pls_train_model_LOO)\n\n    # Optimal number of components\n    opt_comp_LOO <- which.min(rmsep_obj$val[1, , -1])\n    min_rmsep  <- min(rmsep_obj$val[1, , -1])\n\n    # --------------------------------------------------------------\n    # Save model summary\n    # --------------------------------------------------------------\n    summary_file <- file.path(\n      output_dir,\n      paste0(\"PLS_model_LOO_summary_\", xrf_el, \".txt\")\n    )\n\n    capture.output(\n      {\n        cat(\"ICP element:\", icp_el, \"\\n\")\n        cat(\"XRF element:\", xrf_el, \"\\n\")\n        cat(\"Optimal number of components (LOO):\", opt_comp_LOO, \"\\n\\n\")\n        summary(pls_train_model_LOO)\n        cat(\"\\n--- Jackknife test ---\\n\")\n        jack.test(pls_train_model_LOO, ncomp = opt_comp_LOO, use.mean = TRUE)\n      },\n      file = summary_file\n    )\n\n    # --------------------------------------------------------------\n    # Save RMSEP plot\n    # --------------------------------------------------------------\n    pdf_file <- file.path(\n      output_dir,\n      paste0(\"PLS_RMSEP_plot_LOO_\", xrf_el, \".pdf\")\n    )\n\n    pdf(pdf_file, width = 4, height = 4)\n    plot(rmsep_obj, legendpos = \"topright\")\n    dev.off()\n\n    # --------------------------------------------------------------\n    # Store summary info\n    # --------------------------------------------------------------\n    results_summary <- rbind(\n      results_summary,\n      data.frame(\n        Element_ICP = icp_el,\n        Element_XRF = xrf_el,\n        Optimal_ncomp_LOO = opt_comp_LOO,\n        Min_RMSEP = min_rmsep\n      )\n    )\n  }\n\n  return(results_summary)\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n## How to run it (exactly matching your setup)\n\n```r\nresults_plsr_loo <- run_plsr_loo_all_elements(\n  df = df,\n  key_elements_xrf = key_elements_xrf,\n  key_elements_icp = key_elements_icp,\n  output_dir = \"Papers_R/2024_DeVleeschouwer/ACE_Calibration/ACE_PLS/Output/PLSR/log_inc\"\n)\n```\n\n---\n\n## What this gives you\n\nFor **each element (Ti, Ca, Mn, Fe, Sr, Zr)**:\n\nu2714 LOO-validated PLSR  \nu2714 Optimal number of components chosen by RMSEP  \nu2714 Jackknife coefficient tests  \nu2714 RMSEP plots saved as PDFs  \nu2714 One text summary per element  \nu2714 All files saved in **the same folder**, consistently named  \n\nAnd `results_plsr_loo` gives you a tidy table you can later merge into:\n\n- model-comparison tables  \n- README summaries  \n- plots of `ncomp` vs element  \n\n---\n\nIf you want, next we can:\n- extend this to **k-fold CV** in the same function  \n- auto-insert `ncomp = opt` into your **prediction pipeline**\n- write a **single combined RMSEP multi-panel PDF** for all elements"

              "Here you go u2014 one **drop-in function** that does all three:\n\n1) **LOO + k-fold CV** (you choose `k`) and picks `ncomp_opt` for each method  \n2) **Auto-inserts `ncomp_opt` into prediction** for a new XRF dataset (`newdata`)  \n3) Writes **one combined multi-panel RMSEP PDF** for *all* elements (and optionally per-element PDFs too)\n\nIt also saves per-element text summaries and returns a clean results table + prediction data.\n\n---\n\n## 1) Function (LOO + k-fold + predictions + combined RMSEP PDF)\n\n```r\nrun_plsr_cv_all_elements <- function(\n  df,\n  key_elements_xrf,\n  key_elements_icp,\n  output_dir,\n  newdata = NULL,                  # optional new XRF dataset for prediction\n  cv_k = 10,                       # k for k-fold CV\n  segments_type = c(\"random\", \"consecutive\", \"interleaved\"),\n  ncomp_max = NULL,                # optional cap; default derived from data\n  scale = TRUE,\n  center = TRUE,\n  save_per_element_rmsep_pdf = TRUE,\n  save_combined_rmsep_pdf = TRUE\n) {\n\n  # Packages\n  require(pls)\n\n  segments_type <- match.arg(segments_type)\n\n  # Checks\n  stopifnot(length(key_elements_xrf) == length(key_elements_icp))\n  stopifnot(all(key_elements_xrf %in% names(df)))\n  stopifnot(all(key_elements_icp %in% names(df)))\n\n  if (!is.null(newdata)) {\n    stopifnot(all(key_elements_xrf %in% names(newdata)))\n  }\n\n  dir.create(output_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)\n\n  # Helper: choose ncomp_max sensibly\n  choose_ncomp_max <- function(n, p) {\n    # Upper bound heuristic to avoid overfitting / degenerate comps\n    max(1L, min(p, n - 2L))\n  }\n\n  # Storage\n  results_summary <- data.frame(\n    Element_ICP = character(),\n    Element_XRF = character(),\n    n_obs = integer(),\n    n_pred = integer(),\n    ncomp_max = integer(),\n    ncomp_opt_LOO = integer(),\n    rmsep_min_LOO = numeric(),\n    ncomp_opt_kfold = integer(),\n    rmsep_min_kfold = numeric(),\n    stringsAsFactors = FALSE\n  )\n\n  preds_list <- list()   # per-element predictions (if newdata provided)\n  rmsep_store <- list()  # RMSEP objects per element (LOO + kfold)\n\n  # Use same CV splits across elements when random segments are used\n  # (keeps comparability). Works because rows used are those non-NA in Y.\n  set.seed(1)\n\n  # ------------------------------------------------------------\n  # Loop elements\n  # ------------------------------------------------------------\n  for (i in seq_along(key_elements_icp)) {\n\n    icp_el <- key_elements_icp[i]\n    xrf_el <- key_elements_xrf[i]\n\n    message(\"Running PLS CV for: \", icp_el)\n\n    # Build modelling frame with complete cases for this Y\n    X_all <- df[, key_elements_xrf, drop = FALSE]\n    y_all <- df[[icp_el]]\n\n    keep <- complete.cases(X_all) & !is.na(y_all)\n    X <- X_all[keep, , drop = FALSE]\n    y <- y_all[keep]\n\n    n <- nrow(X)\n    p <- ncol(X)\n\n    if (n < 5) {\n      warning(\"Skipping \", icp_el, \" (too few complete rows after NA removal).\")\n      next\n    }\n\n    ncomp_max_i <- if (is.null(ncomp_max)) choose_ncomp_max(n, p) else min(ncomp_max, choose_ncomp_max(n, p))\n\n    pls_df <- data.frame(X, Y_test = y)\n\n    # -----------------------\n    # LOO model\n    # -----------------------\n    pls_LOO <- plsr(\n      Y_test ~ .,\n      data = pls_df,\n      validation = \"LOO\",\n      jackknife = TRUE,\n      scale = scale,\n      center = center,\n      ncomp = ncomp_max_i\n    )\n\n    rmsep_LOO <- RMSEP(pls_LOO)\n    # rmsep_LOO$val dims: [estimate, response, ncomp+1] with first = 0 comps\n    loo_vals <- rmsep_LOO$val[1, 1, -1]\n    ncomp_opt_LOO <- which.min(loo_vals)\n    rmsep_min_LOO <- min(loo_vals)\n\n    # -----------------------\n    # k-fold model\n    # -----------------------\n    # pls uses \"CV\" with 'segments' for k-fold\n    # segments = cv_k gives k folds; segment.type controls split behaviour\n    pls_kfold <- plsr(\n      Y_test ~ .,\n      data = pls_df,\n      validation = \"CV\",\n      segments = cv_k,\n      segment.type = segments_type,\n      jackknife = TRUE,\n      scale = scale,\n      center = center,\n      ncomp = ncomp_max_i\n    )\n\n    rmsep_kfold <- RMSEP(pls_kfold)\n    k_vals <- rmsep_kfold$val[1, 1, -1]\n    ncomp_opt_kfold <- which.min(k_vals)\n    rmsep_min_kfold <- min(k_vals)\n\n    # Store RMSEP objects for combined plotting\n    rmsep_store[[xrf_el]] <- list(LOO = rmsep_LOO, kfold = rmsep_kfold)\n\n    # -----------------------\n    # Save per-element text summary (includes both CV types)\n    # -----------------------\n    summary_file <- file.path(output_dir, paste0(\"PLS_model_CV_summary_\", xrf_el, \".txt\"))\n    capture.output(\n      {\n        cat(\"ICP element:\", icp_el, \"\\n\")\n        cat(\"XRF elements used:\", paste(key_elements_xrf, collapse = \", \"), \"\\n\")\n        cat(\"Rows used (complete cases):\", n, \"\\n\")\n        cat(\"ncomp_max:\", ncomp_max_i, \"\\n\\n\")\n\n        cat(\"=== LOO CV ===\\n\")\n        cat(\"Optimal ncomp (LOO):\", ncomp_opt_LOO, \"\\n\")\n        cat(\"Min RMSEP (LOO):\", rmsep_min_LOO, \"\\n\\n\")\n        print(summary(pls_LOO))\n        cat(\"\\n--- Jackknife test (LOO optimum) ---\\n\")\n        print(jack.test(pls_LOO, ncomp = ncomp_opt_LOO, use.mean = TRUE))\n\n        cat(\"\\n\\n=== k-fold CV ===\\n\")\n        cat(\"k:\", cv_k, \" segment.type:\", segments_type, \"\\n\")\n        cat(\"Optimal ncomp (k-fold):\", ncomp_opt_kfold, \"\\n\")\n        cat(\"Min RMSEP (k-fold):\", rmsep_min_kfold, \"\\n\\n\")\n        print(summary(pls_kfold))\n        cat(\"\\n--- Jackknife test (k-fold optimum) ---\\n\")\n        print(jack.test(pls_kfold, ncomp = ncomp_opt_kfold, use.mean = TRUE))\n      },\n      file = summary_file\n    )\n\n    # -----------------------\n    # Save per-element RMSEP PDFs (optional)\n    # -----------------------\n    if (save_per_element_rmsep_pdf) {\n      pdf(file.path(output_dir, paste0(\"PLS_RMSEP_LOO_\", xrf_el, \".pdf\")), width = 4, height = 4)\n      plot(rmsep_LOO, legendpos = \"topright\", main = paste0(xrf_el, \" (LOO)\"))\n      dev.off()\n\n      pdf(file.path(output_dir, paste0(\"PLS_RMSEP_kfold_\", xrf_el, \".pdf\")), width = 4, height = 4)\n      plot(rmsep_kfold, legendpos = \"topright\", main = paste0(xrf_el, \" (k=\", cv_k, \")\"))\n      dev.off()\n    }\n\n    # -----------------------\n    # Auto prediction pipeline (optional):\n    # Fit \"final\" model using chosen optimum (default: k-fold optimum)\n    # Then predict for newdata.\n    # -----------------------\n    n_pred <- 0L\n    if (!is.null(newdata)) {\n\n      X_new <- newdata[, key_elements_xrf, drop = FALSE]\n      # allow NAs in newdata: predictions will be NA where predictors missing\n      can_pred <- complete.cases(X_new)\n      n_pred <- sum(can_pred)\n\n      # Fit final model using k-fold optimum ncomp\n      final_model <- plsr(\n        Y_test ~ .,\n        data = pls_df,\n        validation = \"none\",\n        scale = scale,\n        center = center,\n        ncomp = ncomp_opt_kfold\n      )\n\n      pred_vec <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(X_new))\n      pred_vec[can_pred] <- as.numeric(predict(final_model, newdata = X_new[can_pred, , drop = FALSE], ncomp = ncomp_opt_kfold))\n\n      preds_list[[icp_el]] <- data.frame(\n        row_id = seq_len(nrow(X_new)),\n        Element_ICP = icp_el,\n        Element_XRF = xrf_el,\n        ncomp_used = ncomp_opt_kfold,\n        Pred = pred_vec\n      )\n\n      # Save per-element predictions CSV\n      write.csv(\n        preds_list[[icp_el]],\n        file = file.path(output_dir, paste0(\"PLS_predictions_kfoldOpt_\", xrf_el, \".csv\")),\n        row.names = FALSE\n      )\n    }\n\n    # -----------------------\n    # Append row to results table\n    # -----------------------\n    results_summary <- rbind(\n      results_summary,\n      data.frame(\n        Element_ICP = icp_el,\n        Element_XRF = xrf_el,\n        n_obs = n,\n        n_pred = n_pred,\n        ncomp_max = ncomp_max_i,\n        ncomp_opt_LOO = ncomp_opt_LOO,\n        rmsep_min_LOO = rmsep_min_LOO,\n        ncomp_opt_kfold = ncomp_opt_kfold,\n        rmsep_min_kfold = rmsep_min_kfold,\n        stringsAsFactors = FALSE\n      )\n    )\n  }\n\n  # ------------------------------------------------------------\n  # Combined RMSEP multi-panel PDF (optional)\n  # Two pages: LOO and k-fold\n  # ------------------------------------------------------------\n  if (save_combined_rmsep_pdf && length(rmsep_store) > 0) {\n\n    els <- names(rmsep_store)\n    m <- length(els)\n\n    # Simple grid: try to make it ~square\n    ncol <- ceiling(sqrt(m))\n    nrow <- ceiling(m / ncol)\n\n    pdf(file.path(output_dir, \"PLS_RMSEP_ALL_ELEMENTS_multiPanel.pdf\"),\n        width = 4 * ncol, height = 4 * nrow)\n\n    #               "This is a **classic namespace / method-masking issue**, and the error message is actually very diagnostic once you know what to look for.\n\n---\n\n## What the error means\n\n```r\nError in select(., c(Site, depth, SH20_mean_age, SH20_mean_95CI, all_of(xrf_icp_elements1))) : \n  unused argument (...)\n```\n\nThis **does not** mean your column names are wrong.\n\nIt means that **the `select()` function being called is *not* `dplyr::select()`**.\n\nInstead, R is calling **another `select()` method** (most commonly from **`MASS`**, sometimes `stats`), which:\n\n- does **not** accept tidyselect helpers (`all_of()`)\n- does **not** accept column vectors wrapped in `c()`\n- therefore throws `unused argument`\n\n---\n\n## Why this happens (very common in your workflow)\n\nYou are using the **`pls` package**, and very often people also have:\n\n```r\nlibrary(MASS)\n```\n\nloaded earlier in the session.\n\n`MASS` defines its own `select()` function, which **masks `dplyr::select()`**:\n\n```r\nMASS::select()\ndplyr::select()\n```\n\nWhen masked, `%>% select()` silently calls the wrong one.\n\nYou can confirm this with:\n\n```r\nselect\n```\n\nor\n\n```r\nconflicts()\n```\n\n---\n\n## Two separate issues in your line\n\n### u274c Issue 1: wrong `select()` function\n\nYou *must* explicitly call `dplyr::select()`.\n\n### u274c Issue 2: incorrect syntax for `select()`\n\nIn **`dplyr::select()`**, you **do not wrap column names in `c()`** when mixing symbols and helpers.\n\n---\n\n## u2705 Correct, robust fix (recommended)\n\n```r\ndf0 <- ACE_matched_xrf_icp_log_inc %>%\n  dplyr::select(\n    Site,\n    depth,\n    SH20_mean_age,\n    SH20_mean_95CI,\n    dplyr::all_of(xrf_icp_elements1)\n  ) %>%\n  tidyr::drop_na()\n```\n\nThis solves **both problems**:\n- forces the correct `select()`\n- uses correct tidyselect syntax\n\n---\n\n## Alternative (base R safe version)\n\nIf you *really* want to avoid tidyverse issues before passing to `pls`:\n\n```r\ncols <- c(\"Site\", \"depth\", \"SH20_mean_age\", \"SH20_mean_95CI\", xrf_icp_elements1)\ndf0  <- ACE_matched_xrf_icp_log_inc[, cols]\ndf0  <- df0[stats::complete.cases(df0), ]\n```\n\nThis is **100% namespace-safe** and often preferable just before modelling.\n\n---\n\n## Why this keeps happening in PLS workflows\n\nYour workflow typically includes:\n\n```r\nlibrary(pls)\nlibrary(MASS)\nlibrary(dplyr)\n```\n\nWhen loaded in this order:\n\n- `MASS::select()` masks `dplyr::select()`\n- `%>% select()` fails *silently* until helpers are used\n- error only appears once `all_of()` or `c()` is passed\n\n---\n\n## Best practice going forward (strongly recommended)\n\nAt the **top of your script**, add:\n\n```r\nconflicted::conflict_prefer(\"select\", \"dplyr\")\n```\n\nor always write:\n\n```r\ndplyr::select(...)\n```\n\nfor any modelling pipeline.\n\n---\n\n## TL;DR\n\n**You get this error because:**\n\n1. `select()` is coming from **`MASS`**, not `dplyr`\n2. `dplyr::select()` does **not** accept `c(...)` wrapping\n\n**Fix it with:**\n\n```r\ndplyr::select(col1, col2, all_of(vec))\n```\n\nIf you want, next I can:\n- audit your full PLS pipeline for other hidden namespace traps\n- give you a **u201csafe modelling preambleu201d** you can paste at the top of every               "**VIP scores** (***Variable Importance in Projection***) are a standard diagnostic from **PLS / PLSR (Partial Least Squares regression)** that quantify **how important each predictor variable is** in explaining the response across the latent components of the model.\n\nThey are especially useful in your kind of **multivariate XRF u2192 ICP-MS calibration**, where predictors are correlated and coefficients alone are hard to interpret.\n\n---\n\n## What a VIP score measures (intuition)\n\nA VIP score answers:\n\n> **u201cHow much does this predictor contribute, overall, to explaining the response variable in the PLS model?u201d**\n\nIt combines **three things at once**:\n\n1. How strongly the variable loads onto each PLS component  \n2. How much variance in **Y** each component explains  \n3. How many components are used in the model  \n\nSo unlike raw coefficients:\n- it is **scale-independent**\n- it reflects **global importance**, not just one component\n- it works well under **multicollinearity**\n\n---\n\n## Formal definition (what the maths is doing)\n\nFor predictor \\( j \\), the VIP score is:\n\n\\[\n\\text{VIP}_j\n=\n\\sqrt{\n\\frac{p \\; \\sum_{a=1}^{A}\n\\left( SSY_a \\cdot w_{ja}^2 \\right)}\n{\\sum_{a=1}^{A} SSY_a}\n}\n\\]\n\nWhere:\n\n- \\( p \\) = number of predictors  \n- \\( A \\) = number of PLS components used  \n- \\( SSY_a \\) = sum of squares of **Y** explained by component \\( a \\)  \n- \\( w_{ja} \\) = weight of variable \\( j \\) on component \\( a \\)\n\nIn words:\n> **Variables get higher VIPs if they strongly load on components that explain a lot of Y variance.**\n\n---\n\n## How to interpret VIP values (rules of thumb)\n\n| VIP value | Interpretation |\n|----------:|----------------|\n| **> 1.0** | Important predictor (commonly used threshold) |\n| 0.8u20131.0  | Moderately important / borderline |\n| < 0.8    | Low importance |\n| u226a 0.5    | Negligible |\n\nu26a0ufe0f These are **heuristics**, not hard statistical tests.\n\n---\n\n## Why VIPs are ideal for your XRFu2013ICP workflow\n\nIn your calibration problem:\n\n- XRF elements are **strongly correlated**\n- regression coefficients can:\n  - change sign across components\n  - shrink due to collinearity\n- RF importance u2260 linear interpretability\n- PLS components are abstract\n\n**VIPs give you:**\n\n- element-level importance (Ti, Ca, Sr, Zr, u2026)\n- comparability **across models and elements**\n- a principled way to justify **dropping or retaining predictors**\n- a defensible explanation in methods sections\n\nThis is exactly why VIPs are widely used in **chemo-metrics, spectroscopy, and geochemical calibration**.\n\n---\n\n## VIP vs coefficients (important distinction)\n\n| Coefficients | VIP |\n|-------------|-----|\n| Component-specific | Global across components |\n| Sensitive to scaling | Scale-invariant |\n| Hard to interpret with collinearity | Robust to collinearity |\n| Can cancel across components | Cannot cancel |\n\nA variable can have:\n- **small coefficients** but **high VIP** u2192 important but distributed across components  \n- **large coefficient** but **low VIP** u2192 influential in one weak component only  \n\n---\n\n## VIPs are **not** p-values\n\nImportant caveat:\n\n- VIP scores are **descriptive**, not inferential\n- No null hypothesis\n- No confidence intervals by default\n\nFor inference you correctly complement VIPs with:\n- **jackknife tests** (which you already run)\n- CV-based performance (RMSEP)\n\nThat combination is best practice.\n\n---\n\n## Typical sentence you can use in a paper\n\n> u201cVariable importance in projection (VIP) scores were used to assess the relative contribution of individual XRF elements to the PLSR models. Predictors with VIP > 1 were considered influential in explaining ICP-MS concentrations.u201d\n\n---\n\n## Want this next?\n\nI can:\n- add **VIP extraction + plots** to your PLS function  \n- compute VIPs at **optimum ncomp (LOO or k-fold)**  \n- generate **VIP heatmaps across sites/elements**  \n- show how VIPs differ between **PLS-LOO vs PLS-k**\n\nJust tell me which output you want first."
