Copy/paste into R and run. I kept reasonable defaults but allow customization.\n\n---\n\n```r\n# Full, integrated validation + reporting function (Option C: rmarkdown preferred, fallback to base PDF)\n# Requires: ggplot2, gridExtra, utils. rmarkdown optional (auto-detected).\n#\n# Usage example after the function is defined:\n# Ti_results <- validate_element_pro(\n#   Ti_ICP ~ Ti,\n#   data = ACE_dataset,\n#   sd_col = \"Ti_ICP_sd\",\n#   cv_method = \"kfold\",\n#   k = 10,\n#   boot_iter = 500,             # reduce for speed; set >=2000 for production\n#   boot_seed = 123,\n#   save_plots = TRUE,\n#   plot_dir = \"validation_plots\",\n#   save_report = TRUE,\n#   report_file = \"Ti_validation_report.pdf\",\n#   report_format = \"pdf\"        # \"pdf\" or \"html\"\n# )\n#\n# Then: Ti_results$predict_new(newdata = Ti_XRF_input, save_results = TRUE)\n#\nvalidate_element_pro <- function(\n  formula,\n  data,\n  sd_col,\n  cv_method = c(\"kfold\", \"LOOCV\"),\n  k = 10,\n  train_frac = 0.6,\n  external_test = NULL,\n  save_plots = TRUE,\n  plot_dir = \"validation_plots\",\n  plot_format = \"png\",\n  boot_iter = 200,          # default 200 for speed; increase (e.g. 2000) for full bootstrap\n  boot_seed = 123,\n  save_report = TRUE,\n  report_file = \"validation_report.pdf\",\n  report_format = c(\"pdf\", \"html\"),\n  report_method = c(\"auto\"), # \"auto\" -> try rmarkdown then fallback\n  verbose = TRUE\n) {\n  library(ggplot2)\n  library(gridExtra)\n  report_format <- match.arg(report_format)\n  cv_method <- match.arg(cv_method)\n  if (!dir.exists(plot_dir) && save_plots) dir.create(plot_dir, recursive = TRUE)\n  \n  # helper for saving a plot\n  save_plot <- function(p, name, width = 6, height = 5) {\n    if (!save_plots) return(NULL)\n    fname <- file.path(plot_dir, paste0(name, \".\", plot_format))\n    ggplot2::ggsave(fname, plot = p, width = width, height = height)\n    if(verbose) message(\"Saved plot: \", fname)\n  }\n  \n  # safe model frame extraction\n  mf_all <- model.frame(formula, data)\n  response_name <- all.vars(formula)[1]\n  predictor_name <- all.vars(formula)[2]\n  \n  # 1) Train/test split or use external_test\n  if (!is.null(external_test)) {\n    train_data <- data\n    test_data <- external_test\n  } else {\n    set.seed(123)\n    n <- nrow(data)\n    train_index <- sample(seq_len(n), size = floor(train_frac * n))\n    train_data <- data[train_index, , drop = FALSE]\n    test_data <- data[-train_index, , drop = FALSE]\n  }\n  \n  # internal helper to fit two-stage WLS on a dataset and return final lm object\n  fit_two_stage_wls <- function(form, df, sd_col_name) {\n    # Stage1 weights column\n    df$w1 <- 1 / (df[[sd_col_name]]^2)\n    stage1 <- lm(form, data = df, weights = w1)\n    # Stage2 weights based on absolute residuals\n    abs_res <- abs(stage1$residuals)\n    fit_vals <- stage1$fitted.values\n    # if abs_res or fit_vals length <=1, fallback to equal weights\n    if (length(abs_res) <= 1) {\n      df$stage2_wt <- rep(1, nrow(df))\n    } else {\n      df$stage2_wt <- 1 / lm(abs_res ~ fit_vals)$fitted.values^2\n      # guard against Inf/NA weights\n      df$stage2_wt[!is.finite(df$stage2_wt)] <- median(df$stage2_wt[is.finite(df$stage2_wt)], na.rm = TRUE)\n      if (any(!is.finite(df$stage2_wt))) df$stage2_wt <- rep(1, nrow(df))\n    }\n    final <- lm(form, data = df, weights = stage2_wt)\n    attr(final, \"data\") <- df  # store the df with weights for diagnostics if needed\n    return(final)\n  }\n  \n  # 2) Cross-validation: either k-fold on train_data or LOOCV on train_data\n  if (cv_method == \"kfold\") {\n    n_train <- nrow(train_data)\n    if (k > n_train) {\n      warning(\"k > n_train; setting k = n_train\")\n      k <- n_train\n    }\n    set.seed(123)\n    folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = n_train))\n    preds_cv <- rep(NA, n_train)\n    rmse_folds <- numeric(k)\n    r2_folds <- numeric(k)\n    for (i in seq_len(k)) {\n      tr <- train_data[folds != i, , drop = FALSE]\n      te <- train_data[folds == i, , drop = FALSE]\n      mod_i <- fit_two_stage_wls(formula, tr, sd_col)\n      p <- predict(mod_i, newdata = te)\n      obs <- model.response(model.frame(formula, te))\n      preds_cv[which(folds == i)] <- p\n      rmse_folds[i] <- sqrt(mean((obs - p)^2))\n      SSE <- sum((obs - p)^2)\n      SST <- sum((obs - mean(obs))^2)\n      r2_folds[i] <- ifelse(SST == 0, NA, 1 - SSE/SST)\n    }\n    CV_RMSEP <- mean(rmse_folds, na.rm = TRUE)\n    CV_R2 <- mean(r2_folds, na.rm = TRUE)\n    # store train-level CV predictions (aligned with train_data order)\n    train_data$cv_pred <- preds_cv\n  } else { # LOOCV on training set\n    n_train <- nrow(train_data)\n    preds_loo <- numeric(n_train)\n    for (i in seq_len(n_train)) {\n      tr <- train_data[-i, , drop = FALSE]\n      te <- train_data[i, , drop = FALSE]\n      mod_i <- fit_two_stage_wls(formula, tr, sd_col)\n      preds_loo[i] <- predict(mod_i, newdata = te)\n    }\n    obs_train <- model.response(model.frame(formula, train_data))\n    CV_RMSEP <- sqrt(mean((obs_train - preds_loo)^2))\n    SSE_cv <- sum((obs_train - preds_loo)^2)\n    SST_cv <- sum((obs_train - mean(obs_train))^2)\n    CV_R2 <- 1 - SSE_cv / SST_cv\n    train_data$cv_pred <- preds_loo\n  }\n  \n  # 3) Final model on full training set\n  final_model <- fit_two_stage_wls(formula, train_data, sd_col)\n  \n  # Training predictions & metrics\n  train_pred <- predict(final_model, newdata = train_data, interval = \"prediction\")\n  train_obs <- model.response(model.frame(formula, train_data))\n  Train_RMSE <- sqrt(mean((train_obs - train_pred[,1])^2))\n  SSE_train <- sum((train_obs - train_pred[,1])^2)\n  SST_train <- sum((train_obs - mean(train_obs))^2)\n  Train_R2 <- ifelse(SST_train == 0, NA, 1 - SSE_train/SST_train)\n  \n  # 4) Independent test performance (if test_data has the response)\n  # test_data may be external_test that may or may not include sd_col: we only need predictor\n  if (response_name %in% names(test_data)) {\n    test_pred_mat <- predict(final_model, newdata = test_data, interval = \"prediction\")\n    test_pred <- test_pred_mat[,1]\n    test_obs <- model.response(model.frame(formula, test_data))\n    Test_RMSEP <- sqrt(mean((test_obs - test_pred)^2))\n    SSE_test <- sum((test_obs - test_pred)^2)\n    SST_test <- sum((test_obs - mean(test_obs))^2)\n    Test_R2 <- ifelse(SST_test == 0, NA, 1 - SSE_test/SST_test)\n  } else {\n    test_pred_mat <- predict(final_model, newdata = test_data, interval = \"prediction\")\n    test_pred <- test_pred_mat[,1]\n    test_obs <- rep(NA, length(test_pred))\n    Test_RMSEP <- NA\n    Test_R2 <- NA\n  }\n  \n  # 5) LOOCV on full dataset (for RMSEP_full and R2_LOOCV) - optional but requested\n  n_total <- nrow(data)\n  pred_LOO_full <- numeric(n_total)\n  for (i in seq_len(n_total)) {\n    tr <- data[-i, , drop = FALSE]\n    te <- data[i, , drop = FALSE]\n    mod_i <- fit_two_stage_wls(formula, tr, sd_col)\n    pred_LOO_full[i] <- predict(mod_i, newdata = te)\n  }\n  full_obs <- model.response(model.frame(formula, data))\n  RMSEP_LOOCV <- sqrt(mean((full_obs - pred_LOO_full)^2))\n  SSE_loocv <- sum((full_obs - pred_LOO_full)^2)\n  SST_loocv <- sum((full_obs - mean(full_obs))^2)\n  R2_LOOCV <- ifelse(SST_loocv == 0, NA, 1 - SSE_loocv/SST_loocv)\n  \n  # 6) Model equation text (rounded)\n  coefs <- coef(final_model)\n  if (length(coefs) >= 2) {\n    intercept <- round(coefs[1], 6)\n    slope <- round(coefs[2], 6)\n    model_equation <- paste0(response_name, \" = \", intercept, \" + \", slope, \" * \", predictor_name)\n  } else {\n    model_equation <- paste0(response_name, \" = \", paste(round(coefs,6), collapse = \" + \"))\n  }\n  \n  # 7) Residuals and diagnostic plots\n  final_df <- attr(final_model, \"data\")\n  final_pred <- predict(final_model, newdata = final_df)\n  final_resid <- final_df[[response_name]] - final_pred\n  df_final_diag <- data.frame(fitted = final_pred, residuals = final_resid)\n  \n  p_res_vs_fit <- ggplot(df_final_diag, aes(x = fitted, y = residuals)) +\n    geom_point() +\n    geom_smooth(method = \"loess\", se = TRUE) +\n    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = \"dashed\") +\n    labs(title = \"Residuals vs Fitted (LOESS)\", x = \"Fitted\", y = \"Residuals\") +\n    theme_bw()\n  save_plot(p_res_vs_fit, \"residuals_vs_fitted\")\n  \n  # residual bands approximate (u00b12 * sd of residuals)\n  resid_sd <- sd(final_resid, na.rm = TRUE)\n  p_res_band <- p_res_vs_fit + geom_hline(yintercept = c(2*resid_sd, -2*resid_sd), linetype = \"dotdash\", color = \"red\")\n  save_plot(p_res_band, \"residuals_vs_fitted_bands\")\n  \n  # QQ plot\n  p_qq <- ggplot(df_final_diag, aes(sample = residuals)) +\n    stat_qq() +\n    stat_qq_line() +\n    labs(title = \"Q-Q Plot of Residuals\") + theme_bw()\n  save_plot(p_qq, \"qq_plot\")\n  \n  # Observed vs Predicted (training) with LOESS and PI ribbon\n  df_train_plot <- data.frame(obs = train_obs, pred = train_pred[,1], lwr = train_pred[,2], upr = train_pred[,3])\n  p_train_obs_pred <- ggplot(df_train_plot, aes(x = obs, y = pred)) +\n    geom_point(color = \"blue\") +\n    geom_smooth(method = \"loess\", se = TRUE) +\n    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), alpha = 0.15) +\n    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = \"dashed\") +\n    labs(title = \"Training: Observed vs Predicted\", x = \"Observed\", y = \"Predicted\") + theme_bw()\n  save_plot(p_train_obs_pred, \"training_obs_vs_pred\")\n  \n  # CV plot: use train_data$cv_pred if available\n  if (\"cv_pred\" %in% names(train_data)) {\n    df_cv_plot <- data.frame(obs = model.response(model.frame(formula, train_data)), pred = train_data$cv_pred)\n  } else {\n    df_cv_plot <- data.frame(obs = train_obs, pred = train_pred[,1])\n  }\n  p_cv_plot <- ggplot(df_cv_plot, aes(x = obs, y = pred)) +\n    geom_point(color = \"red\") +\n    geom_smooth(method = \"loess\", se = TRUE) +\n    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = \"dashed\") +\n    labs(title = paste0(\"Cross-Validation (\", cv_method, \") Observed vs Predicted\"), x = \"Observed\", y = \"Predicted\") + theme_bw()\n  save_plot(p_cv_plot, \"cv_obs_vs_pred\")\n  \n  # Test plot\n  if (!all(is.na(test_obs))) {\n    df_test_plot <- data.frame(obs = test_obs, pred = test_pred, lwr = test_pred_mat[,2], upr = test_pred_mat[,3])\n  } else {\n    df_test_plot <- data.frame(obs = rep(NA, length(test_pred)), pred = test_pred, lwr = test_pred_mat[,2], upr = test_pred_mat[,3])\n  }\n  p_test_plot <- ggplot(df_test_plot, aes(x = obs, y = pred)) +\n    geom_point(color = \"darkgreen\") +\n    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), alpha = 0.12) +\n    geom_smooth(method = \"loess\", se = TRUE) +\n    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = \"dashed\") +\n    labs(title = \"Test Set: Observed vs Predicted\", x = \"Observed\", y = \"Predicted\") + theme_bw()\n  save_plot(p_test_plot, \"test_obs_vs_pred\")\n  \n  # 8) Bootstrap prediction uncertainty (resampling training set and refit)\n  if (!is.null(boot_iter) && boot_iter > 0) {\n    set.seed(boot_seed)\n    n_train <- nrow(train_data)\n    # pre-allocate matrices\n    boot_train_preds <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_train, ncol = boot_iter)\n    n_test <- nrow(test_data)\n    boot_test_preds <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_test, ncol = boot_iter)\n    if(verbose) message(\"Starting bootstrap with \", boot_iter, \" iterations (this may take time)...\")\n    for (b in seq_len(boot_iter)) {\n      idx <- sample(seq_len(n_train), replace = TRUE)\n      boot_tr <- train_data[idx, , drop = FALSE]\n      mod_b <- tryCatch({\n        fit_two_stage_wls(formula, boot_tr, sd_col)\n      }, error = function(e) {\n        NULL\n      })\n      if (!is.null(mod_b)) {\n        # predict on original training (out-of-bag not used here; we produce bootstrap distribution of predictions)\n        boot_train_preds[, b] <- predict(mod_b, newdata = train_data)\n        # predict on test set (if present)\n        boot_test_preds[, b] <- predict(mod_b, newdata = test_data)\n      } else {\n        boot_train_preds[, b] <- NA\n        boot_test_preds[, b] <- NA\n      }\n    }\n    # compute bootstrap means & percentile intervals\n    boot_train_mean <- apply(boot_train_preds, 1, mean, na.rm = TRUE)\n    boot_train_lwr <- apply(boot_train_preds, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)\n    boot_train_upr <- apply(boot_train_preds, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)\n    boot_test_mean <- apply(boot_test_preds, 1, mean, na.rm = TRUE)\n    boot_test_lwr <- apply(boot_test_preds, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)\n    boot_test_upr <- apply(boot_test_preds, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)\n    \n    # attach bootstrap outputs to df for plotting/saving\n    df_train_plot$boot_mean <- boot_train_mean\n    df_train_plot$boot_lwr <- boot_train_lwr\n    df_train_plot$boot_upr <- boot_train_upr\n    df_test_plot$boot_mean <- boot_test_mean\n    df_test_plot$boot_lwr <- boot_test_lwr\n    df_test_plot$boot_upr <- boot_test_upr\n    \n    # bootstrap RMSEP on test (if test has obs)\n    if (!all(is.na(test_obs))) {\n      boot_test_rmsep <- sqrt(mean((test_obs - boot_test_mean)^2, na.rm = TRUE))\n    } else {\n      boot_test_rmsep <- NA\n    }\n  } else {\n    boot_train_mean <- boot_train_lwr <- boot_train_upr <- NULL\n    boot_test_mean <- boot_test_lwr <- boot_test_upr <- NULL\n    boot_test_rmsep <- NA\n  }\n  \n  # Save extra plots: bootstrap train predictions with ribbon if available\n  if (!is.null(boot_train_mean)) {\n    p_train_boot <- ggplot(df_train_plot, aes(x = obs, y = pred)) +\n      geom_point(color = \"blue\") +\n      geom_line(aes(y = boot_mean), color = \"orange\") +\n      geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = boot_lwr, ymax = boot_upr), alpha = 0.12, fill = \"orange\") +\n      geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = \"dashed\") +\n      labs(title = \"Bootstrap (train): Predicted mean and 95% PI\") + theme_bw()\n    save_plot(p_train_boot, \"bootstrap_train_preds\")\n  }\n  if (!is.null(boot_test_mean)) {\n    p_test_boot <- ggplot(df_test_plot, aes(x = obs, y = pred)) +\n      geom_point(color = \"darkgreen\") +\n      geom_line(aes(y = boot_test_mean), color = \"orange\") +\n      geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = boot_test_lwr, ymax = boot_test_upr), alpha = 0.12, fill = \"orange\") +\n      geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = \"dashed\") +\n      labs(title = \"Bootstrap (test): Predicted mean and 95% PI\") + theme_bw()\n    save_plot(p_test_boot, \"bootstrap_test_preds\")\n  }\n  \n  # 9) Summary table\n  summary_table <- data.frame(\n    Metric = c(\"Training R2\", \"Training RMSE\", \"CV R2\", \"CV RMSEP\",\n               \"Test R2\", \"Test RMSEP\", \"LOOCV RMSEP (full)\", \"LOOCV R2 (full)\", \"Bootstrap test RMSEP (mean)\"),\n    Value = c(Train_R2, Train_RMSE, CV_R2, CV_RMSEP,\n              Test_R2, Test_RMSEP, RMSEP_LOOCV, R2_LOOCV, boot_test_rmsep)\n  )\n  \n  # 10) Helper: predict_new with bootstrap option\n  predict_new <- function(newdata, predictor_col = NULL, unit = NULL, save_results = FALSE, output_file = \"predictions_new.csv\", include_boot = FALSE) {\n    if (is.null(predictor_col)) predictor_col <- predictor_name\n    if (!predictor_col %in% names(newdata)) stop(\"predictor_col not found in newdata\")\n    preds_mat <- predict(final_model, newdata = newdata, interval = \"prediction\")\n    results <- data.frame(\n      XRF_input = newdata[[predictor_col]],\n      Predicted = preds_mat[,1],\n      PI_lower = preds_mat[,2],\n      PI_upper = preds_mat[,3]\n    )\n    names(results)[2:4] <- paste0(response_name, c(\"_pred\",\"_PI_lower\",\"_PI_upper\"))\n    if (!is.null(unit)) attr(results, \"units\") <- unit\n    attr(results, \"model_equation\") <- model_equation\n    attr(results, \"cv_method\") <- cv_method\n    attr(results, \"k\") <- ifelse(cv_method == \"kfold\", k, NA)\n    if (include_boot && !is.null(boot_iter) && boot_iter > 0) {\n      # perform bootstrap predictions for newdata using saved boot iterations if available\n      # If boot matrices exist, we refit boot models and predict newdata\n      set.seed(boot_seed)\n      n_new <- nrow(newdata)\n      boot_new_preds <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_new, ncol = boot_iter)\n      n_train <- nrow(train_data)\n      for (b in seq_len(boot_iter)) {\n        idx <- sample(seq_len(n_train), replace = TRUE)\n        boot_tr <- train_data[idx, , drop = FALSE]\n        mod_b <- tryCatch(fit_two_stage_wls(formula, boot_tr, sd_col), error = function(e) NULL)\n        if (!is.null(mod_b)) {\n          boot_new_preds[,b] <- predict(mod_b, newdata = newdata)\n        } else {\n          boot_new_preds[,b] <- NA\n        }\n      }\n      results[[paste0(response_name, \"_boot_mean\")]] <- apply(boot_new_preds, 1, mean, na.rm = TRUE)\n      results[[paste0(response_name, \"_boot_PI_lower\")]] <- apply(boot_new_preds, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)\n      results[[paste0(response_name, \"_boot_PI_upper\")]] <- apply(boot_new_preds, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)\n    }\n    if (save_results) {\n      write.csv(results, output_file, row.names = FALSE)\n      if (verbose) message(\"Saved new predictions to: \", output_file)\n    }\n    return(results)\n  }\n  \n  # 11) Reporting (Option C): prefer rmarkdown; fallback to base PDF\n  if (save_report) {\n    # check rmarkdown availability\n    has_rmd <- requireNamespace(\"rmarkdown\", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace(\"knitr\", quietly = TRUE)\n    if (report_format == \"html\") has_rmd <- has_rmd # for html we require rmarkdown\n    if (has_rmd) {\n      # create a temporary Rmd file that embeds key results and saved plots\n      rmd_file <- tempfile(fileext = \".Rmd\")\n      plots_list <- list(\n        training = file.path(plot_dir, paste0(\"training_obs_vs_pred.\", plot_format)),\n        test = file.path(plot_dir, paste0(\"test_obs_vs_pred.\", plot_format)),\n        cv = file.path(plot_dir, paste0(\"cv_obs_vs_pred.\", plot_format)),\n        residuals = file.path(plot_dir, paste0(\"residuals_vs_fitted.\", plot_format)),\n        qq = file.path(plot_dir, paste0(\"qq_plot.\", plot_format))\n      )\n      # Ensure plots exist (they were saved earlier)\n      rmd_text <- c(\n        \"---\",\n        \"title: \\\"Validation report\\\"\",\n        \"output: pdf_document\",\n        \"---\",\n        \"\",\n        \"```{r setup, include=FALSE}\",\n        \"knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE)\",\n        \"library(knitr)\",\n        \"```\",\n        \"\",\n        \"## Model\",\n        \"\",\n        paste0(\"- Formula: `\", deparse(formula), \"`\"),\n        paste0(\"- Equation: `\", model_equation, \"`\"),\n        \"\",\n        \"## Summary table\",\n        \"\",\n        \"```{r summary}\",\n        \"summary_table <- as.data.frame(\", deparse(summary_table), \")\",\n        \"knitr::kable(summary_table)\",\n        \"```\",\n        \"\",\n        \"## Plots\",\n        \"\"\n      )\n      # add lines for each saved plot if present\n      for (nm in names(plots_list)) {\n        path <- plots_list[[nm]]\n        if (file.exists(path)) {\n          rmd_text <- c(rmd_text, paste0(\"### \", nm), \"\", paste0(\"![](\", path, \")\"), \"\")\n        }\n      }\n      # write Rmd and render\n      writeLines(rmd_text, con = rmd_file)\n      out_file <- tryCatch({\n        rmarkdown::render(rmd_file, output_file = report_file, quiet = !verbose)\n      }, error = function(e) {\n        if (verbose) message(\"rmarkdown render failed: \", e$message)\n        return(NULL)\n      })\n      if (!is.null(out_file) && verbose) message(\"Report generated: \", out_file)\n    } else {\n      # fallback: create a multi-page PDF using base device (or PNGs)\n      if (report_format == \"pdf\") {\n        pdf(report_file, width = 8, height = 10)\n        gridExtra::grid.arrange(ggplotGrob(p_train_obs_pred), top = \"Training: Observed vs Predicted\")\n        gridExtra::grid.arrange(ggplotGrob(p_cv_plot), top = paste(\"CV:\", cv_method))\n        gridExtra::grid.arrange(ggplotGrob(p_test_plot), top = \"Test: Observed vs Predicted\")\n        gridExtra::grid.arrange(ggplotGrob(p_res_vs_fit), top = \"Residuals vs Fitted\")\n        gridExtra::grid.arrange(ggplotGrob(p_qq), top = \"Q-Q Plot\")\n        dev.off()\n        if (verbose) message(\"Fallback PDF report saved to: \", report_file)\n      } else {\n        # html fallback: write a simple HTML with embedded PNGs\n        htmlf <- sub(\"\\\\.pdf$\", \".html\", report_file)\n        html_lines <- c(\"<html><body>\",\n                        \"<h1>Validation Report</h1>\",\n                        paste0(\"<p>Formula: \", deparse(formula), \"</p>\"),\n                        paste0(\"<p>Equation: \", model_equation, \"</p>\",\n                               \"<h2>Plots</h2>\"))\n        # embed images\n        imgs <- list.files(plot_dir, pattern = paste0(\"\\\\.\", plot_format, \"$\"), full.names = TRUE)\n        for (img in imgs) {\n          html_lines <- c(html_lines, paste0(\"<img src='\", img, \"' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;'><br>\"))\n        }\n        html_lines <- c(html_lines, \"</body></html>\")\n        writeLines(html_lines, con = htmlf)\n        if (verbose) message(\"Fallback HTML report saved to: \", htmlf)\n      }\n    }\n  } # end save_report\n  \n  # assemble returned result\n  out <- list(\n    model = final_model,\n    equation = model_equation,\n    summary_table = summary_table,\n    Train_R2 = Train_R2,\n    Train_RMSE = Train_RMSE,\n    CV_R2 = CV_R2,\n    CV_RMSEP = CV_RMSEP,\n    Test_R2 = Test_R2,\n    Test_RMSEP = Test_RMSEP,\n    RMSEP_LOOCV = RMSEP_LOOCV,\n    R2_LOOCV = R2_LOOCV,\n    plots = list(\n      train = p_train_obs_pred,\n      cv = p_cv_plot,\n      test = p_test_plot,\n      residuals = p_res_vs_fit,\n      qq = p_qq\n    ),\n    bootstrap = list(\n      iter = boot_iter,\n      seed = boot_seed,\n      train_boot_mean = if (!is.null(boot_train_mean)) boot_train_mean else NULL,\n      train_boot_lwr = if (!is.null(boot_train_lwr)) boot_train_lwr else NULL,\n      train_boot_upr = if (!is.null(boot_train_upr)) boot_train_upr else NULL,\n      test_boot_mean = if (!is.null(boot_test_mean)) boot_test_mean else NULL,\n      test_boot_lwr = if (!is.null(boot_test_lwr)) boot_test_lwr else NULL,\n      test_boot_upr = if (!is.null(boot_test_upr)) boot_test_upr else NULL\n    ),\n    predict_new = predict_new,\n    parameters = list(\n      cv_method = cv_method,\n      k = ifelse(cv_method == \"kfold\", k, NA),\n      train_frac = train_frac,\n      external_test_used = !is.null(external_test),\n      boot_iter = boot_iter\n    )\n  )\n  \n  class(out) <- \"validate_element_pro\"\n  return(out)\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n# Quick notes & tips\n\n- **Boot iterations:** `boot_iter = 200` is a good compromise for testing; use `>=2000` for more stable bootstrap intervals (but it will take much longer).  \n- **RMarkdown:** if you want a polished PDF/HTML report make sure `rmarkdown` + `knitr` are installed. If not, the function will create a neat multi-page PDF using base R and `gridExtra`.  \n- **Saving plots:** set `save_plots = TRUE` u2014 they will be saved to `plot_dir`. The report will reference those saved files.  \n- **Predicting new data:** use `res$predict_new(newdata = Ti_XRF_input, include_boot = TRUE, save_results = TRUE)` to get bootstrap intervals for new inputs and save results automatically.  \n- **Performance:** bootstrap and LOOCV are the most time-consuming bits. Reduce `boot_iter` for quick tests.\n\n---\n\nIf you like, I can also:\n\n- Create a small reproducible demonstration with simulated data to show outputs and the report.  \n- Add functionality to cache bootstrap models to re-use them for multiple `predict_new()` calls (speeds repeated predictions).  \n\nWant a simulated demo run now (with `boot_iter=200` to keep runtime reasonable)?"

              "Great u2014 below is the **complete, ready-to-run R function** that implements **everything** you asked for, with **Option C** for bootstrap CSVs (both summary and full distribution), and saves **individual plots**, **combined summary PDF + CSV**, and **bootstrap PDF + CSVs** into the element-specific folder:\n\n`\"Papers_R/2024_DeVleeschouwer/FigureS6/Data/Output/Validation/<ELEMENT>\"`\n\nKey features implemented:\n- element parameter (e.g. `\"Ti\"`), and `Ti_results` style object can be assigned by the caller\n- train/test split or external test set\n- k-fold CV or LOOCV\n- two-stage WLS (w1, stage2_wt stored)\n- training / CV / test metrics (Ru00b2, RMSE, RMSEP)\n- training/CV/test/diagnostic plots saved individually as PDF\n- combined summary tables saved as one PDF and one CSV\n- bootstrap: saved as combined PDF plots, CSV summary (mean/lwr/upr), CSV distribution (one column per bootstrap iter)\n- predict_new helper attached to results, optionally returns bootstrap predictions for new data\n- report generation: tries rmarkdown, falls back to base PDF\n- robust handling of missing sd column in test data\n- creates directories if needed\n\nCopy/paste the function into your R session and call it as shown in the usage example below.\n\n---\n\n```r\n# Full master function: validate_and_export\n# --------------------------------------------------------\n# Dependencies: ggplot2, gridExtra, utils. rmarkdown/knitr optional.\n# Usage example at end.\n# --------------------------------------------------------\n\nvalidate_and_export <- function(\n  element,                    # string, e.g. \"Ti\"\n  formula,                    # e.g. Ti_ICP ~ Ti\n  data,                       # training/calibration dataset (data.frame)\n  sd_col,                     # string, name of SD column for response, e.g. \"Ti_ICP_sd\"\n  output_base = \"Papers_R/2024_DeVleeschouwer/FigureS6/Data/Output/Validation\",\n  cv_method = c(\"kfold\", \"LOOCV\"),\n  k = 10,\n  train_frac = 0.6,\n  external_test = NULL,\n  boot_iter = 200,            # increase to 2000+ for production\n  boot_seed = 123,\n  save_plots = TRUE,\n  save_summary_pdf = TRUE,\n  save_bootstrap_files = TRUE,\n  report_file = NULL,         # if NULL -> <output_dir>/<element>_Model_Report.pdf\n  report_format = c(\"pdf\", \"html\"),\n  save_individual_plots = TRUE,\n  verbose = TRUE\n) {\n  # --- libs\n  if (!requireNamespace(\"ggplot2\", quietly = TRUE)) stop(\"Install ggplot2 first.\")\n  if (!requireNamespace(\"gridExtra\", quietly = TRUE)) stop(\"Install gridExtra first.\")\n  report_format <- match.arg(report_format)\n  cv_method <- match.arg(cv_method)\n  \n  # Prepare paths\n  output_dir <- file.path(output_base, element)\n  plots_dir  <- file.path(output_dir, \"plots\")\n  tables_dir <- file.path(output_dir, \"tables\")\n  bootstrap_dir <- file.path(output_dir, \"bootstrap\")\n  dirs <- c(output_dir, plots_dir, tables_dir, bootstrap_dir)\n  for (d in dirs) if (!dir.exists(d)) dir.create(d, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)\n  \n  # default report file\n  if (is.null(report_file)) {\n    report_file <- file.path(output_dir, paste0(element, \"_Model_Report.pdf\"))\n  }\n  \n  # helper to optionally print messages\n  msg <- function(...) if (verbose) message(...)\n  \n  # safe model.frame extraction\n  mf_all <- model.frame(formula, data)\n  response_name <- all.vars(formula)[1]\n  predictor_name <- all.vars(formula)[2]\n  \n  # 1) Train/test split or external_test\n  if (!is.null(external_test)) {\n    train_data <- data\n    test_data <- external_test\n  } else {\n    set.seed(123)\n    n <- nrow(data)\n    train_index <- sample(seq_len(n), size = floor(train_frac * n))\n    train_data <- data[train_index, , drop = FALSE]\n    test_data <- data[-train_index, , drop = FALSE]\n  }\n  \n  # internal fit function (two-stage wls)\n  fit_two_stage_wls <- function(form, df, sd_col_name) {\n    df <- as.data.frame(df)\n    if (!(sd_col_name %in% names(df))) stop(paste0(\"sd_col '\", sd_col_name, \"' not found in data frame.\"))\n    df$w1 <- 1 / (df[[sd_col_name]]^2)\n    stage1 <- lm(form, data = df, weights = w1)\n    abs_res <- abs(stage1$residuals)\n    fit_vals <- stage1$fitted.values\n    if (length(abs_res) <= 1) {\n      df$stage2_wt <- rep(1, nrow(df))\n    } else {\n      # if the lm(abs_res ~ fit_vals) fails or returns Inf, have a fallback\n      tmp <- try(lm(abs_res ~ fit_vals), silent = TRUE)\n      if (inherits(tmp, \"try-error\")) {\n        df$stage2_wt <- rep(1, nrow(df))\n      } else {\n        df$stage2_wt <- 1 / fitted(tmp)^2\n        # handle Inf/NAs\n        if (!any(is.finite(df$stage2_wt))) df$stage2_wt <- rep(1, nrow(df))\n        df$stage2_wt[!is.finite(df$stage2_wt)] <- median(df$stage2_wt[is.finite(df$stage2_wt)], na.rm = TRUE)\n      }\n    }\n    final <- lm(form, data = df, weights = stage2_wt)\n    attr(final, \"data_with_weights\") <- df\n    return(final)\n  }\n  \n  # 2) Cross-validation (k-fold or LOOCV) on training set\n  if (cv_method == \"kfold\") {\n    n_train <- nrow(train_data)\n    if (k > n_train) {\n      warning(\"k > n_train; setting k = n_train\")\n      k <- n_train\n    }\n    set.seed(123)\n    folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = n_train))\n    preds_cv <- rep(NA, n_train)\n    rmse_folds <- numeric(k)\n    r2_folds <- numeric(k)\n    for (i in seq_len(k)) {\n      tr <- train_data[folds != i, , drop = FALSE]\n      te <- train_data[folds == i, , drop = FALSE]\n      mod_i <- fit_two_stage_wls(formula, tr, sd_col)\n      p <- predict(mod_i, newdata = te)\n      obs <- model.response(model.frame(formula, te))\n      preds_cv[which(folds == i)] <- p\n      rmse_folds[i] <- sqrt(mean((obs - p)^2))\n      SSE <- sum((obs - p)^2)\n      SST <- sum((obs - mean(obs))^2)\n      r2_folds[i] <- ifelse(SST == 0, NA, 1 - SSE/SST)\n    }\n    CV_RMSEP <- mean(rmse_folds, na.rm = TRUE)\n    CV_R2 <- mean(r2_folds, na.rm = TRUE)\n    train_data$cv_pred <- preds_cv\n  } else {\n    n_train <- nrow(train_data)\n    preds_loo <- numeric(n_train)\n    for (i in seq_len(n_train)) {\n      tr <- train_data[-i, , drop = FALSE]\n      te <- train_data[i, , drop = FALSE]\n      mod_i <- fit_two_stage_wls(formula, tr, sd_col)\n      preds_loo[i] <- predict(mod_i, newdata = te)\n    }\n    obs_train <- model.response(model.frame(formula, train_data))\n    CV_RMSEP <- sqrt(mean((obs_train - preds_loo)^2))\n    SSE_cv <- sum((obs_train - preds_loo)^2)\n    SST_cv <- sum((obs_train - mean(obs_train))^2)\n    CV_R2 <- ifelse(SST_cv == 0, NA, 1 - SSE_cv / SST_cv)\n    train_data$cv_pred <- preds_loo\n  }\n  \n  # 3) Final model on training set\n  final_model <- fit_two_stage_wls(formula, train_data, sd_col)\n  train_pred_mat <- predict(final_model, newdata = train_data, interval = \"prediction\")\n  train_obs <- model.response(model.frame(formula, train_data))\n  Train_RMSE <- sqrt(mean((train_obs - train_pred_mat[,1])^2))\n  SSE_train <- sum((train_obs - train_pred_mat[,1])^2)\n  SST_train <- sum((train_obs - mean(train_obs))^2)\n  Train_R2 <- ifelse(SST_train == 0, NA, 1 - SSE_train/SST_train)\n  \n  # 4) Test predictions\n  test_pred_mat <- predict(final_model, newdata = test_data, interval = \"prediction\")\n  test_pred <- test_pred_mat[,1]\n  if (response_name %in% names(test_data)) {\n    test_obs <- model.response(model.frame(formula, test_data))\n    Test_RMSEP <- sqrt(mean((test_obs - test_pred)^2))\n    SSE_test <- sum((test_obs - test_pred)^2)\n    SST_test <- sum((test_obs - mean(test_obs))^2)\n    Test_R2 <- ifelse(SST_test == 0, NA, 1 - SSE_test / SST_test)\n  } else {\n    test_obs <- rep(NA, length(test_pred))\n    Test_RMSEP <- NA\n    Test_R2 <- NA\n  }\n  \n  # 5) LOOCV on full dataset for RMSEP_full & R2_LOOCV\n  n_total <- nrow(data)\n  pred_LOO_full <- numeric(n_total)\n  for (i in seq_len(n_total)) {\n    tr <- data[-i, , drop = FALSE]\n    te <- data[i, , drop = FALSE]\n    mod_i <- fit_two_stage_wls(formula, tr, sd_col)\n    pred_LOO_full[i] <- predict(mod_i, newdata = te)\n  }\n  full_obs <- model.response(model.frame(formula, data))\n  RMSEP_LOOCV <- sqrt(mean((full_obs - pred_LOO_full)^2))\n  SSE_loocv <- sum((full_obs - pred_LOO_full)^2)\n  SST_loocv <- sum((full_obs - mean(full_obs))^2)\n  R2_LOOCV <- ifelse(SST_loocv == 0, NA, 1 - SSE_loocv/SST_loocv)\n  \n  # 6) Model equation text\n  coefs <- coef(final_model)\n  if (length(coefs) >= 2) {\n    intercept <- round(coefs[1], 6)\n    slope <- round(coefs[2], 6)\n    model_equation <- paste0(response_name, \" = \", intercept, \" + \", slope, \" * \", predictor_name)\n  } else {\n    model_equation <- paste0(response_name, \" = \", paste(round(coefs,6), collapse = \" + \"))\n  }\n  \n  # 7) Plots: training, CV, test, residuals, QQ\n  library(ggplot2)\n  library(gridExtra)\n  # training plot\n  df_train_plot <- data.frame(obs = train_obs, pred = train_pred_mat[,1], lwr = train_pred_mat[,2], upr = train_pred_mat[,3])\n  p_train <- ggplot(df_train_plot, aes(x = obs, y = pred)) +\n    geom_point(color = \"blue\") +\n    geom_smooth(method = \"loess\", se = TRUE) +\n    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), alpha = 0.15) +\n    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = \"dashed\") +\n    labs(title = paste0(element, \" Training: Observed vs Predicted\"), x = \"Observed\", y = \"Predicted\") + theme_bw()\n  if (save_individual_plots) {\n    pdf(file.path(plots_dir, paste0(element, \"_training_plot.pdf\")), width = 7, height = 6)\n    print(p_train); dev.off()\n    msg(\"Saved:\", file.path(plots_dir, paste0(element, \"_training_plot.pdf\")))\n  }\n  \n  # CV plot\n  if (\"cv_pred\" %in% names(train_data)) {\n    df_cv_plot <- data.frame(obs = model.response(model.frame(formula, train_data)), pred = train_data$cv_pred)\n  } else {\n    df_cv_plot <- df_train_plot\n  }\n  p_cv <- ggplot(df_cv_plot, aes(x = obs, y = pred)) +\n    geom_point(color = \"red\") +\n    geom_smooth(method = \"loess\", se = TRUE) +\n    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = \"dashed\") +\n    labs(title = paste0(element, \" CV: Observed vs Predicted\"), x = \"Observed\", y = \"Predicted\") + theme_bw()\n  if (save_individual_plots) {\n    pdf(file.path(plots_dir, paste0(element, \"_cv_plot.pdf\")), width = 7, height = 6)\n    print(p_cv); dev.off()\n    msg(\"Saved:\", file.path(plots_dir, paste0(element, \"_cv_plot.pdf\")))\n  }\n  \n  # test plot\n  df_test_plot <- data.frame(obs = test_obs, pred = test_pred, lwr = test_pred_mat[,2], upr = test_pred_mat[,3])\n  p_test <- ggplot(df_test_plot, aes(x = obs, y = pred)) +\n    geom_point(color = \"darkgreen\") +\n    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), alpha = 0.12) +\n    geom_smooth(method = \"loess\", se = TRUE) +\n    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = \"dashed\") +\n    labs(title = paste0(element, \" Test: Observed vs Predicted\"), x = \"Observed\", y = \"Predicted\") + theme_bw()\n  if (save_individual_plots) {\n    pdf(file.path(plots_dir, paste0(element, \"_test_plot.pdf\")), width = 7, height = 6)\n    print(p_test); dev.off()\n    msg(\"Saved:\", file.path(plots_dir, paste0(element, \"_test_plot.pdf\")))\n  }\n  \n  # residuals vs fitted + bands and QQ\n  final_df <- attr(final_model, \"data_with_weights\")\n  final_pred <- aes(x = fitted, y = residuals)) +\n    geom_point() +\n    geom_smooth(method = \"loess\", se = TRUE) +\n    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = \"dashed\") +\n    labs(title = paste0(element, \" Residuals vs Fitted (LOESS)\"), x = \"Fitted\", y = \"Residuals\") + theme_bw()\n  if (save_individual_plots) {\n    pdf(file.path(plots_dir, paste0(element, \"_residuals_vs_fitted.pdf\")), width = 7, <- p_res_fit + geom_hline(yintercept = c(2*resid_sd, -2*resid_sd), linetype = \"dotdash\", color = \"red\")\n  if (save_individual_plots) {\n    pdf(file.path(plots_dir, paste0(element, write.csv(boot_sum_df, file.path(bootstrap_dir, paste0(element, \"_BootstrapTrainSummary.csv\")), row.names = FALSE)\n      msg(\"Saved:\", file.path(bootstrap_dir, paste0(element, \"_BootstrapTrainSummary.csv\")))\n      # Distribution CSV (wide)\n      boot_train_df_wide <- data.frame(id = seq_len(n_train), boot_train_matrix)\n      names(boot_train_df_wide) <- c(\"id\", msg(\"Saved:\", file.path(bootstrap_dir, paste0(element, \"_BootstrapTrainDistribution.csv\")))\n      \n      # Test bootstrap CSVs\n      boot_test_sum_df <- data.frame(\n        id =               "use linear regression models in plots only in this and reproduce the whole revised code # Full master function: validate_and_export\n# --------------------------------------------------------\n# Dependencies: ggplot2, gridExtra, utils. rmarkdown/knitr optional.\n# Usage example at end.\n# --------------------------------------------------------\n\nvalidate_and_export <- function(\n  element,                    # string, e.g. \"Ti\"\n  formula,                    # e.g. Ti_ICP ~ Ti\n  data,                       # training/calibration dataset (data.frame)\n  sd_col,                     # string, name of SD column for response, e.g. \"Ti_ICP_sd\"\n  output_base = \"Papers_R/2024_DeVleeschouwer/FigureS6/Data/Output/Validation\",\n  cv_method = c(\"kfold\", \"LOOCV\"),\n  k = 10,\n  train_frac = 0.6,\n  external_test = NULL,\n  boot_iter = 200,            # increase to 2000+ for production\n  boot_seed = 123,\n  save_plots = TRUE,\n  save_summary_pdf = TRUE,\n  save_bootstrap_files = TRUE,\n  report_file = NULL,         # if NULL -> <output_dir>/<element>_Model_Report.pdf\n  report_format = c(\"pdf\", \"html\"),\n  save_individual_plots = TRUE,\n  verbose = TRUE\n) {\n  # --- libs\n  if (!requireNamespace(\"ggplot2\", quietly = TRUE)) stop(\"Install ggplot2 first.\")\n  if (!requireNamespace(\"gridExtra\", quietly = TRUE)) stop(\"Install gridExtra first.\")\n  report_format <- match.arg(report_format)\n  cv_method <- match.arg(cv_method)\n  \n  # Prepare paths\n  output_dir <- file.path(output_base, element)\n  plots_dir  <- file.path(output_dir, \"plots\")\n  tables_dir <- file.path(output_dir, \"tables\")\n  bootstrap_dir <- file.path(output_dir, \"bootstrap\")\n  dirs <- c(output_dir, plots_dir, tables_dir, bootstrap_dir)\n  for (d in dirs) if (!dir.exists(d)) dir.create(d, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)\n  \n  # default report file\n  if (is.null(report_file)) {\n    report_file <- file.path(output_dir, paste0(element, \"_Model_Report.pdf\"))\n  }\n  \n  # helper to optionally print messages\n  msg <- function(...) if (verbose) message(...)\n  \n  # safe model.frame extraction\n  mf_all <- model.frame(formula, data)\n  response_name <- all.vars(formula)[1]\n  predictor_name <- all.vars(formula)[2]\n  \n  # 1) Train/test split or external_test\n  if (!is.null(external_test)) {\n    train_data <- data\n    test_data <- external_test\n  } else {\n    set.seed(123)\n    n <- nrow(data)\n    train_index <- sample(seq_len(n), size = floor(train_frac * n))\n    train_data <- data[train_index, , drop = FALSE]\n    test_data <- data[-train_index, , drop = FALSE]\n  }\n  \n  # internal fit function (two-stage wls)\n  fit_two_stage_wls <- function(form, df, sd_col_name) {\n    df <- as.data.frame(df)\n    if (!(sd_col_name %in% names(df))) stop(paste0(\"sd_col '\", sd_col_name, \"' not found in data frame.\"))\n    df$w1 <- 1 / (df[[sd_col_name]]^2)\n    stage1 <- lm(form, data = df, weights = w1)\n    abs_res <- abs(stage1$residuals)\n    fit_vals <- stage1$fitted.values\n    if (length(abs_res) <= 1) {\n      df$stage2_wt <- rep(1, nrow(df))\n    } else {\n      # if the lm(abs_res ~ fit_vals) fails or returns Inf, have a fallback\n      tmp <- try(lm(abs_res ~ fit_vals), silent = TRUE)\n      if (inherits(tmp, \"try-error\")) {\n        df$stage2_wt <- rep(1, nrow(df))\n      } else {\n        df$stage2_wt <- 1 / fitted(tmp)^2\n        # handle Inf/NAs\n        if (!any(is.finite(df$stage2_wt))) df$stage2_wt <- rep(1, nrow(df))\n        df$stage2_wt[!is.finite(df$stage2_wt)] <- median(df$stage2_wt[is.finite(df$stage2_wt)], na.rm = TRUE)\n      }\n    }\n    final <- lm(form, data = df, weights = stage2_wt)\n    attr(final, \"data_with_weights\") <- df\n    return(final)\n  }\n  \n  # 2) Cross-validation (k-fold or LOOCV) on training set\n  if (cv_method == \"kfold\") {\n    n_train <- nrow(train_data)\n    if (k > n_train) {\n      warning(\"k > n_train; setting k = n_train\")\n      k <- n_train\n    }\n    set.seed(123)\n    folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = n_train))\n    preds_cv <- rep(NA, n_train)\n    rmse_folds <- numeric(k)\n    r2_folds <- numeric(k)\n    for (i in seq_len(k)) {\n      tr <- train_data[folds != i, , drop = FALSE]\n      te <- train_data[folds == i, , drop = FALSE]\n      mod_i <- fit_two_stage_wls(formula, tr, sd_col)\n      p <- predict(mod_i, newdata = te)\n      obs <- model.response(model.frame(formula, te))\n      preds_cv[which(folds == i)] <- p\n      rmse_folds[i] <- sqrt(mean((obs - p)^2))\n      SSE <- sum((obs - p)^2)\n      SST <- sum((obs - mean(obs))^2)\n      r2_folds[i] <- ifelse(SST == 0, NA, 1 - SSE/SST)\n    }\n    CV_RMSEP <- mean(rmse_folds, na.rm = TRUE)\n    CV_R2 <- mean(r2_folds, na.rm = TRUE)\n    train_data$cv_pred <- preds_cv\n  } else {\n    n_train <- nrow(train_data)\n    preds_loo <- numeric(n_train)\n    for (i in seq_len(n_train)) {\n      tr <- train_data[-i, , drop = FALSE]\n      te <- train_data[i, , drop = FALSE]\n      mod_i <- fit_two_stage_wls(formula, tr, sd_col)\n      preds_loo[i] <- predict(mod_i, newdata = te)\n    }\n    obs_train <- model.response(model.frame(formula, train_data))\n    CV_RMSEP <- sqrt(mean((obs_train - preds_loo)^2))\n    SSE_cv <- sum((obs_train - preds_loo)^2)\n    SST_cv <- sum((obs_train - mean(obs_train))^2)\n    CV_R2 <- ifelse(SST_cv == 0, NA, 1 - SSE_cv / SST_cv)\n    train_data$cv_pred <- preds_loo\n  }\n  \n  # 3) Final model on training set\n  final_model <- fit_two_stage_wls(formula, train_data, sd_col)\n  train_pred_mat <- predict(final_model, newdata = train_data, interval = \"prediction\")\n  train_obs <- model.response(model.frame(formula, train_data))\n  Train_RMSE <- sqrt(mean((train_obs - train_pred_mat[,1])^2))\n  SSE_train <- sum((train_obs - train_pred_mat[,1])^2)\n  SST_train <- sum((train_obs - mean(train_obs))^2)\n  Train_R2 <- ifelse(SST_train == 0, NA, 1 - SSE_train/SST_train)\n  \n  # 4) Test predictions\n  test_pred_mat <- predict(final_model, newdata = test_data, interval = \"prediction\")\n  test_pred <- test_pred_mat[,1]\n  if (response_name %in% names(test_data)) {\n    test_obs <- model.response(model.frame(formula, test_data))\n    Test_RMSEP <- sqrt(mean((test_obs - test_pred)^2))\n    SSE_test <- sum((test_obs - test_pred)^2)\n    SST_test <- sum((test_obs - mean(test_obs))^2)\n    Test_R2 <- ifelse(SST_test == 0, NA, 1 - SSE_test / SST_test)\n  } else {\n    test_obs <- rep(NA, length(test_pred))\n    Test_RMSEP <- NA\n    Test_R2 <- NA\n  }\n  \n  # 5) LOOCV on full dataset for RMSEP_full & R2_LOOCV\n  n_total <- nrow(data)\n  pred_LOO_full <- numeric(n_total)\n  for (i in seq_len(n_total)) {\n    tr <- data[-i, , drop = FALSE]\n    te <- data[i, , drop = FALSE]\n    mod_i <- fit_two_stage_wls(formula, tr, sd_col)\n    pred_LOO_full[i] <- predict(mod_i, newdata = te)\n  }\n  full_obs <- model.response(model.frame(formula, data))\n  RMSEP_LOOCV <- sqrt(mean((full_obs - pred_LOO_full)^2))\n  SSE_loocv <- sum((full_obs - pred_LOO_full)^2)\n  SST_loocv <- sum((full_obs - mean(full_obs))^2)\n  R2_LOOCV <- ifelse(SST_loocv == 0, NA, 1 - SSE_loocv/SST_loocv)\n  \n  # 6) Model equation text\n  coefs <- coef(final_model)\n  if (length(coefs) >= 2) {\n    intercept <- round(coefs[1], 6)\n    slope <- round(coefs[2], 6)\n    model_equation <- paste0(response_name, \" = \", intercept, \" + \", slope, \" * \", predictor_name)\n  } else {\n    model_equation <- paste0(response_name, \" = \", paste(round(coefs,6), collapse = \" + \"))\n  }\n  \n  # 8) Bootstrap: produce train/test bootstrap distributions & summary\n  boot_train_mean <- boot_train_lwr <- boot_train_upr <- NULL\n  boot_test_mean <- boot_test_lwr <- boot_test_upr <- NULL\n  boot_train_matrix <- boot_test_matrix <- NULL\n  boot_test_rmsep <- NA\n  if (!is.null(boot_iter) && boot_iter > 0) {\n    set.seed(boot_seed)\n    n_train <- nrow(train_data)\n    n_test <- nrow(test_data)\n    boot_train_matrix <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_train, ncol = boot_iter)\n    boot_test_matrix  <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_test,  ncol = boot_iter)\n    msg(\"Starting bootstrap (\", boot_iter, \" iterations)...\")\n    for (b in seq_len(boot_iter)) {\n      idx <- sample(seq_len(n_train), replace = TRUE)\n      boot_tr <- train_data[idx, , drop = FALSE]\n      mod_b <- tryCatch(fit_two_stage_wls(formula, boot_tr, sd_col), error = function(e) NULL)\n      if (!is.null(mod_b)) {\n        boot_train_matrix[,b] <- predict(mod_b, newdata = train_data)\n        boot_test_matrix[,b]  <- predict(mod_b, newdata = test_data)\n      } else {\n        boot_train_matrix[,b] <- NA\n        boot_test_matrix[,b]  <- NA\n      }\n    }\n    # 10) Attach predict_new helper (with bootstrap option to regenerate boot predictions if requested)\n  predict_new <- function(newdata, predictor_col = NULL, unit = NULL, save_results = FALSE, output_csv = NULL, include_boot = FALSE, boot_iter_local = boot_iter) {\n    if (is.null(predictor_col)) predictor_col <- predictor_name\n    if (!predictor_col %in% names(newdata)) stop(\"predictor_col not found in newdata\")\n    preds_mat <- predict(final_model, newdata = newdata, interval = \"prediction\")\n    results <- data.frame(XRF_input = newdata[[predictor_col]], Predicted = preds_mat[,1], PI_lower = preds_mat[,2], PI_upper = preds_mat[,3])\n    names(results)[2:4] <- paste0(response_name, c(\"_pred\",\"_PI_lower\",\"_PI_upper\"))\n    if (!is.null(unit)) attr(results, \"units\") <- unit\n    attr(results, \"model_equation\") <- model_equation\n    attr(results, \"cv_method\") <- cv_method\n    attr(results, \"k\") <- ifelse(cv_method == \"kfold\", k, NA)\n    # Linear model prediction on ORIGINAL (log) scale ---\n  pred_mat <- predict(final_model,\n                      newdata = newdata,\n                      interval = \"prediction\")\n\n  # extract fitted and PI bounds on log scale\n  log_fit <- pred_mat[, \"fit\"]\n  log_lwr <- pred_mat[, \"lwr\"]\n  log_upr <- pred_mat[, \"upr\"]\n\n  # --- 2. `sd_col` u2192 analytical uncertainty (used as weights)\n- `train_frac` u2192 proportion of data for training (default 60%)\n- `k` u2192 number of CV folds (default 10)\n- `boot_iter` u2192 number of bootstrap iterations\n- `output_dir` u2192 where to save everything\n\nThe function then:\n\n- Creates a directory:  \n  ```\n  /Validation/<element>/\n  ```\n- Creates subfolders:\n  ```\n  plots/\n  bootstrap/\n  tables/\n  ```\n- Extracts predictor & response names from the formula.\n\n---\n\n## **2ufe0fu20e3 Model Fitting u2014 *Two-Stage Weighted Least Squares***\n\nThe calibration uses a **two-stage WLS regression**:\n\n### Stage 1  \nWeights = **1 / SDu00b2**  \nFits the initial model.\n\n### Stage 2  \nModels |residuals| vs fitted values  \nComputes new weights = **1 / (predicted residual variance)u00b2**  \nRefits the final model using these refined weights.\n\nThis method accounts for **heteroscedasticity** and gives a better calibration.\n\n---\n\n## **3ufe0fu20e3 Cross-Validation (CV)**\n\nThe function performs **k-fold CV** on the TRAIN dataset only:\n\nFor each fold:\n\n1. Fit the 2-stage WLS model  \n2. Predict the held-out fold  \n3. Compute:  \n   - Root Mean Squared Error of Prediction (RMSEP)  \n   - Ru00b2 (predictive)\n\nThe function returns:\n\n- **CV_RMSEP** (average)  \n- **CV_R2**  \n- A scatterplot of OBS vs PRED (with linear trendline)\n\n---\n\n## **4ufe0fu20e3 Test-Set Validation**\n\nUses the withheld TEST data.\n\nComputes:\n\n- **Test_RMSEP**  \n- **Test_R2**\n\nProduces a **Test Observed vs Predicted plot** with:\n\n- Linear regression smooth  \n- Prediction interval ribbon  \n\n---\n\n## **5ufe0fu20e3 LOOCV (Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation)**\n\nPerformed on the **full dataset**.\n\nComputes:\n\n- **LOOCV_RMSEP**  \n- **LOOCV_R2**\n\nThis gives an unbiased estimate of predictive power.\n\n---\n\n## **6ufe0fu20e3 Diagnostic Plots**\n\nThe function generates:\n\n### u2714 Training Observed vs Predicted (with PI)\n### u2714 CV Observed vs Predicted  \n### u2714 Test Observed vs Predicted (with PI)\n### u2714 Residuals vs Fitted (LM smooth, u00b12SD lines)\n### u2714 Qu2013Q plot of residuals\n\nAll plots:\n\n- Printed on **screen**\n- Saved to **PDFs** in the elementu2019s `/plots/` folder\n\n---\n\n## **7ufe0fu20e3 Prediction Intervals**\n\nUsing:\n\n```r\npredict(final_model, interval = \"prediction\")\n```\n\nThe function adds PI ribbons onto plots.\n\n---\n\n## **8ufe0fu20e3 Summary Table**\n\nCreates a summary table containing:\n\n| Metric | Description |\n|--------|-------------|\n| Train_R2 | Fit quality on training data |\n| Train_RMSE | RMSE on training data |\n| CV_R2 | Cross-validated predictive Ru00b2 |\n| CV_RMSEP | Cross-validated RMSEP |\n| Test_R2 | Test-set predictive Ru00b2 |\n| Test_RMSEP | Test-set RMSEP |\n| LOOCV_R2 | Leave-one-out CV Ru00b2 |\n| LOOCV_RMSEP | Leave-one-out RMSEP |\n\nSaved as:\n\n- `<element>_SummaryTable.csv`\n- `<element>_SummaryTable.pdf`\n\n---\n\n## **9ufe0fu20e3 Bootstrap Uncertainty Analysis**\n\nRuns `boot_iter` bootstrap samples (default = 500):\n\nEach iteration:\n\n1. Resamples the training data  \n2. Refits the full 2-stage WLS model  \n3. Predicts training + test data  \n4. Stores prediction distributions  \n\nComputes:\n\n- Mean bootstrapped prediction  \n- 95% bootstrap confidence intervals  \n- Bootstrapped RMSEP  \n- Uncertainty plots for training + test\n\nExports:\n\n### ud83dudcc4 Bootstrapped RMSEP PDF:  \n```\nbootstrap/<element>_Bootstrap_RMSEP.pdf\n```\n\n### ud83dudcca RMSEP CSV:  \n```\nbootstrap/<element>_Bootstrap_RMSEP.csv\n```\n\n### ud83dudcc4 Bootstrapped predictions:\n- Summary CSV  \n- Full bootstrap matrix CSV  \n\n### ud83dudcc8 Bootstrap plots:\nSaved to `bootstrap/`.\n\n---\n\n## **ud83dudd1f Combined Validation Report (Multi-page PDF)**\n\nCreates:\n\n```\n<element>_Validation_Report.pdf\n```\n\nPages include:\n\n1. Summary table  \n2. Training plot  \n3. CV plot  \n4. Test plot  \n5. Residuals vs fitted  \n6. QQ plot  \n7. Bootstrap plots  \n\nIf RMarkdown is available u2192 beautiful PDF report.  \nIf not u2192 simple multi-page PDF fallback.\n\n---\n\n## **1ufe0fu20e31ufe0fu20e3 Prediction Function for New Input Data**\n\nYou can run:\n\n```r\nTi_preds <- Ti_results$predict_new(Ti_XRF_input)\n```\n\nIt returns:\n\n### u2714 log-scale fitted values  \n### u2714 ppm-scale predictions  \n### u2714 ppm-scale prediction intervals  \n### u2714 optional bootstrap uncertainty  \n### u2714 optional CSV export\n\nThe new columns include:\n\n- `Ti_ICP_pred_ppm`\n- `Ti_ICP_ppm_PI_lower`\n- `Ti_ICP_ppm_PI_upper`\n- (optional bootstrap)\n  - `Ti_ICP_boot_mean_ppm`\n  - `Ti_ICP_boot_lwr_ppm`\n  - `Ti_ICP_boot_upr_ppm`\n\n---\n\n# u2b50 FINAL RESULT: WHAT THE FUNCTION PRODUCES\n\nInside:\n\n```\nValidation/Ti/\n```\n\nYou get:\n\n## ud83dudcc1 `/plots/`\n- Training plot\n- CV plot\n- Test plot\n- Residuals vs fitted\n- Residuals u00b12SD\n- QQ plot\n\n## ud83dudcc1 `/bootstrap/`\n- Bootstrap RMSEP PDF\n- Bootstrap RMSEP CSV\n- Bootstrap prediction summary files\n- Bootstrap distribution matrices\n\n## ud83dudcc1 `/tables/`\n- Summary table PDF  \n- Summary table CSV  \n- Model coefficients CSV  \n\n## ud83dudcc4 Main validation report:\n```\nTi_Validation_Report.pdf\n```\n\n## ud83dudd2e Prediction helper\n`Ti_results$predict_new()`  \nreturns ppm predictions for new XRF data.\n\n## ud83dudce6 Return object\nIncludes:\n\n- model  \n- Ru00b2 and RMSEP metrics  \n- plots  \n- bootstrap intervals  \n- prediction function  \n- directories used  \n\n---\n\n# ud83cudf89 In summary\n\nThe function is a **complete calibration-validation-uncertainty pipeline**, producing:\n\n- A validated WLS model  \n- Cross-validation metrics  \n- Test set performance  \n- LOOCV performance  \n- Diagnostic plots  \n- Bootstrap uncertainty  \n- Multi-page report  \n- Prediction tool for new XRF samples (in ppm with PIs)  \n\nIt's publication-ready and accepts any element as input.\n\n---\n\nIf you'd like, I can also:\n\n### ud83dudd27 Make a wrapper to run **all elements automatically**  \n### ud83dudcca Add biasu2013variance decomposition  \n### ud83dudcc9 Add Blandu2013Altman plots  \n### u2728 Add interactive HTML reports  \n\nWould you like any of those?"

              "In Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression you commonly encounter **two different Ru00b2 values**, and the distinction can be confusing. Here is the clear difference:\n\n---\n\n# u2705 **1. Ru00b2 (Explained Variance on the Training Data)**\n\nThis is the **in-sample Ru00b2** computed directly from the PLS model on the same data used to fit it.\n\n- Measures how well the PLS components explain the variance of **Y** *during training*.\n- Often reported per component (u201cRu00b2Y(cum)u201d in SIMCA/Unscrambler, etc.).\n- It tends to **increase as more components are added** (can overestimate performance).\n- Formula:  \n  \\[\n  R^2 = 1 - \\frac{\\sum (y_i - \\hat{y}_i)^2}{\\sum (y_i - \\bar{y})^2}\n  \\]\n\nThis Ru00b2 evaluates **model fit**, not predictive ability.\n\n---\n\n# u2705 **2. Ru00b2 of Predictions (Ru00b2pred, Qu00b2, or External Prediction Ru00b2)**\n\nThis is **out-of-sample Ru00b2**, calculated using predictions on data **not used to fit the model**:\n\n### Two common cases:\n### **a) Cross-Validation Ru00b2 (often called Qu00b2)**\n- Predicted values come from **cross-validation folds**.\n- Measures predictive performance on unseen data.\n- Typically **lower** than training Ru00b2.\n- Used to assess whether adding components improves prediction.\n\n### **b) External Test Set Ru00b2**\n- Predictions on a separate test set.\n- Gold standard for model predictive power.\n\nFormula is the same as above but using **predicted values for unseen data**:\n\\[\nR^2_{\\text{pred}} = 1 - \\frac{\\sum (y_i - \\hat{y}_{i,\\text{pred}})^2}{\\sum (y_i - \\bar{y})^2}\n\\]\n\nThis Ru00b2 evaluates **true predictive performance**, not training fit.\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudccc **Why they differ**\n\n| Metric | Data used | What it measures | Typical magnitude |\n|-------|-----------|------------------|-------------------|\n| **Ru00b2** | Training data | How well model fits training data | Higher |\n| **Ru00b2pred** (Qu00b2 or external Ru00b2) | Unseen data (CV/test set) | Predictive accuracy | Lower |\n\nPLS can overfit if too many components are used. Training Ru00b2 may remain high, while Ru00b2pred dropsu2014indicating poor generalization.\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudccc Example difference in practice\n\n| #Components | Ru00b2 (train) | Qu00b2 / Ru00b2pred |\n|------------|------------|-------------|\n| 1 | 0.72 | 0.68 |\n| 2 | 0.88 | 0.74 |\n| 8 | 0.99 | 0.10 u2190 overfitting |\n\n---\n\n# u2714ufe0f Summary\n\n**Ru00b2 = how well the model fits the training data**  \n**Ru00b2pred = how well the model predicts new/unseen data**  \n\nBoth are useful, but **Ru00b2pred is what determines real performance**.\n\n---\n\nIf you want, I can also show you how to compute both (in R or Python), or help interpret your specific PLS output."
            ]

              "**Leverage** and **Cooku2019s Distance** are both diagnostic measures used in regression analysis to understand how individual data points influence the fitted model.\n\n---\n\n## **Leverage**\n**What it shows:**  \nHow unusual a data pointu2019s **predictor (X) values** are compared to the rest of the dataset.\n\n**Key ideas:**\n- Points with high leverage have extreme or outlying X-values.\n- High leverage points *pull* the regression line toward themselves.\n- A point can have high leverage without being a bad pointu2014it simply has the *potential* to strongly influence the model.\n\n**Interpretation:**\n- Leverage values range from 0 to 1.\n- A common rule of thumb:  \n  High leverage if  \n  \\[\n  h_i > \\frac{2p}{n}\n  \\]  \n  where \\( p \\) = number of parameters, \\( n \\) = sample size.\n\n---\n\n## **Cooku2019s Distance**\n**What it shows:**  \nHow much a data point *actually influences* the estimated regression coefficients when it is removed.\n\n**Key ideas:**\n- Combines both **leverage** (unusual X) and **residual size** (unusual Y).\n- A large Cooku2019s distance indicates that removing the point would change the model substantially.\n\n**Interpretation:**\n- Cooku2019s distance values typically small for non-influential points.\n- A common threshold:  \n  \\[\n  D_i > \\frac{4}{n}\n  \\]  \n  suggests an influential point.\n\n---\n\n## **In short**\n- **Leverage** = u201cIs this point unusual in X?u201d  \n- **Cooku2019s Distance** = u201cDoes this point strongly affect the fitted model?u201d  \n- A point needs both unusual X (high leverage) and a large error (large residual) to have a big Cook's distance.\n\n---\n\nIf you'd like, I can show an example with a visualization or explain how to calculate them."
            ]

              "Below is a clean way to **add K-fold cross-validation** to your existing weighted regression workflow in R.\n\nYou have two good options:\n\n---\n\n# u2705 **Option 1 u2014 Add K-fold CV using `caret` (simple + works with weights)**\n\n```r\nlibrary(caret)\n\n# Define cross-validation setup\ntrain_control <- trainControl(\n  method = \"cv\",      # k-fold CV\n  number = 10,        # 10 folds\n  savePredictions = \"final\"\n)\n\n# Fit weighted regression using caret\nACE_cv_model <- train(\n  Dry_mass ~ coh_inc,\n  data = ACE_Subsample_xrf_matched,\n  method = \"lm\",\n  weights = ACE_wt_wt,     # <-- your WLS weights here\n  trControl = train_control,\n  metric = \"RMSE\"\n)\n\nACE_cv_model\n```\n\n### **This gives you:**\n- CV RMSE  \n- CV Ru00b2  \n- Fold-by-fold predictions  \n- Training summary\n\n---\n\n# u2705 **Option 2 u2014 Manual K-fold CV using `boot::cv.glm`**\n\n`cv.glm` handles **weights** correctly if passed in the model input.\n\n```r\nlibrary(boot)\n\n# Fit your weighted model first\nACE_wls_wt <- lm(Dry_mass ~ coh_inc, \n                 data = ACE_Subsample_xrf_matched, \n                 weights = ACE_wt_wt)\n\n# Perform 10-fold cross-validation\nset.seed(123)\nACE_cv <- cv.glm(\n  data = ACE_Subsample_xrf_matched,\n  glmfit = ACE_wls_wt,\n  K = 10\n)\n\nACE_cv$delta   # CV error (raw and adjusted)\n```\n\n### Output:\n- `delta[1]` = raw CV error  \n- `delta[2]` = adjusted CV error (preferred)\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudd27 If you want **LOOCV**\n```r\nACE_loocv <- cv.glm(\n  data = ACE_Subsample_xrf_matched,\n  glmfit = ACE_wls_wt\n)\n\nACE_loocv$delta\n```\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudccc **Where to place this in your script**\n\nHere it is inserted into your workflow:\n\n```r\nACE_model_wt <- lm(Dry_mass ~ coh_inc, data = ACE_Subsample_xrf_matched,\n                   weight = 1/Dry_mass_err^2)\n\nACE_wt_wt <- 1 / lm(abs(ACE_model_wt$residuals) ~ ACE_model_wt$fitted.values)$fitted.values^2\n\nACE_wls_wt <- lm(Dry_mass ~ coh_inc, \n                 data = ACE_Subsample_xrf_matched, \n                 weights = ACE_wt_wt)\n\n# ---- CROSS VALIDATION ----\nlibrary(boot)\n\nset.seed(123)\nACE_cv <- cv.glm(\n  data = ACE_Subsample_xrf_matched,\n  glmfit = ACE_wls_wt,\n  K = 10\n)\n\nprint(ACE_cv$delta)\n\n# ---- MODEL CHECKS ----\nsummary(ACE_wls_wt)\nglance(ACE_wls_wt)\nmodel_performance(ACE_wls_wt)\ncheck_model(ACE_wls_wt)\n\nggsave(\"Papers_R/2024_DeVleeschouwer/FigureS12/Data/Output/OLS_WLS/ACE/DM_WLS_wt_performance.pdf\",\n       height = 30, width = 30, dpi = 600, units = \"cm\")\n```\n\n---\n\n# If you want, I can also:\nu2705 add repeated CV  \nu2705 compute cross-validated AIC  \nu2705 plot CV predicted vs. observed  \nu2705 wrap everything into a reusable function\n\nJust tell me!"

              "To compute the **depth error associated with the depth difference**, you must propagate the uncertainty from the two rows used in the subtraction.\n\n### u2714ufe0f Error propagation for a difference  \nIf  \n```\ndepth_diff = depth_next u2013 depth_current\n```  \nand each depth has an uncertainty (error):  \n```\nerr_current  = depth_err (row i)\nerr_next     = depth_err (row i+1)\n```\n\nThen the **combined uncertainty** (standard error propagation) is:\n\n\\[\n\\text{depth\\_diff\\_err} = \\sqrt{err\\_current^2 + err\\_next^2}\n\\]\n\nThis is standard error propagation for subtraction of two independent measurements.\n\n---\n\n## u2705 R code to compute both depth difference AND its propagated error\n\n```r\nACE_xrf_icpms_matched <- ACE_xrf_icpms_matched %>%\n  arrange(Site, sample) %>%\n  group_by(Site) %>%\n  mutate(\n    depth_next        = lead(depth),\n    depth_next_err    = lead(depth_err),\n\n    depth_next_diff   = depth_next - depth,\n\n    depth_diff_err = sqrt(depth_err^2 + depth_next_err^2)\n  ) %>%\n  ungroup()\n```\n\n### Result columns created\n- **depth_next_diff** = difference between next depth and current\n- **depth_diff_err** = propagated uncertainty  \n- Last row of each Site will have `NA` because there is no next depth.\n\n---\n\n## u2714ufe0f Example with your data\n\n| depth | depth_err | next depth | next depth_err |\n|-------|-----------|------------|----------------|\n| 0.6   | 0.55      | 4.5        | 0.55           |\n\nDepth difference:\n```\n4.5 u2013 0.6 = 3.9\n```\n\nError propagation:\n```\nsqrt(0.55^2 + 0.55^2) = 0.777\n```\n\n---\n\nIf you want the error expressed differently (e.g., relative error, percentages), just tell me!"

              "The **standard error (SE)** is a measure of how precisely a sample statistic (usually the mean) estimates the population value.\n\n### u2705 **Standard Error of the Mean (SEM)**\n\n\\[\nSE = \\frac{s}{\\sqrt{n}}\n\\]\n\nWhere:\n\n- \\( s \\) = sample standard deviation  \n- \\( n \\) = number of observations  \n\n---\n\n### u2714ufe0f In R, if you already have a numeric vector `x`:\n\n```r\nse <- sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(x)))\n```\n\n---\n\n### Alternative formulas depending on context:\n\n#### **1. Standard error of a difference of two values**  \nIf  \n\\[\nz = x - y\n\\]\n\nThen:\n\n\\[\nSE_z = \\sqrt{SE_x^2 + SE_y^2}\n\\]\n\n#### **2. Standard error of a sum**  \n\n\\[\nSE_{x+y} = \\sqrt{SE_x^2 + SE_y^2}\n\\]\n\n#### **3. Standard error of a proportion**  \n\n\\[\nSE_p = \\sqrt{\\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\n\\]\n\n---\n\nIf you tell me **what you want the standard error of** (e.g., accrate_err, thickness, depth differences), I can provide the exact formula and R code for your specific case."

              "In the output of **`psych::describe()`**, two of the columns you seeu2014**`trimmed`** and **`mad`**u2014are **robust statistics** that complement the standard mean and standard deviation. Here's what they mean:\n\n---\n\n### **1. `trimmed`**\n- **Definition:** The **trimmed mean**.\n- **How it is calculated:** Usually the **10% trimmed mean** by default in `psych::describe()`.  \n  - This means it **removes the lowest 10% and highest 10% of values** and then calculates the mean of the remaining 80%.  \n- **Purpose:**  \n  - Reduces the influence of **outliers** on the mean.  \n  - Gives a more **robust central tendency** if the data is skewed or has extreme values.\n\n**Example:**  \n```r\nx = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 100)\nmean(x)         # 22\nmean(x, trim=0.1) # 3 (10% trimmed mean)\n```\n\n---\n\n### **2. `mad`**\n- **Definition:** The **Median Absolute Deviation**.\n- **How it is calculated:**  \n\\[\n\\text{MAD} = \\text{median}(|x_i - \\text{median}(x)|)\n\\]  \n- **Purpose:**  \n  - Measures **spread or variability** like standard deviation but is **robust to outliers**.  \n  - Useful when your data is skewed or contains extreme values.  \n- Often used in robust statistics instead of `sd`.\n\n**Example:**  \n```r\nx = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 100)\nmad(x)   # 1.4826  (after default scaling factor)\nsd(x)    # 43.2   (very sensitive to outlier)\n```\n\n---\n\n### **Summary Table of Key Stats in `psych::describe()`**\n\n| Column    | Meaning |\n|-----------|---------|\n| mean      | Arithmetic mean |\n| sd        | Standard deviation |\n| trimmed   | 10% trimmed mean (robust to outliers) |\n| mad       | Median absolute deviation (robust spread measure) |\n| min / max | Minimum / maximum |\n| range     | max - min |\n| median    | Median |\n| skew      | Skewness (asymmetry) |\n| kurtosis  | Kurtosis (tailedness) |\n| se        | Standard error of the mean |\n| Q0.25 / Q0.75 | 25th / 75th percentile (1st and 3rd quartiles) |\n\n---\n\nIf you want, I can **highlight which of these stats are recommended for skewed sedimentary datasets like DMAR or C_org_pc** to make your reporting more robust."

              "**Skewness** is a statistical measure of the **asymmetry of a data distribution** around its mean. It tells you whether your data is **balanced**, **leaning left**, or **leaning right**.\n\n---\n\n### **1. Definition**\nFor a dataset \\(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n\\) with mean \\(\\bar{x}\\) and standard deviation \\(s\\), the **sample skewness** is often calculated as:\n\n\\[\n\\text{Skewness} = \\frac{n}{(n-1)(n-2)} \\sum_{i=1}^{n} \\left(\\frac{x_i - \\bar{x}}{s}\\right)^3\n\\]\n\n---\n\n### **2. Interpretation**\n\n| Skewness Value | Shape of Distribution |\n|----------------|--------------------|\n| u2248 0            | Symmetric (normal-like) |\n| < 0            | Left-skewed / negative skew (long tail on the left) |\n| > 0            | Right-skewed / positive skew (long tail on the right) |\n\n- **Positive skew:** Most data points are **smaller**, with a few very **large values** stretching the tail to the right.\n- **Negative skew:** Most data points are **larger**, with a few very **small values** stretching the tail to the left.\n\n---\n\n### **3. Use in `psych::describe()`**\n\n- `skew` column reports the **sample skewness** for each variable.  \n- Helps **detect asymmetry** in your data before using statistical tests or reporting summary statistics.  \n- For example, DMAR or C_org_pc data often have **positive skew** because most values are small, with a few large accumulation rates.\n\n---\n\n### **4. Quick R example**\n\n```r\nx <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 10)\npsych::describe(x)$skew\n# Output: 1.603 (positively skewed)\n```\n\n- The distribution has a **long right tail**.\n\n---\n\nSkewness is especially important in **sediment or environmental datasets**, where data are often **non-normal**, so median, trimmed mean, and MAD are useful alongside skew to describe distributions robustly.  \n\nIf you want, I can explain **how skewness affects which statistics (mean, median, DMAR) to report** for your sediment cores."
            ]

            "parts": [
              "**Kurtosis** is a statistical measure that describes the **u201ctailednessu201d or peakedness** of a data distribution. It tells you how heavy or light the tails of your distribution are compared to a normal distribution.\n\n---\n\n### **1. Definition**\n\nFor a dataset \\(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n\\) with mean \\(\\bar{x}\\) and standard deviation \\(s\\), the sample kurtosis is often calculated as:\n\n\\[\n\\text{Kurtosis} = \\frac{n(n+1)}{(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)} \\sum_{i=1}^{n} \\left(\\frac{x_i - \\bar{x}}{s}\\right)^4 - \\frac{3(n-1)^2}{(n-2)(n-3)}\n\\]\n\n- The subtraction of 3 makes the **kurtosis of a normal distribution = 0**. This is called **excess kurtosis**.\n\n---\n\n### **2. Interpretation**\n\n| Kurtosis Value | Shape of Distribution |\n|----------------|--------------------|\n| u2248 0            | Mesokurtic u2013 similar to normal distribution |\n| > 0            | Leptokurtic u2013 sharper peak, heavy tails (more outliers) |\n| < 0            | Platykurtic u2013 flatter peak, light tails (fewer outliers) |\n\n- **Leptokurtic**: Data are more concentrated near the mean and in the tails u2192 more extreme values.  \n- **Platykurtic**: Data are more spread out, flatter peak, fewer extreme values.\n\n---\n\n### **3. Use in `psych::describe()`**\n\n- `kurtosis` column reports the **excess kurtosis** of each variable.  \n- Helps identify whether your data have **heavy tails**, which can influence:\n  - Mean and standard deviation reliability\n  - Statistical tests assuming normality\n\n---\n\n### **4. Quick R example**\n\n```r\nx <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 10)\npsych::describe(x)$kurtosis\n# Output: 1.75 (leptokurtic, heavy tails)\n```\n\n- Indicates **more extreme values than a normal distribution** would have.\n\n---\n\n### **5. Why it matters for your sediment data**\n\n- Environmental and sedimentary data (like DMAR, C_org_pc) often have **leptokurtic distributions** due to rare extreme events (e.g., rapid deposition layers).  \n- Knowing kurtosis helps decide whether to **use robust statistics** (median, trimmed mean, MAD) instead of relying solely on mean u00b1 sd.  \n\n---\n\nIf you want, I can make a **table explaining which stats (mean, median, MAD, skew, kurtosis) are best for reporting DMAR and C_org_pc** depending on skewness and kurtosis."

              "A **Random Forest Regression model** is a machine-learning method that predicts a continuous (numeric) value by combining the results of many decision trees.\n\nHereu2019s a clear breakdown:\n\n---\n\n## ud83cudf32 What is a Random Forest?\nA **Random Forest** is an ensemble (group) of many decision trees.  \nEach tree makes its own prediction, and the forest *averages* those predictions to get the final result.\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudccc How Random Forest Regression Works\n1. **Bootstrap sampling**  \n   The algorithm randomly samples the training data *with replacement* to build many different subsets.\n\n2. **Decision trees are trained**  \n   For each tree:\n   - A random subset of **rows** is selected (bootstrap sample).\n   - A random subset of **columns (features)** is selected at each split.\n   - The tree grows fully or until stopping rules.\n\n3. **Prediction**  \n   - Every tree predicts a numeric value.\n   - The final prediction is the **average** of all tree predictions.\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudca1 Why use it?\n### Advantages\n- Handles **nonlinear relationships** extremely well  \n- Works well with **large numbers of features**  \n- Robust to **outliers**  \n- Resistant to **overfitting** compared to a single tree  \n- Provides **variable importance** measures  \n\n### Limitations\n- Less interpretable than simple models  \n- Can be slower for very large datasets  \n- Predictions are averages, so they may smooth out extreme values\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudcca When to use Random Forest Regression?\nUse it when:\n- You want strong prediction accuracy  \n- Relationships between variables are complex or nonlinear  \n- You have many predictors (e.g., XRF spectra, sensor data, geochemical data)\n\n---\n\n## ud83euddea Example in R\n\n```r\nlibrary(randomForest)\n\nrf_model <- randomForest(\n  x = df_xrf_matrix,\n  y = df_icp_matrix,\n  ntree = 500,\n  importance = TRUE\n)\n```\n\n---\n\nIf you want, I can compare **Random Forest vs PLSR**, or show how to choose hyperparameters, tune the model, or plot predictions."

              "Below is a **complete, practical comparison** of **Random Forest vs PLSR**, plus **how to tune hyperparameters** and **plot predictions**.  \nIu2019ll give everything in a clean, usable R workflow.\n\n---\n\n# ud83cudf32 Random Forest vs ud83dudcc9 PLSR  \n### u2714ufe0f When to use each model?\n\n| Feature | **Random Forest (RF)** | **Partial Least Squares Regression (PLSR)** |\n|--------|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------|\n| **Type** | Non-parametric ensemble | Linear, latent-variable regression |\n| **Relationships** | Captures *complex, nonlinear* patterns | *Linear* relationships |\n| **Works with high-dimensional predictors** | Yes | Yes |\n| **Collinearity handling** | Excellent | Designed for it |\n| **Interpretability** | Moderate (variable importance) | High (loadings, scores) |\n| **Overfitting risk** | Low (ensemble) | Can overfit if components are not tuned |\n| **Speed** | Slower | Very fast |\n| **Best for** | Complex chemistry signals, noisy data, large feature sets | High-dim spectral data with relatively linear relationships |\n| **Outputs** | Variable importance, proximity measures | Latent variables, coefficients |\n\n**For XRF u2192 ICP calibration:**  \n- u2714ufe0f **RF** handles nonlinearities and interactions in spectral data  \n- u2714ufe0f **PLSR** is often standard in chemometrics  \n- u26a1 Best practice: **compare both and choose by cross-validation RMSE**\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudd27 1. Hyperparameters for Random Forest\nThe most important ones:\n\n### **ntree**  \nNumber of trees (larger u2192 more stable).  \nCommon range: **300u20132000**.\n\n### **mtry**  \nNumber of predictors tried at each split.  \n- Regression default: u221ap  \n- Tune over:  \n  ```r\n  mtry_grid <- c( floor(sqrt(p)), p/3, p/2 )\n  ```\n\n### **nodesize**  \nMinimum samples per terminal node (controls tree depth).  \nSmaller u2192 more complex trees.  \nTry: **1, 5, 10**\n\n---\n\n# ud83euddea 2. Hyperparameter tuning for Random Forest (caret)\n```r\nlibrary(caret)\nlibrary(randomForest)\n\nset.seed(123)\n\ntune_grid <- expand.grid(\n  mtry = c(5, 10, 20, 30)\n)\n\nctrl <- trainControl(\n  method = \"cv\",\n  number = 10\n)\n\nrf_tuned <- train(\n  x = df_xrf_matrix,\n  y = df_icp_matrix,\n  method = \"rf\",\n  metric = \"RMSE\",\n  tuneGrid = tune_grid,\n  trControl = ctrl,\n  ntree = 500\n)\n\nrf_tuned\n```\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudd04 3. Hyperparameter tuning for PLSR (components)\n```r\nlibrary(pls)\n\npls_tuned <- plsr(\n  df_icp_matrix ~ df_xrf_matrix,\n  ncomp = 30,\n  validation = \"CV\",\n  scale = TRUE,\n  center = TRUE\n)\n\n# Choose optimal components\nopt_comp <- which.min(RMSEP(pls_tuned)$val[1,,])\nopt_comp\n```\n\n---\n\n# u2714ufe0f 4. Fit final models\n\n### Random Forest\n```r\nrf_final <- randomForest(\n  x = df_xrf_matrix,\n  y = df_icp_matrix,\n  ntree = 500,\n  mtry = rf_tuned$bestTune$mtry,\n  importance = TRUE\n)\n```\n\n### PLSR\n```r\npls_final <- plsr(\n  df_icp_matrix ~ df_xrf_matrix,\n  ncomp = opt_comp,\n  scale = TRUE,\n  center = TRUE,\n  validation = \"none\"\n)\n```\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudcc8 5. Plot Predictions vs Actual\n\n## Random Forest Predictions\n```r\nrf_pred <- predict(rf_final, df_xrf_matrix)\n\nplot(df_icp_matrix, rf_pred,\n     xlab = \"Actual ICP\",\n     ylab = \"Predicted (RF)\")\nabline(0,1)\n```\n\n## PLSR Predictions\n```r\npls_pred <- predict(pls_final, df_xrf_matrix, ncomp = opt_comp)\n\nplot(df_icp_matrix, pls_pred,\n     xlab = \"Actual ICP\",\n     ylab = \"Predicted (PLSR)\")\nabline(0,1)\n```\n\n---\n\n# u2b50 Summary: Which is better?\n\n### Choose **Random Forest** if:\n- Your XRF u2192 ICP relationship is nonlinear  \n- You want maximum predictive accuracy  \n- You want a robust model that handles noise\n\n### Choose **PLSR** if:\n- You want interpretability (loadings, components)  \n- Relationship is mostly linear  \n- You prefer traditional chemometric modeling\n\n---\n\nIf you want, I can also generate:  \nu2705 Side-by-side RMSE comparison  \nu2705 Multi-element (multivariate) RF calibration  \nu2705 Variable importance plots  \nJust say the word!"

              "Here is a **clear, practical comparison of Random Forest (RF), PLSR, and Support Vector Regression (SVR)** u2014 focused on chemometric calibration (e.g., XRF u2192 ICP).\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudd25 **Random Forest vs PLSR vs SVR (Support Vector Regression)**\n\n## ud83eudde0 1. Conceptual Overview  \n| Model | Type | Handles Nonlinearity | Typical Strength |\n|-------|------|----------------------|-------------------|\n| **Random Forest** | Tree ensemble | u2714ufe0f Strong | Robust, high accuracy, resistant to overfitting |\n| **PLSR** | Linear latent-variable model | u274c Mostly linear | Interpretable, traditional chemometrics |\n| **SVR** | Kernel-based margin model | u2714ufe0f Very strong | Works well with complex but smooth relationships |\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudccc 2. How They Work (Simple Explanation)\n\n### ud83cudf32 **Random Forest (RF)**\n- Builds many decision trees on random subsets.  \n- Final prediction = **average of trees**.  \n- Great for messy, nonlinear data.\n\n### ud83dudcc9 **PLSR**\n- Reduces X to a small number of **latent components** explaining covariance with Y.  \n- Assumes **linear relationship** between latent variables and response.\n\n### u2699ufe0f **Support Vector Regression (SVR)**\n- Finds a function that fits data **within a margin (u03b5-insensitive loss)**.  \n- Can use kernels:\n  - RBF (Gaussian) u2014 most common  \n  - Linear  \n  - Polynomial  \n- Very strong for **smooth nonlinear relationships**.\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudcc8 3. Prediction Performance (Typical Behaviors)\n\n| Feature | **RF** | **PLSR** | **SVR** |\n|--------|--------|----------|---------|\n| **Linear relationships** | Good | u2714ufe0f Excellent | Good |\n| **Nonlinear relationships** | u2714ufe0f Very good | Pooru2013Moderate | u2714ufe0f Excellent |\n| **Overfitting risk** | Low | Moderate | High if not tuned |\n| **Noise robustness** | u2714ufe0f High | Moderate | Moderate |\n| **Small datasets** | Good | u2714ufe0f Very good | u274c Can overfit easily |\n| **Large feature sets (spectra)** | Good | u2714ufe0f Excellent | Good |\n| **Speed** | Medium | u2714ufe0f Fast | Slow for large data |\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudcca 4. Interpretability\n\n| Category | RF | PLSR | SVR |\n|----------|----|------|-----|\n| Easy to explain? | Medium | u2714ufe0f High | Low |\n| Latent components? | No | u2714ufe0f Yes | No |\n| Variable importance | u2714ufe0f Yes | Yes | Limited |\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudd27 5. Hyperparameters to Tune\n\n### ud83cudf32 Random Forest\n| Param | Meaning |\n|-------|---------|\n| `mtry` | # of variables tested at each split |\n| `ntree` | # of trees |\n| `nodesize` | Min samples per leaf |\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudcc9 PLSR\n| Param | Meaning |\n|-------|---------|\n| `ncomp` | Number of latent components |\n\n---\n\n### u2699ufe0f SVR (RBF kernel)\nMost important:\n\n| Param | Meaning |\n|-------|---------|\n| `C` | penalty strength (controls margin width) |\n| `epsilon` | tolerance for prediction error |\n| `gamma` | kernel width (controls nonlinearity) |\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudd2c 6. R Code: Fit & Tune All Three Models\n\n## Libraries\n```r\nlibrary(caret)\nlibrary(pls)\nlibrary(randomForest)\nlibrary(e1071)\n```\n\n---\n\n## u2714ufe0f PLSR Tuning\n```r\npls_tuned <- plsr(\n  df_icp_matrix ~ df_xrf_matrix,\n  ncomp = 30,\n  validation = \"CV\",\n  scale = TRUE,\n  center = TRUE\n)\nbest_comp <- which.min(RMSEP(pls_tuned)$val[1,,])\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83cudf32 Random Forest Tuning\n```r\nrf_grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(5, 10, 20, 30))\n\nctrl <- trainControl(method = \"cv\", number = 10)\n\nrf_tuned <- train(\n  x = df_xrf_matrix,\n  y = df_icp_matrix,\n  method = \"rf\",\n  tuneGrid = rf_grid,\n  trControl = ctrl,\n  ntree = 500\n)\n```\n\n---\n\n## u2699ufe0f SVR Tuning (RBF kernel)\n```r\nsvr_grid <- expand.grid(\n  sigma = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.1),\n  C = c(1, 10, 100),\n  epsilon = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.1)\n)\n\nsvr_tuned <- train(\n  x = df_xrf_matrix,\n  y = df_icp_matrix,\n  method = \"svmRadial\",\n  tuneLength = 10,\n  trControl = ctrl\n)\n```\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudcc8 7.
