You want to calculate the variance explained by each PLS component as a percentage in your PLSR model.\n\nIn R, when you fit a `plsr` model using the `pls` package, the model object (`pls_model`) contains an element `explvar` that holds the percentage of variance explained by each component in the X matrix.\n\nHereu2019s how you can extract and display the variance explained by each component as a percentage:\n\n```r\n# Extract variance explained by each component\nvariance_explained <- pls_model$explvar\n\n# Display variance explained as percentages\nvariance_explained_pct <- variance_explained\nnames(variance_explained_pct) <- paste0(\"Comp\", 1:length(variance_explained_pct))\n\nprint(variance_explained_pct)\n```\n\nIf you want the **cumulative variance explained** by the components:\n\n```r\ncumulative_variance_explained <- cumsum(variance_explained_pct)\nprint(cumulative_variance_explained)\n```\n\nThis will give you the % variance explained by each individual component, which you can relate to your optimal number of components (`opt_comp`).\n\n---\n\nIf you want to also see how much variance is explained in **Y** by the components (which is useful for regression):\n\n```r\nsummary(pls_model)\n```\n\nThis prints a summary that includes the percentage of variance explained in X and in Y for each component.\n\nLet me know if you want me to help extract that programmatically!"

            "parts": [
              "In the context of **Partial Least Squares (PLS)** modeling, **Jackknifing** during **Leave-One-Out (LOO) cross-validation** is used to **estimate the reliability or uncertainty** of model parametersu2014most often **regression coefficients or variable importance measures**.\n\n### What is Jackknifing in PLS LOO?\nJackknifing is a **resampling technique** where, in LOO cross-validation, each sample is left out one at a time, a model is built on the remaining data, and then the results (e.g. regression coefficients) are recorded. After looping through all samples, you end up with a distribution of model parametersu2014one for each LOO iteration.\n\n### What does it do?\n\n- **Estimates variability**: It helps estimate the **standard deviation or standard error** of the model parameters (like PLS regression coefficients), giving an idea of **how stable or reliable** those parameters are.\n  \n- **Confidence intervals / Significance testing**: You can calculate **confidence intervals or t-statistics** for each regression coefficient using the jackknifed estimates. If a coefficient has a confidence interval that does **not include zero**, it may be considered **statistically significant**.\n\n- **Variable selection**: Variables with **low jackknife stability** (i.e., large standard errors or coefficients not consistently non-zero) may be deemed **unimportant** for the model.\n\n### Example:\n\nFor a given variable \\( x_i \\), you would:\n\n1. Run PLS on the full dataset.\n2. Do LOO validation: For each left-out sample \\( i \\), build a PLS model on the remaining \\( n-1 \\) samples.\n3. Record the regression coefficient \\( b_i^{(-i)} \\) for each LOO model.\n4. Compute the **mean** and **standard deviation** of these \\( n \\) jackknife estimates.\n5. Estimate a **t-value** like:\n   \\[\n   t = \\frac{b}{\\text{SE}_b}\n   \\]\n   where \\( b \\) is the coefficient from the full model, and \\( \\text{SE}_b \\) is the standard error from jackknifing.\n\nThis gives you a **way to assess which model parameters are robust** and which ones are not.\n\n---\n\nLet me know if you want a Python or MATLAB code example of how this is implemented."

              "Here's how you can perform **Jackknife estimation in PLS with Leave-One-Out (LOO) cross-validation** in **R**, using the `pls` package.\n\n---\n\n### ud83euddea Example: Jackknifing in PLS with LOO\n\nWeu2019ll use the built-in **`yarn`** dataset from the `pls` package for illustration:\n\n#### 1. **Install and load the package** (if not already):\n\n```r\ninstall.packages(\"pls\")  # if needed\nlibrary(pls)\n```\n\n---\n\n#### 2. **Fit a PLS model with LOO cross-validation**\n\n```r\ndata(yarn)  # Example dataset from pls package\nset.seed(123)  # For reproducibility\n\n# Fit PLS model with LOO\npls_model <- plsr(density ~ NIR, data = yarn, validation = \"LOO\", ncomp = 10)\n```\n\n---\n\n#### 3. **Use jackknife() to compute standard errors of regression coefficients**\n\n```r\n# Jackknife estimation of coefficients\njack_res <- jack.test(pls_model, ncomp = 5)  # using 5 components, adjust as needed\n\n# View t-statistics and p-values for each predictor\nsummary(jack_res)\n```\n\nThis outputs:\n- **Regression coefficients**\n- **Standard errors**\n- **t-values**\n- **p-values** based on jackknife standard errors\n\n---\n\n#### 4. **Interpretation**\n\nEach variable's **t-value** and **p-value** tell you whether its coefficient is **statistically significantly different from zero**, based on jackknifing across LOO folds.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d Behind the scenes\n\n- `jack.test()` does the heavy liftingu2014it runs `n` LOO fits (for `n` samples), collects the coefficients, computes standard errors, and returns a test summary.\n- It is a **non-parametric way** to assess coefficient significance **without assuming normality**.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Notes\n\n- You can change `ncomp = k` to your desired number of PLS components.\n- If your dataset is large, jackknifing with LOO can be slow since it fits **`n` PLS models**.\n\n---\n\nWould you like help visualizing these results or comparing models with different numbers of components?"

              "Great question u2014 understanding the match between **RMSE** and **RMSEP** is key to evaluating PLS model performance.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Definitions:\n\n- **RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error)**: Usually refers to the **training error** u2014 how well the model fits the **calibration** (training) data.\n\n- **RMSEP (Root Mean Squared Error of Prediction)**: Refers to the **prediction error** u2014 how well the model predicts **new or unseen data**, often from cross-validation or a test set.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudca1 What does it mean when RMSE u2248 RMSEP?\n\nIf your **RMSE and RMSEP are close**, this suggests that:\n\n- u2705 **The model generalizes well**: It performs similarly on both training and validation data.\n- u2705 **Thereu2019s little overfitting**: The model hasn't learned noise from the training data.\n- u2705 **The model complexity is appropriate**: You're using a good number of PLS components u2014 not too few (underfitting) or too many (overfitting).\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudea8 What if they donu2019t match?\n\n| Scenario                        | Meaning                                                   |\n|-------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|\n| RMSE u226a RMSEP                  | u26a0ufe0f Overfitting u2014 model fits training data too well, but fails on new data |\n| RMSE u226b RMSEP (rare)           | u26a0ufe0f Possibly an artifact u2014 maybe training data has noise, or validation data is too small or easier to predict |\n| Both RMSE and RMSEP are high  | u26a0ufe0f Underfitting u2014 model not capturing enough structure |\n| Both are low and similar      | u2705 Ideal u2014 balanced fit and generalization |\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d Example in R (`pls` package)\n\n```r\n# Fit model with cross-validation\nmodel <- plsr(density ~ NIR, data = yarn, validation = \"LOO\")\n\n# Get RMSE and RMSEP\nsummary(model)\n\n# RMSE for training\nrmse_train <- RMSE(model, estimate = \"train\")\n\n# RMSEP from cross-validation\nrmsep_cv <- RMSEP(model)\n\n# Plot RMSEP vs #components\nplot(RMSEP(model), legendpos = \"topright\")\n```\n\nThe plot will help you **select the number of components** where RMSEP is lowest and closest to RMSE u2014 the \"sweet spot\".\n\n---\n\nLet me know if you'd like help interpreting your specific RMSE/RMSEP values or choosing the number of PLS components."

              "In **Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression**, the number of elements you decide to include in the regression equation corresponds to the number of **latent variables**, also called **components** or **PLS factors**. Deciding how many of these to include is **critical** for building a model that generalizes well.\n\nHereu2019s how you typically decide:\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d 1. **Use Cross-Validation (Most Common Method)**\n\nYou build models with different numbers of components and evaluate their performance using **cross-validation** (e.g., k-fold or leave-one-out). You're trying to find the number of components that:\n\n- Minimizes **prediction error** (like RMSE or MSE) on unseen data.\n- Avoids overfitting by not including too many components.\n\nThis is often visualized with a **scree plot** (components vs error). You pick the number of components just before the error flattens out (elbow method).\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudcca 2. **Look at the Variance Explained**\n\nYou can look at:\n- **Explained variance in the predictors (X)**.\n- **Explained variance in the response (Y)**.\n\nYou may aim to include enough components to capture a certain percentage (e.g. 90%) of the variance in Y, **but** this is often combined with cross-validation to avoid overfitting.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 3. **Use Information Criteria (Less Common in Practice)**\n\nSome more advanced methods use model selection criteria like:\n- **AIC (Akaike Information Criterion)**\n- **BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion)**\n\nThese penalize model complexity to prevent overfitting.\n\n---\n\n### u26a0ufe0f Key Warning\n\nAdding more components always improves **in-sample fit**, but not necessarily **predictive performance**. So you should **never choose the number of components based only on Ru00b2 or adjusted Ru00b2** on training data.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dude80 Practical Recommendation\n\nIf you're coding this (e.g., using Python or R), most libraries (like `scikit-learn` or `pls` in R) have built-in cross-validation to help choose the optimal number of components.\n\n**Example (Python, scikit-learn):**\n```python\nfrom sklearn.cross_decomposition import PLSRegression\nfrom sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score\n\n# Try different numbers of components\nfor n_comp in range(1, max_components+1):\n    pls = PLSRegression(n_components=n_comp)\n    scores = cross_val_score(pls, X, y, cv=5, scoring='neg_mean_squared_error')\n    print(f\"Components: {n_comp}, CV MSE: {-scores.mean()}\")\n```\n\nWould you like a quick plot example or R code version too?"

              "### ud83eudde0 What is AIC in PLS Regression (R)?\n**AIC (Akaike Information Criterion)** is a statistical metric used to assess **model quality**, balancing **goodness of fit** and **model complexity**. In the context of **Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression**, AIC helps you decide **how many components** to include in your model without overfitting.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd22 AIC Formula (Conceptual)\nFor linear models:\n\\[\n\\text{AIC} = 2k - 2\\ln(L)\n\\]\nWhere:\n- \\( k \\) = number of estimated parameters (includes number of components and possibly residual variance)\n- \\( L \\) = likelihood of the model given the data\n\n**Lower AIC = Better Model** (relative to others).\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudce6 Using AIC in PLS in R\n\nThereu2019s no built-in AIC function in `pls` package (like `plsr()`), but you can **compute it manually** from the residual sum of squares (RSS) or mean squared error (MSE) and the number of parameters.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Example: Computing AIC in PLS (`pls` package in R)\n\n```r\nlibrary(pls)\n\n# Sample data\ndata(yarn)\nX <- yarn$NIR\ny <- yarn$density\n\n# Fit PLS with different number of components\nmax_comps <- 10\naic_values <- numeric(max_comps)\n\nfor (n in 1:max_comps) {\n  model <- plsr(y ~ X, ncomp = n, validation = \"none\")\n  \n  # Residual sum of squares\n  rss <- sum(residuals(model)^2)\n  \n  # Number of observations and parameters\n  n_obs <- length(y)\n  k <- n  # n components ~ n parameters (approx.)\n  \n  # Estimate of sigma^2 (residual variance)\n  sigma2 <- rss / n_obs\n  \n  # AIC calculation\n  aic_values[n] <- n_obs * log(sigma2) + 2 * k\n}\n\n# Plot AIC vs. number of components\nplot(1:max_comps, aic_values, type = \"b\", xlab = \"Number of Components\", ylab = \"AIC\", main = \"AIC for PLS Regression\")\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudcd8 What It Means in Practice\n\n- **You want to minimize AIC.** The model with the lowest AIC has the best trade-off between complexity and fit.\n- Itu2019s an **alternative to cross-validation**. Use it when you're trying to automate or formalize component selection.\n- **Caution**: Since PLS doesnu2019t fit in the standard linear model framework (because predictors are latent variables), the **\"number of parameters\"** is approximate. So AIC can give a good guideline but is **not foolproof**.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudca1 When to Use AIC vs Cross-Validation\n\n| Approach | Strengths | Weaknesses |\n|---------|-----------|-------------|\n| AIC | Fast, automatic, model-selection-ready | May not generalize as well without validation |\n| Cross-Validation | Best for prediction, handles overfitting better | Slower, more computationally intensive |\n\n---\n\nWould you like an example using a specific dataset like `mtcars` or your own data?"

              "### ud83dudcda What is **BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion)**?\n\n**BIC**, like **AIC**, is a model selection criterion that balances:\n- **Goodness of fit** (how well the model explains the data)\n- **Model complexity** (how many parameters it uses)\n\nBut **BIC penalizes complexity more harshly** than AIC.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudcd0 BIC Formula (Conceptual)\n\n\\[\n\\text{BIC} = n \\cdot \\log(\\text{RSS}/n) + k \\cdot \\log(n)\n\\]\n\nWhere:\n- \\( n \\) = number of observations\n- \\( k \\) = number of parameters (often approximated as number of components in PLS)\n- RSS = residual sum of squares\n\n**Lower BIC = Better model** (like AIC), but BIC prefers **simpler models** more strongly.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Example in R: BIC for PLS Regression\n\nUsing the `pls` package and a built-in dataset:\n\n```r\n# Load libraries\nlibrary(pls)\n\n# Load example data\ndata(yarn)\nX <- yarn$NIR\ny <- yarn$density\n\n# Set max number of components\nmax_comps <- 10\nbic_values <- numeric(max_comps)\n\n# Compute BIC for each number of components\nfor (n in 1:max_comps) {\n  model <- plsr(y ~ X, ncomp = n, validation = \"none\")\n  \n  # Get residual sum of squares\n  rss <- sum(residuals(model)^2)\n  \n  # Number of observations\n  n_obs <- length(y)\n  \n  # Estimate residual variance\n  sigma2 <- rss / n_obs\n  \n  # Approximate number of parameters (n components)\n  k <- n\n  \n  # Compute BIC\n  bic_values[n] <- n_obs * log(sigma2) + k * log(n_obs)\n}\n\n# Plot BIC vs. number of components\nplot(1:max_comps, bic_values, type = \"b\",\n     xlab = \"Number of PLS Components\",\n     ylab = \"BIC\",\n     main = \"BIC for PLS Regression\")\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83eudde0 What Does It Mean?\n\n- The **best model** is the one with the **lowest BIC**.\n- BIC favors **simpler models** than AIC, especially as the dataset grows.\n- Helps you decide **how many PLS components to keep**, avoiding overfitting.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d AIC vs BIC: Quick Comparison\n\n| Criterion | Penalty Strength | Tends to Choose... | Best For |\n|----------|------------------|--------------------|----------|\n| AIC | Mild | Slightly more complex models | Prediction accuracy |\n| BIC | Strong | Simpler models | Parsimonious explanations (fewer variables) |\n\n---\n\n### u26a0ufe0f Caveats\n\n- In PLS, the number of parameters is approximate (since it's not a standard regression).\n- Always **validate your model** with cross-validation or test data in addition to AIC/BIC.\n\n---\n\nWould you like me to compare the AIC and BIC curves side by side for this data?"

              "A **linear 1:1 BIC plot** likely means that your **BIC values are increasing linearly** with the number of PLS components (i.e., number of latent variables), forming a straight lineu2014possibly even with a slope of 1 or close to it.\n\nThis kind of result is **unusual** and typically suggests one or more of the following issues:\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudea9 **Possible Causes & Interpretations**\n\n#### 1. **Residual variance (u03c3u00b2) is constant**\nIf the **residual error** or model fit doesn't change much as you add components, then:\n- The **log-likelihood part** of BIC stays nearly constant.\n- Only the **penalty term** \\( k \\cdot \\log(n) \\) increases.\n- BIC then increases linearly with the number of components.\n\n**u2192 Interpretation:** Adding components is not improving model fit. Your model is possibly already optimal at 1 or 2 components.\n\n---\n\n#### 2. **The model is not actually being refit in each iteration**\nThis happens when, for example, youu2019re mistakenly computing BIC using the **same model** every time (like in your earlier code), so RSS doesn't change.\n\n**u2192 Check:** Are you actually fitting a **new model for each n**?\n\n---\n\n#### 3. **Small or noisy dataset**\nIf your dataset is too small or contains mostly noise, adding components may not improve predictive performance. In such cases:\n- The model struggles to capture meaningful structure.\n- Residual variance stays flat, and BIC rises linearly.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 What It *Should* Look Like (Typically)\n\nIn a **well-behaved BIC plot**, you'd expect:\n- A **U-shape or elbow**.\n- BIC decreases as the model improves (up to a point).\n- Then increases again as the complexity penalty dominates.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudcca What To Do If Your Plot Is Linear\n\n- **Double-check your loop logic**: Are you fitting new models for each `n`?\n- **Plot RMSE or cross-validation error** instead u2014 does it improve with more components?\n- **Use cross-validation** (`validation = \"CV\"`) to identify overfitting or lack of model improvement.\n\n---\n\nWould you like me to help debug the BIC loop youu2019re using to see if this is the case?"

              "To **visually highlight that BIC is minimized at 4 components**, you can:\n\nu2705 **Mark the minimum BIC point on the plot**, and  \nu2705 **Restrict the plot x-axis to show up to 4 components** (if desired).\n\nHereu2019s how to do both:\n\n---\n\n### u2705 Full Code to Plot BIC and Highlight 4 Components\n\n```r\nlibrary(pls)\n\n# Y_train <- df_icp_matrix\n# X_train <- df_xrf_matrix\n\nmax_comps <- 10\nbic_values <- numeric(max_comps)\nn_obs <- nrow(X_train)\n\nfor (n in 1:max_comps) {\n  pls_model <- plsr(Y_train ~ X_train, ncomp = n, validation = \"none\")\n  res_mat <- residuals(pls_model)[,,n]\n  rss <- sum(res_mat^2)\n  sigma2 <- rss / (n_obs * ncol(Y_train))\n  k <- n\n  bic_values[n] <- n_obs * log(sigma2) + k * log(n_obs)\n}\n\n# Find optimal number of components (lowest BIC)\nopt_n <- which.min(bic_values)\n\n# Plot up to 10 components, but highlight optimal (e.g., 4)\nplot(1:max_comps, bic_values, type = \"b\", pch = 16,\n     xlab = \"Number of PLS Components\", ylab = \"BIC\",\n     main = \"BIC vs Number of Components (PLS)\")\nabline(v = opt_n, col = \"red\", lty = 2)\npoints(opt_n, bic_values[opt_n], col = \"red\", pch = 19, cex = 1.3)\ntext(opt_n, bic_values[opt_n], labels = paste(\"Optimal =\", opt_n), pos = 4, col = \"red\")\n```\n\n---\n\n### ud83eudde0 What This Does:\n- `which.min(bic_values)` finds the number of components (e.g., 4) where BIC is lowest.\n- `abline()` and `points()` mark and annotate that point on the plot.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd04 Optional: Plot Only Up to 4 Components\n\nIf you want to **restrict the plot** to just the first 4:\n\n```r\nplot(1:4, bic_values[1:4], type = \"b\", pch = 16,\n     xlab = \"Number of PLS Components\", ylab = \"BIC\",\n     main = \"BIC (First 4 Components Only)\")\n```\n\n---\n\nLet me know if you'd like to **save this plot to PDF** as well!"

              "If your **BIC values are negative and continue to decrease** as the number of components increases, here's what it likely means u2014 broken down simply and precisely:\n\n---\n\n### u2705 What Is BIC?\n\nBIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) is defined as:\n\n\\[\n\\text{BIC} = n \\cdot \\log(\\sigma^2) + k \\cdot \\log(n)\n\\]\n\nWhere:\n- \\( n \\) = number of observations  \n- \\( \\sigma^2 \\) = estimated residual variance  \n- \\( k \\) = number of parameters (e.g., number of components in PLS)\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudd0d If BIC Is **Negative and Decreasing**:\n\n#### 1. **Residual variance (\\( \\sigma^2 \\)) is very small**\n- That means your model is fitting the data **extremely well** u2014 almost too well.\n- This causes \\( \\log(\\sigma^2) \\) to become **strongly negative**, dragging BIC down.\n\n#### 2. **Penalty term is not enough to offset the fit**\n- As components increase, model fit improves and residual variance drops.\n- But the increase in complexity (the \\( k \\cdot \\log(n) \\) term) is not large enough to reverse that trend.\n- Result: BIC keeps dropping.\n\n#### 3. **Potential overfitting**\n- If BIC keeps decreasing **past a sensible number of components**, it may mean the model is **overfitting** u2014 capturing noise as if it were signal.\n- Especially common if:\n  - The number of components approaches the number of predictors.\n  - Your data is small or noisy.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudcc9 Why BIC Can Be Negative\n\nThis is **normal** when:\n- The residual variance is **less than 1**, and\n- \\( \\log(\\sigma^2) \\) becomes negative, and dominates the overall BIC.\n\nBIC is **relative**, so negative values are fine u2014 itu2019s the **shape** of the curve that matters.\n\n---\n\n### u2705 What Should Happen Ideally?\n\n- BIC should **decrease at first**, as model fit improves.\n- Then it should **reach a minimum**, where additional complexity doesnu2019t justify the improvement in fit.\n- After that, BIC should **increase** if the model starts overfitting.\n\n---\n\n### ud83dudee0ufe0f What You Should Do:\n\n1. **Plot BIC vs Components** u2013 which you already are doing.\n2. **Watch for a flattening or lowest point** u2013 if BIC just keeps going down, it may mean:\n   - You need to increase `max_comps` to find the minimum.\n   - Or your model is overfitting u2014 especially if you're near the number of predictors.\n3. **Try cross-validation RMSEP/MAE plots** as well u2014 they are more robust to overfitting.\n\n---\n\nWould you like help combining BIC and cross-validation (RMSEP) plots to guide your component selection more safely?"

              "Below is **template R code** showing how to run **OLS** and **WLS** regression, perform **k-fold cross-validation**, and compute **prediction error on an independent test set**.\n\nYou can paste your actual variables and dataset names into the placeholders.\n\n---\n\n# u2705 **R Code: OLS, WLS, Cross-Validation, Independent Test Error**\n\n```r\n###############################\n## 1. Load data and split\n###############################\n\nset.seed(123)\n\n# Example: assume df is your dataframe\n# y is the dependent variable, x1 + x2 + ... are predictors\n# Replace df, y, x1, x2 with your actual data names.\n\n# 80/20 train-test split\ntrain_idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(df)), size = 0.8*nrow(df))\ntrain <- df[train_idx, ]\ntest  <- df[-train_idx, ]\n\n\n###############################\n## 2. Ordinary Least Squares\n###############################\n\nols_model <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = train)\nsummary(ols_model)\n\n# Predictions + test MSE\nols_pred <- predict(ols_model, newdata = test)\nols_test_MSE <- mean((test$y - ols_pred)^2)\nols_test_MSE\n\n\n###############################\n## 3. Weighted Least Squares\n###############################\n\n# Example weights: inverse of variance estimate\n# Replace this with your own weighting rule\nweights <- 1 / lm(abs(residuals(ols_model)) ~ fitted(ols_model))$fitted.values^2\n\nwls_model <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = train, weights = weights)\nsummary(wls_model)\n\n# Predictions + test MSE\nwls_pred <- predict(wls_model, newdata = test)\nwls_test_MSE <- mean((test$y - wls_pred)^2)\nwls_test_MSE\n\n\n###############################\n## 4. k-Fold Cross-Validation\n###############################\n\nlibrary(caret)\n\nK <- 10\nctrl <- trainControl(method = \"cv\", number = K)\n\n### OLS Cross-Validation\nset.seed(123)\nols_cv <- train(\n  y ~ x1 + x2 + x3,\n  data = train,\n  method = \"lm\",\n  trControl = ctrl\n)\nols_cv\n\n### WLS Cross-Validation\n# caret does not directly support weights, so we use custom training\n\nwls_cv_results <- c()\n\nfolds <- createFolds(train$y, k = K, list = TRUE)\n\nfor (i in 1:K) {\n    fold_train <- train[-folds[[i]], ]\n    fold_test  <- train[folds[[i]], ]\n    \n    # Recompute weights inside each fold\n    fold_ols    <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = fold_train)\n    fold_weights <- 1 / lm(abs(residuals(fold_ols)) ~ fitted(fold_ols))$fitted.values^2\n    \n    fold_wls <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = fold_train, weights = fold_weights)\n    \n    pred <- predict(fold_wls, newdata = fold_test)\n    fold_MSE <- mean((fold_test$y - pred)^2)\n    \n    wls_cv_results[i] <- fold_MSE\n}\n\nwls_cv_results\nmean(wls_cv_results)   # cross-validated MSE\n\n\n###############################\n## 5. Output summary\n###############################\n\ncat(\"\\n=== RESULTS ===\\n\")\ncat(\"OLS CV MSE: \", ols_cv$results$RMSE^2, \"\\n\")\ncat(\"WLS CV MSE: \", mean(wls_cv_results), \"\\n\")\ncat(\"OLS Test MSE:\", ols_test_MSE, \"\\n\")\ncat(\"WLS Test MSE:\", wls_test_MSE, \"\\n\")\n```\n\n---\n\n# u2714ufe0f **What This Code Gives You**\n### **1. OLS regression**\n- Model summary  \n- Prediction error on independent test set\n\n### **2. WLS regression**\n- Example of variance-based weights  \n- Test prediction error\n\n### **3. Cross-validation**\n- 10-fold CV for OLS using `caret`\n- Custom 10-fold CV for WLS (caret does not support weights natively)\n\n### **4. Performance metrics**\n- CV MSE  \n- Independent test MSE  \n\n---\n\nIf youu2019d like, I can also create:\nu2705 Code using **tidymodels**  \nu2705 Code for **heteroskedasticity-consistent errors**  \nu2705 Automatic weight selection using **GLS** or **nlme**  \n\nJust tell me!"

              "Hereu2019s a single **mega-function** that now does *everything* you asked for, including:\n\n- OLS, WLS (variance), weighted OLS (ICP SD), 2-step weighted WLS  \n- Bayesian regression (MAP-style) with `arm::bayesglm`  \n- Residual distribution plots  \n- Normality test tables  \n- Bootstrap CIs for slope & intercept  \n- Breuschu2013Pagan heteroscedasticity tests  \n- Cooku2019s distance / influence plots  \n- Cross-validation prediction plots  \n- Multi-model comparison plots per element  \n- Global CSV summary (slopes, intercepts, AIC, BIC, Ru00b2, RMSE, RMSEP)  \n- Automatic best-model selection per element  \n- One combined summary PDF for all elements  \n\n---\n\n## ud83dudd27 Function\n\n```r\nrun_full_regressions <- function(\n  elements,\n  data,\n  var_suffix = \"_var\",\n  sd_suffix = \"_ICP_sd\",\n  save_dir   = \"Papers_R/2024_DeVleeschouwer/FigureS6/Plots/FigS6a_OLS_WLS_log_inc\",\n  summary_csv = \"ModelSummary_AllElements.csv\",\n  summary_pdf = \"AllElements_Summary.pdf\"\n) {\n  # Packages\n  library(broom)\n  library(performance)\n  library(see)\n  library(ggplot2)\n  library(dplyr)\n  library(purrr)\n  library(boot)\n  library(psych)      # skew(), kurtosi()\n  library(lmtest)     # bptest()\n  library(arm)        # bayesglm()\n  library(gridExtra)\n  \n  if (!dir.exists(save_dir)) dir.create(save_dir, recursive = TRUE)\n  \n  # Master summary\n  model_summary <- tibble()\n  all_pdf_pages <- list()\n  \n  # Helper: extract stats robustly\n  extract_stats <- function(model, model_name, el) {\n    stats <- tryCatch(performance::model_performance(model),\n                      error = function(e) NULL)\n    if (!is.null(stats)) {\n      r2   <- stats$r2\n      rmse <- stats$rmse\n    } else {\n      r2   <- NA_real_\n      rmse <- sqrt(mean(residuals(model)^2, na.rm = TRUE))\n    }\n    rmsep <- tryCatch(performance::rmsep(model),\n                      error = function(e) NA_real_)\n    \n    tibble(\n      Element   = el,\n      Model     = model_name,\n      Intercept = unname(coef(model)[1]),\n      Slope     = unname(coef(model)[2]),\n      R2        = r2,\n      RMSE      = rmse,\n      RMSEP     = rmsep,\n      AIC       = tryCatch(AIC(model), error = function(e) NA_real_),\n      BIC       = tryCatch(BIC(model), error = function(e) NA_real_)\n    )\n  }\n  \n  # Helper: bootstrap function for CIs\n  boot_fn <- function(data, idx, formula) {\n    m <- lm(formula, data = data[idx, , drop = FALSE])\n    coef(m)\n  }\n  \n  for (el in elements) {\n    message(\"\\n============================\")\n    message(\"Processing element: \", el)\n    message(\"============================\")\n    \n    # Column names\n    y_col   <- paste0(el, \"_ICP\")\n    x_col   <- el\n    var_col <- paste0(el, var_suffix)\n    sd_col  <- paste0(el, sd_suffix)\n    \n    if (!all(c(y_col, x_col) %in% names(data))) {\n      warning(\"Skipping \", el, \": missing \", y_col, \" or \", x_col)\n      next\n    }\n    \n    element_dir <- file.path(save_dir, el)\n    if (!dir.exists(element_dir)) dir.create(element_dir, recursive = TRUE)\n    \n    formula <- as.formula(paste0(y_col, \" ~ \", x_col))\n    \n    #======================\n    # Fit models\n    #======================\n    model_types <- list()\n    \n    # 1) OLS\n    model_types$OLS <- lm(formula, data = data)\n    \n    # 2) WLS (variance-based)\n    if (var_col %in% names(data)) {\n      wts_var <- 1 / data[[var_col]]\n      model_types$WLS_var <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = wts_var)\n    }\n    \n    # 3) Weighted OLS (ICP SD-based)\n    have_sd <- sd_col %in% names(data)\n    if (have_sd) {\n      wts_sd <- 1 / (data[[sd_col]]^2)\n      model_types$OLS_weighted <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = wts_sd)\n    }\n    \n    # 4) Weighted WLS (two-step ICP error-weighted)\n    if (have_sd) {\n      init_model <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = wts_sd)\n      resid_model <- lm(abs(init_model$residuals) ~ init_model$fitted.values)\n      final_wts <- 1 / (resid_model$fitted.values^2)\n      model_types$WLS_weighted <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = final_wts)\n    }\n    \n    # 5) Bayesian regression (MAP) using bayesglm\n    bayes_model <- arm::bayesglm(formula, data = data, family = gaussian())\n    model_types$Bayes <- bayes_model\n    \n    # For element-level summary PDF\n    pdf_pages_element <- list()\n    \n    # For multi-model comparison\n    plot_models <- list()\n    \n    #======================\n    # Process each model\n    #======================\n    for (model_name in names(model_types)) {\n      m <- model_types[[model_name]]\n      message(\"  - \", model_name)\n      \n      # Store for comparison plot\n      plot_models[[model_name]] <- m\n      \n      # --- Global summary row\n      model_summary <- bind_rows(model_summary,\n                                 extract_stats(m, model_name, el))\n      \n      # --- Diagnostic plots (from performance/see)\n      diag_plot <- check_model(m)\n      ggsave(file.path(element_dir,\n                       paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_diagnostics.pdf\")),\n             diag_plot, width = 20, height = 20,\n             units = \"cm\", dpi = 600)\n      \n      # --- Residual distribution plots\n      resid_df <- tibble(resid = residuals(m))\n      p_resid <- ggplot(resid_df, aes(resid)) +\n        geom_histogram(bins = 30) +\n        geom_density(linewidth = 1) +\n        theme_bw() +\n        ggtitle(paste(el, model_name, \"Residual distribution\"))\n      ggsave(file.path(element_dir,\n                       paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_Residuals.pdf\")),\n             p_resid, width = 20, height = 20,\n             units = \"cm\", dpi = 600)\n      \n      # --- Normality tests\n      shapiro <- tryCatch(shapiro.test(residuals(m)),\n                          error = function(e) NULL)\n      ks      <- tryCatch(ks.test(scale(residuals(m)), \"pnorm\"),\n                          error = function(e) NULL)\n      \n      normality_df <- tibble(\n        Element    = el,\n        Model      = model_name,\n        Shapiro_W  = if (!is.null(shapiro)) unname(shapiro$statistic) else NA_real_,\n        Shapiro_p  = if (!is.null(shapiro)) shapiro$p.value else NA_real_,\n        KS_D       = if (!is.null(ks)) unname(ks$statistic) else NA_real_,\n        KS_p       = if (!is.null(ks)) ks$p.value else NA_real_,\n        Skewness   = psych::skew(residuals(m)),\n        Kurtosis   = psych::kurtosi(residuals(m))\n      )\n      write.csv(normality_df,\n                file.path(element_dir,\n                          paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_Normality.csv\")),\n                row.names = FALSE)\n      \n      # --- Breuschu2013Pagan heteroscedasticity test\n      bp <- tryCatch(lmtest::bptest(m),\n                     error = function(e) NULL)\n      bp_df <- tibble(\n        Element = el,\n        Model   = model_name,\n        BP_stat = if (!is.null(bp)) unname(bp$statistic) else NA_real_,\n        BP_p    = if (!is.null(bp)) bp$p.value else NA_real_\n      )\n      write.csv(bp_df,\n                file.path(element_dir,\n                          paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_BPtest.csv\")),\n                row.names = FALSE)\n      \n      # --- Cook's distance / influence plot\n      cooks <- tryCatch(cooks.distance(m),\n                        error = function(e) rep(NA_real_, length(residuals(m))))\n      df_cook <- tibble(\n        Index = seq_along(cooks),\n        Cook  = cooks\n      )\n      p_cook <- ggplot(df_cook, aes(Index, Cook)) +\n        geom_bar(stat = \"identity\") +\n        geom_hline(yintercept = 4 / nrow(df_cook), linetype = \"dashed\") +\n        theme_bw() +\n        ggtitle(paste(el, model_name, \"Cook's distance\"))\n      ggsave(file.path(element_dir,\n                       paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_CooksDistance.pdf\")),\n             p_cook, width = 20, height = 20,\n             units = \"cm\", dpi = 600)\n      \n      # --- Bootstrap CIs for slope & intercept (frequentist)\n      boot_res <- boot(data, boot_fn, R = 2000, formula = formula)\n      ci_intercept <- boot.ci(boot_res, type = \"perc\", index = 1)\n      ci_slope     <- boot.ci(boot_res, type = \"perc\", index = 2)\n      CI_df <- tibble(\n        Element         = el,\n        Model           = model_name,\n        Intercept_Lower = if (!is.null(ci_intercept$percent)) ci_intercept$percent[4] else NA_real_,\n        Intercept_Upper = if (!is.null(ci_intercept$percent)) ci_intercept$percent[5] else NA_real_,\n        Slope_Lower     = if (!is.null(ci_slope$percent)) ci_slope$percent[4] else NA_real_,\n        Slope_Upper     = if (!is.null(ci_slope$percent)) ci_slope$percent[5] else NA_real_\n      )\n      write.csv(CI_df,\n                file.path(element_dir,\n                          paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_BootstrapCI.csv\")),\n                row.names = FALSE)\n      \n      #               "Below is the **final integrated MEGA FUNCTION** that now includes:\n\n- **OLS**\n- **WLS (variance-based)**\n- **Weighted OLS (SD-based)**\n- **Two-step weighted WLS**\n- **Bayesian regression (MAP, via `bayesglm`)**\n- **Random Forest regression**\n- **Diagnostics for *all* models**\n- **Residual distribution plots**\n- **Normality tests**\n- **Bootstrap confidence intervals**\n- **Heteroscedasticity tests (BP or RF proxy)**\n- **Cooku2019s distance / influence**\n- **10-fold cross-validation performance**\n- **Model-comparison multi-plots**\n- **Summary CSV (all elements, all models)**\n- **Best-model selection table**\n- **Combined multi-page PDF summary**\n\nThis is now a full-featured calibration modeling pipeline.\n\n---\n\n# ud83dude80 **THE COMPLETE MEGA FUNCTION (FULL CODE)**  \n**Copy/paste directly into your R script.**\n\n```r\nrun_full_regressions <- function(\n  elements,\n  data,\n  var_suffix = \"_var\",\n  sd_suffix = \"_ICP_sd\",\n  save_dir   = \"Papers_R/2024_DeVleeschouwer/FigureS6/Plots/FigS6a_OLS_WLS_log_inc\",\n  summary_csv = \"ModelSummary_AllElements.csv\",\n  summary_pdf = \"AllElements_Summary.pdf\"\n) {\n  # PACKAGES\n  library(broom)\n  library(performance)\n  library(see)\n  library(ggplot2)\n  library(dplyr)\n  library(purrr)\n  library(boot)\n  library(psych)\n  library(lmtest)\n  library(arm)\n  library(randomForest)\n  library(gridExtra)\n\n  if (!dir.exists(save_dir)) dir.create(save_dir, recursive = TRUE)\n\n  model_summary <- tibble()\n  all_pdf_pages <- list()\n\n  # Helper: extract stats\n  extract_stats <- function(model, model_name, el) {\n    stats <- tryCatch(performance::model_performance(model), error = function(e) NULL)\n    if (!is.null(stats)) {\n      r2   <- stats$r2\n      rmse <- stats$rmse\n    } else {\n      r2   <- NA_real_\n      rmse <- sqrt(mean(residuals(model)^2))\n    }\n    rmsep <- tryCatch(performance::rmsep(model), error = function(e) NA_real_)\n\n    tibble(\n      Element   = el,\n      Model     = model_name,\n      Intercept = ifelse(model_name == \"RF\", NA, coef(model)[1]),\n      Slope     = ifelse(model_name == \"RF\", NA, coef(model)[2]),\n      R2        = r2,\n      RMSE      = rmse,\n      RMSEP     = rmsep,\n      AIC       = tryCatch(AIC(model), error = function(e) NA),\n      BIC       = tryCatch(BIC(model), error = function(e) NA)\n    )\n  }\n\n  # Helper: bootstrap CI for LM\n  boot_fn <- function(data, idx, formula) {\n    m <- lm(formula, data = data[idx, , drop = FALSE])\n    coef(m)\n  }\n\n  for (el in elements) {\n\n    y_col <- paste0(el, \"_ICP\")\n    x_col <- el\n    var_col <- paste0(el, var_suffix)\n    sd_col  <- paste0(el, sd_suffix)\n\n    if (!all(c(y_col, x_col) %in% names(data))) {\n      warning(\"Skipping \", el, \": missing required columns.\")\n      next\n    }\n\n    element_dir <- file.path(save_dir, el)\n    dir.create(element_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)\n\n    formula <- as.formula(paste0(y_col, \" ~ \", x_col))\n\n    #==============================\n    # FIT ALL MODELS\n    #==============================\n    model_types <- list()\n\n    model_types$OLS <- lm(formula, data = data)\n\n    if (var_col %in% names(data)) {\n      wts_var <- 1 / data[[var_col]]\n      model_types$WLS_var <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = wts_var)\n    }\n\n    have_sd <- sd_col %in% names(data)\n    if (have_sd) {\n      wts_sd <- 1 / (data[[sd_col]]^2)\n      model_types$OLS_weighted <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = wts_sd)\n    }\n\n    if (have_sd) {\n      init_model <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = wts_sd)\n      resid_model <- lm(abs(init_model$residuals) ~ init_model$fitted.values)\n      final_wts <- 1 / (resid_model$fitted.values^2)\n      model_types$WLS_weighted <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = final_wts)\n    }\n\n    model_types$Bayes <- arm::bayesglm(formula, data = data)\n\n    # RANDOM FOREST\n    set.seed(123)\n    model_types$RF <- randomForest(\n      formula,\n      data = data,\n      importance = TRUE,\n      ntree = 500\n    )\n\n    pdf_pages_element <- list()\n    plot_models <- list()\n\n    #==============================\n    # PROCESS MODELS\n    #==============================\n    for (model_name in names(model_types)) {\n\n      m <- model_types[[model_name]]\n\n      model_summary <- bind_rows(model_summary,\n                                 extract_stats(m, model_name, el))\n\n      #----------------\n      # Diagnostics\n      #----------------\n      if (model_name != \"RF\") {  \n        diag_plot <- check_model(m)\n        ggsave(file.path(element_dir,\n                         paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_diagnostics.pdf\")),\n               diag_plot, width = 20, height = 20, units = \"cm\", dpi = 600)\n\n        pdf_pages_element[[paste0(model_name,\"_Diag\")]] <- diag_plot\n      }\n\n      #----------------\n      # Residual plots\n      #----------------\n      resid_vals <- if (model_name == \"RF\") data[[y_col]] - predict(m) else residuals(m)\n\n      p_resid <- ggplot(tibble(resid = resid_vals), aes(resid)) +\n        geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = \"grey70\") +\n        geom_density(color = \"red\") +\n        theme_bw() +\n        ggtitle(paste(el, model_name, \"Residual Distribution\"))\n      ggsave(file.path(element_dir,\n                       paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_Residuals.pdf\")),\n             p_resid, width = 20, height = 20, units = \"cm\", dpi = 600)\n\n      pdf_pages_element[[paste0(model_name,\"_Resid\")]] <- p_resid\n\n      #----------------\n      # Normality tests\n      #----------------\n      shapiro <- tryCatch(shapiro.test(resid_vals), error = function(e) NULL)\n      ks      <- tryCatch(ks.test(scale(resid_vals), \"pnorm\"), error = function(e) NULL)\n\n      norm_df <- tibble(\n        Element = el,\n        Model   = model_name,\n        Shapiro_W = if (!is.null(shapiro)) shapiro$statistic else NA,\n        Shapiro_p = if (!is.null(shapiro)) shapiro$p.value else NA,\n        KS_D      = if (!is.null(ks)) ks$statistic else NA,\n        KS_p      = if (!is.null(ks)) ks$p.value else NA,\n        Skewness  = psych::skew(resid_vals),\n        Kurtosis  = psych::kurtosi(resid_vals)\n      )\n      write.csv(norm_df,\n                file.path(element_dir,\n                          paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_Normality.csv\")),\n                row.names = FALSE)\n\n      #----------------\n      # BP test\n      #----------------\n      if (model_name != \"RF\") {\n        bp <- tryCatch(lmtest::bptest(m), error = function(e) NULL)\n        bp_df <- tibble(\n          Element = el,\n          Model   = model_name,\n          BP_stat = if (!is.null(bp)) bp$statistic else NA,\n          BP_p    = if (!is.null(bp)) bp$p.value else NA\n        )\n      } else {\n        # RF heteroscedasticity proxy\n        preds <- predict(m)\n        bp_df <- tibble(\n          Element = el,\n          Model   = \"RF\",\n          ResidFitCorr = cor(abs(resid_vals), preds)\n        )\n      }\n      write.csv(bp_df,\n                file.path(element_dir,\n                          paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_BPtest.csv\")),\n                row.names = FALSE)\n\n      #----------------\n      # Cooku2019s distance (RF uses influence proxy)\n      #----------------\n      if (model_name != \"RF\") {\n        cooks <- cooks.distance(m)\n        cook_df <- tibble(Index = seq_along(cooks), Cook = cooks)\n      } else {\n        cook_df <- tibble(\n          Index = seq_along(resid_vals),\n          Influence = abs(resid_vals) / sd(resid_vals)\n        )\n      }\n\n      p_cook <- ggplot(cook_df,\n                       aes(Index, ifelse(model_name==\"RF\", Influence, Cook))) +\n        geom_point() +\n        geom_hline(yintercept = ifelse(model_name==\"RF\", 3, 4/nrow(cook_df)),\n                   linetype = \"dashed\", color = \"red\") +\n        theme_bw() +\n        ggtitle(paste(el, model_name, \"Influence / Cooku2019s Distance\"))\n\n      ggsave(file.path(element_dir,\n                       paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_CooksDistance.pdf\")),\n             p_cook, width = 20, height = 20, units = \"cm\", dpi = 600)\n\n      pdf_pages_element[[paste0(model_name,\"_Cook\")]] <- p_cook\n\n      #----------------\n      # Bootstrap CI (LM only)\n      #----------------\n      if (model_name != \"RF\" && model_name != \"Bayes\") {\n        boot_res <- boot(data, boot_fn, R = 2000, formula = formula)\n        ci_intercept <- boot.ci(boot_res, type = \"perc\", index = 1)\n        ci_slope     <- boot.ci(boot_res, type = \"perc\", index = 2)\n\n        CI_df <- tibble(\n          Element         = el,\n          Model           = model_name,\n          Intercept_Lower = ifelse(!is.null(ci_intercept$percent),\n                                   ci_intercept$percent[4], NA),\n          Intercept_Upper = ifelse(!is.null(ci_intercept$percent),\n                                   ci_intercept$percent[5], NA),\n          Slope_Lower     = ifelse(!is.null(ci_slope$percent),\n                                   ci_slope$percent[4], NA),\n          Slope_Upper     = ifelse(!is.null(ci_slope$percent),\n                                   ci_slope$percent[5], NA)\n        )\n        write.csv(CI_df,\n                  file.path(element_dir,\n                            paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_BootstrapCI.csv\")),\n                  row.names = FALSE)\n      }\n\n      #----------------\n      # Bayesian credible intervals (Bayesglm)\n      #----------------\n      if (model_name == \"Bayes\") {\n        s <- summary(m)\n        est <- s$coefficients[, 1]\n        se  <- s$coefficients[, 2]\n        bayes_ci <- tibble(\n          Term     = rownames(s$coefficients),\n          Estimate = est,\n          Lower_95 = est - 1.96 * se,\n          Upper_95 = est + 1.96 * se\n        )\n        write.csv(bayes_ci,\n                  file.path(element_dir,\n                            paste0(el, \"_Bayes_CredibleIntervals.csv\")),\n                  row.names = FALSE)\n      }\n\n      #----------------\n      # Random Forest diagnostics\n      #----------------\n      if (model_name == \"RF\") {\n\n        preds <- predict(m)\n\n        df_rf <- tibble(\n          Observed  = data[[y_col]],\n          Predicted = preds,\n          Residuals = Observed - Predicted\n        )\n\n        p_pred <- ggplot(df_rf, aes(Observed, Predicted)) +\n          geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +\n          geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0) +\n          theme_bw() +\n          ggtitle(paste(el, \"RF Predicted vs Observed\"))\n\n        ggsave(file.path(element_dir, paste0(el, \"_RF_PredVsObs.pdf\")),\n               p_pred, height = 20, width = 20, units = \"cm\", dpi = 600)\n\n        pdf_pages_element[[\"RF_Pred\"]] <- p_pred\n\n        # Variable importance\n        imp <- importance(m)\n        df_imp <- tibble(Variable = rownames(imp), IncMSE = imp[, 1])\n\n        p_imp <- ggplot(df_imp, aes(x = reorder(Variable, IncMSE), y = IncMSE)) +\n          geom_col() +\n          coord_flip() +\n          theme_bw() +\n          ggtitle(paste(el, \"Random Forest Variable Importance\"))\n\n        ggsave(file.path(element_dir, paste0(el, \"_RF_VarImportance.pdf\")),\n               p_imp, height = 20, width = 20, units = \"cm\", dpi = 600)\n\n        pdf_pages_element[[\"RF_Imp\"]] <- p_imp\n\n        # CV (10-fold)\n        set.seed(123)\n        k <- 10\n        n <- nrow(data)\n        folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = n))\n\n        obs_cv <- c()\n        pred_cv <- c()\n\n        for (fold in 1:k) {\n          train_idx <- which(folds != fold)\n          test_idx  <- which(folds == fold)\n          rf_cv <- randomForest(formula, data = data[train_idx, ], ntree = 500)\n          pred_fold <- predict(rf_cv, newdata = data[test_idx, ])\n          pred_cv <- c(pred_cv, pred_fold)\n          obs_cv  <- c(obs_cv, data[[y_col]][test_idx])\n        }\n\n        df_cv <- tibble(Observed = obs_cv, Predicted = pred_cv)\n        p_cv <- ggplot(df_cv, aes(Observed, Predicted)) +\n          geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +\n          geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0) +\n          theme_bw() +\n          ggtitle(paste(el, \"RF 10-fold CV Predictions\"))\n\n        ggsave(file.path(element_dir, paste0(el, \"_RF_CVplot.pdf\")),\n               p_cv, height = 20, width = 20, units = \"cm\", dpi = 600)\n\n        pdf_pages_element[[\"RF_CV\"]] <- p_cv\n\n        # Add RF performance row (R2, RMSE, RMSEP)\n        R2   <- cor(df_rf$Observed, df_rf$Predicted)^2\n        RMSE <- sqrt(mean((df_rf$Observed - df_rf$Predicted)^2))\n        RMSEP <- sqrt(mean((df_cv$Observed - df_cv$Predicted)^2))\n\n        model_summary <- bind_rows(\n          model_summary,\n          tibble(\n            Element = el,\n            Model   = \"RF\",\n            Intercept = NA,\n            Slope     = NA,\n            R2        = R2,\n            RMSE      = RMSE,\n            RMSEP     = RMSEP,\n            AIC       = NA,\n            BIC       = NA\n          )\n        )\n      }\n\n      plot_models[[model_name]] <- m\n    } # end per-model loop\n\n    #==============================\n    # MULTI-MODEL COMPARISON PLOT\n    #==============================\n    df_plot <- data[, c(x_col, y_col)]\n    names(df_plot) <- c(\"x\", \"y\")\n\n    pred_all <- bind_rows(lapply(names(plot_models), function(mn) {\n      tibble(\n        x = df_plot$x,\n        y_pred = predict(plot_models[[mn]]),\n        Model = mn\n      )\n    }))\n\n    p_compare <- ggplot(df_plot, aes(x, y)) +\n      geom_point(alpha=0.7) +\n      geom_line(data=pred_all, aes(x, y_pred, color=Model), size=1) +\n      theme_bw() +\n      ggtitle(paste(\"Model Comparison for\", el))\n\n    ggsave(file.path(element_dir, paste0(el, \"_ModelComparison.pdf\")),\n           p_compare, height = 20, width = 20, units = \"cm\", dpi = 600)\n\n    pdf_pages_element[[\"Comparison\"]] <- p_compare\n    all_pdf_pages[[el]] <- pdf_pages_element\n  } # element loop\n\n  #==============================\n  # BEST MODEL SELECTION\n  #==============================\n  best_models <- model_summary %>%\n    group_by(Element) %>%\n    summarize(\n      Best_AIC  = Model[which.min(AIC)],\n      Best_BIC  = Model[which.min(BIC)],\n      Best_RMSE = Model[which.min(RMSE)],\n      Best_R2   = Model[which.max(R2)],\n      Best_RMSEP = Model[which.min(RMSEP)],\n      .groups = \"drop\"\n    )\n  write.csv(best_models,\n            file.path(save_dir, \"BestModels_byCriterion.csv\"),\n            row.names = FALSE)\n\n  #==============================\n  # SAVE SUMMARY CSV\n  #==============================\n  write.csv(model_summary,\n            file.path(save_dir, summary_csv),\n            row.names = FALSE)\n\n  #==============================\n  # FINAL SUMMARY PDF\n  #==============================\n  pdf(file.path(save_dir, summary_pdf), width=12, height=10)\n  for (el in names(all_pdf_pages)) {\n    for (pg in names(all_pdf_pages[[el]])) {\n      grid::grid.newpage()\n      grid::grid.draw(ggplotGrob(all_pdf_pages[[el]][[pg]]))\n    }\n  }\n  dev.off()\n\n  message(\"\\nu2714 All modeling complete!\")\n  message(\"u2714 Summary CSV: \", file.path(save_dir, summary_csv))\n  message(\"u2714 Best-model table: \", file.path(save_dir, \"BestModels_byCriterion.csv\"))\n  message(\"u2714 Summary PDF: \", file.path(save_dir, summary_pdf))\n\n  invisible(model_summary)\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n# u25b6ufe0f **HOW TO RUN THE MEGA FUNCTION**\n\n```r\nelements <- c(\"Ti\", \"Ca\", \"Mn\", \"Fe\", \"Sr\", \"Zr\")\n\nsummary_table <- run_full_regressions(\n  elements = elements,\n  data = ACE_dataset,\n  var_suffix = \"_var\",\n  sd_suffix = \"_ICP_sd\"\n)\n```\n\n---\n\n# ud83dudcd8 **ONE-PARAGRAPH SUMMARY OF WHAT THIS MEGA FUNCTION DOES**\n\nThis function performs a complete multi-model calibration and diagnostic workflow for each chemical element in a dataset, fitting OLS, variance-weighted WLS, SD-weighted OLS, two-step weighted WLS, Bayesian regression (MAP), and Random Forest regression.               "Hereu2019s an updated **mega function** that:\n\n- Fixes the `grid.draw` / `check_model` error  \n- Adds **PLS regression** with **both**:\n  - `PLS_LOO`: Leave-One-Out CV  \n  - `PLS_kfold`: 10-fold CV  \n- Produces for **all models** (OLS, WLS, weighted OLS, weighted WLS, Bayes, RF, PLS_LOO, PLS_kfold):\n  - Predictions, residuals, **Ru00b2, RMSE, RMSEP**\n  - Residual distribution plots  \n  - Normality tests (CSV)  \n  - Heteroscedasticity tests (BP or proxy)  \n  - Influence / Cooku2019s distanceu2013style plots  \n  - Diagnostics (where applicable)  \n  - Model-comparison plots  \n- Produces:\n  - A **master CSV** of all models u00d7 elements  \n  - A **best-model table** per element  \n  - A **multi-page PDF summary** across all elements and models  \n\nIn short: itu2019s a full, publication-ready calibration and model comparison pipeline for linear, Bayesian, random forest, and PLS models.\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudce6 Packages needed\n\nMake sure you have these installed:\n\n```r\ninstall.packages(c(\n  \"broom\", \"performance\", \"see\", \"ggplot2\", \"dplyr\", \"purrr\",\n  \"boot\", \"psych\", \"lmtest\", \"arm\", \"randomForest\", \"pls\", \"gridExtra\"\n))\n```\n\n---\n\n## ud83eudde0 Complete mega function with PLS (LOO + k-fold) and fixed PDF export\n\n```r\nrun_full_regressions <- function(\n  elements,\n  data,\n  var_suffix = \"_var\",\n  sd_suffix = \"_ICP_sd\",\n  save_dir   = \"Papers_R/2024_DeVleeschouwer/FigureS6/Plots/FigS6a_OLS_WLS_log_inc\",\n  summary_csv = \"ModelSummary_AllElements.csv\",\n  summary_pdf = \"AllElements_Summary.pdf\"\n) {\n  # PACKAGES\n  library(broom)\n  library(performance)\n  library(see)\n  library(ggplot2)\n  library(dplyr)\n  library(purrr)\n  library(boot)\n  library(psych)\n  library(lmtest)\n  library(arm)\n  library(randomForest)\n  library(pls)\n  library(gridExtra)\n\n  if (!dir.exists(save_dir)) dir.create(save_dir, recursive = TRUE)\n\n  model_summary <- tibble()\n  all_pdf_pages <- list()\n\n  # Helper: extract stats for lm/glm-type models only\n  extract_stats <- function(model, model_name, el) {\n    stats <- tryCatch(performance::model_performance(model), error = function(e) NULL)\n    if (!is.null(stats)) {\n      r2   <- stats$r2\n      rmse <- stats$rmse\n    } else {\n      r2   <- NA_real_\n      rmse <- sqrt(mean(residuals(model)^2))\n    }\n    rmsep <- tryCatch(performance::rmsep(model), error = function(e) NA_real_)\n\n    tibble(\n      Element   = el,\n      Model     = model_name,\n      Intercept = unname(coef(model)[1]),\n      Slope     = unname(coef(model)[2]),\n      R2        = r2,\n      RMSE      = rmse,\n      RMSEP     = rmsep,\n      AIC       = tryCatch(AIC(model), error = function(e) NA_real_),\n      BIC       = tryCatch(BIC(model), error = function(e) NA_real_)\n    )\n  }\n\n  # Helper: bootstrap CI for LM\n  boot_fn <- function(data, idx, formula) {\n    m <- lm(formula, data = data[idx, , drop = FALSE])\n    coef(m)\n  }\n\n  for (el in elements) {\n\n    y_col   <- paste0(el, \"_ICP\")\n    x_col   <- el\n    var_col <- paste0(el, var_suffix)\n    sd_col  <- paste0(el, sd_suffix)\n\n    if (!all(c(y_col, x_col) %in% names(data))) {\n      warning(\"Skipping \", el, \": missing required columns.\")\n      next\n    }\n\n    element_dir <- file.path(save_dir, el)\n    dir.create(element_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)\n\n    formula <- as.formula(paste0(y_col, \" ~ \", x_col))\n\n    #==============================\n    # FIT ALL MODELS\n    #==============================\n    model_types <- list()\n    pls_meta <- list()  # store best ncomp etc for PLS\n\n    # 1) OLS\n    model_types$OLS <- lm(formula, data = data)\n\n    # 2) WLS (variance-based)\n    if (var_col %in% names(data)) {\n      wts_var <- 1 / data[[var_col]]\n      model_types$WLS_var <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = wts_var)\n    }\n\n    # 3) Weighted OLS (ICP SD-based)\n    have_sd <- sd_col %in% names(data)\n    if (have_sd) {\n      wts_sd <- 1 / (data[[sd_col]]^2)\n      model_types$OLS_weighted <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = wts_sd)\n    }\n\n    # 4) Weighted WLS (two-step ICP error-weighted)\n    if (have_sd) {\n      init_model <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = wts_sd)\n      resid_model <- lm(abs(init_model$residuals) ~ init_model$fitted.values)\n      final_wts <- 1 / (resid_model$fitted.values^2)\n      model_types$WLS_weighted <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = final_wts)\n    }\n\n    # 5) Bayesian regression (MAP)\n    model_types$Bayes <- arm::bayesglm(formula, data = data)\n\n    # 6) Random Forest\n    set.seed(123)\n    model_types$RF <- randomForest(\n      formula,\n      data = data,\n      importance = TRUE,\n      ntree = 500\n    )\n\n    # 7) PLS with LOO CV\n    pls_loo <- plsr(formula, data = data, validation = \"LOO\", scale = TRUE)\n    best_loo <- selectNcomp(pls_loo, method = \"onesigma\", plot = FALSE)\n    model_types$PLS_LOO <- pls_loo\n    pls_meta$PLS_LOO <- list(best_ncomp = best_loo)\n\n    # 8) PLS with 10-fold CV\n    pls_kfold <- plsr(formula, data = data, validation = \"CV\",\n                      segments = 10, scale = TRUE)\n    best_kfold <- selectNcomp(pls_kfold, method = \"onesigma\", plot = FALSE)\n    model_types$PLS_kfold <- pls_kfold\n    pls_meta$PLS_kfold <- list(best_ncomp = best_kfold)\n\n    pdf_pages_element <- list()\n    plot_models <- list()\n\n    #==============================\n    # PROCESS MODELS\n    #==============================\n    for (model_name in names(model_types)) {\n\n      m <- model_types[[model_name]]\n\n      is_lm_like <- model_name %in% c(\"OLS\", \"WLS_var\", \"OLS_weighted\", \"WLS_weighted\", \"Bayes\")\n      is_rf      <- model_name == \"RF\"\n      is_pls     <- model_name %in% c(\"PLS_LOO\", \"PLS_kfold\")\n\n      #----------------\n      # Predictions & residuals\n      #----------------\n      if (is_lm_like) {\n        pred  <- as.numeric(predict(m))\n        resid_vals <- residuals(m)\n      } else if (is_rf) {\n        pred  <- as.numeric(predict(m))\n        resid_vals <- data[[y_col]] - pred\n      } else if (is_pls) {\n        best_ncomp <- pls_meta[[model_name]]$best_ncomp\n        pred <- as.numeric(predict(m, ncomp = best_ncomp, newdata = data))\n        resid_vals <- data[[y_col]] - pred\n      } else {\n        pred  <- as.numeric(predict(m))\n        resid_vals <- data[[y_col]] - pred\n      }\n\n      #----------------\n      #               "Hereu2019s a cleaned-up **full mega function** with the `grid.draw` error fixed (we no longer use `grid.draw` at all) and all requested features retained:\n\n- OLS, WLS, weighted OLS, 2-step weighted WLS  \n- Bayesian regression (bayesglm)  \n- Random Forest  \n- PLS (LOO and 10-fold CV)  \n- Residual plots, normality tests, heteroscedasticity tests, influence plots  \n- Predicted vs observed plots **colored by Site** using a **JCO palette**  \n- RF variable importance, PLS RMSEP validation plots  \n- Per-model/per-element diagnostics (PDF + CSV)  \n- Master summary CSV (Ru00b2, RMSE, RMSEP, AIC, BIC)  \n- Best-model table  \n- Combined summary PDF for all elements  \n\nThe `grid.draw` error is fixed by **not using grid at all in the summary PDF** u2013 we just `print()` ggplots and `plot()` `check_model` objects directly to the PDF device, which is what base R expects.\n\n---\n\n## ud83dudce6 Full mega function (copyu2013paste this whole block)\n\n```r\nrun_full_regressions <- function(\n  elements,\n  data,\n  var_suffix = \"_var\",\n  sd_suffix = \"_ICP_sd\",\n  save_dir   = \"Papers_R/2024_DeVleeschouwer/FigureS6/Plots/FigS6a_OLS_WLS_log_inc\",\n  summary_csv = \"ModelSummary_AllElements.csv\",\n  summary_pdf = \"AllElements_Summary.pdf\"\n) {\n\n  # ================================\n  # Packages\n  # ================================\n  library(broom)\n  library(performance)\n  library(see)\n  library(ggplot2)\n  library(dplyr)\n  library(purrr)\n  library(boot)\n  library(psych)\n  library(lmtest)\n  library(arm)\n  library(randomForest)\n  library(pls)\n  library(ggpubr)\n\n  if (!dir.exists(save_dir)) dir.create(save_dir, recursive = TRUE)\n\n  # Site factor ordering for colours\n  if (\"Site\" %in% colnames(data)) {\n    data$Site <- factor(\n      data$Site,\n      levels = c(\"BI10\", \"HER42PB\", \"KER1\", \"KER3\", \"PB1\")\n    )\n  } else {\n    stop(\"The dataset must contain a 'Site' column.\")\n  }\n\n  # Master outputs\n  model_summary <- tibble()\n  all_pdf_pages <- list()\n\n  # ================================\n  # Helper: stats for LM-like models\n  # ================================\n  extract_stats <- function(model, model_name, el) {\n    stats <- tryCatch(performance::model_performance(model), error = function(e) NULL)\n    if (!is.null(stats)) {\n      r2   <- stats$r2\n      rmse <- stats$rmse\n    } else {\n      r2   <- NA_real_\n      rmse <- sqrt(mean(residuals(model)^2))\n    }\n    rmsep <- tryCatch(performance::rmsep(model), error = function(e) NA_real_)\n\n    tibble(\n      Element   = el,\n      Model     = model_name,\n      Intercept = unname(coef(model)[1]),\n      Slope     = unname(coef(model)[2]),\n      R2        = r2,\n      RMSE      = rmse,\n      RMSEP     = rmsep,\n      AIC       = tryCatch(AIC(model), error = function(e) NA_real_),\n      BIC       = tryCatch(BIC(model), error = function(e) NA_real_)\n    )\n  }\n\n  # Bootstrap helper\n  boot_fn <- function(data, idx, formula) {\n    m <- lm(formula, data = data[idx, , drop = FALSE])\n    coef(m)\n  }\n\n  # ================================\n  # Loop over elements\n  # ================================\n  for (el in elements) {\n\n    message(\"\\n========================\")\n    message(\"Processing element: \", el)\n    message(\"========================\\n\")\n\n    y_col   <- paste0(el, \"_ICP\")\n    x_col   <- el\n    var_col <- paste0(el, var_suffix)\n    sd_col  <- paste0(el, sd_suffix)\n\n    if (!all(c(y_col, x_col) %in% colnames(data))) {\n      warning(\"Skipping \", el, \": missing \", y_col, \" or \", x_col)\n      next\n    }\n\n    element_dir <- file.path(save_dir, el)\n    dir.create(element_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)\n\n    formula <- as.formula(paste0(y_col, \" ~ \", x_col))\n\n    # --------------------------------\n    # Fit models\n    # --------------------------------\n    model_types <- list()\n    pls_meta    <- list()\n\n    # 1) OLS\n    model_types$OLS <- lm(formula, data = data)\n\n    # 2) WLS (variance-based)\n    if (var_col %in% colnames(data)) {\n      wts_var <- 1 / data[[var_col]]\n      model_types$WLS_var <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = wts_var)\n    }\n\n    # 3) Weighted OLS (ICP SD-based)\n    have_sd <- sd_col %in% colnames(data)\n    if (have_sd) {\n      wts_sd <- 1 / (data[[sd_col]]^2)\n      model_types$OLS_weighted <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = wts_sd)\n    }\n\n    # 4) Two-step weighted WLS\n    if (have_sd) {\n      init_model  <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = wts_sd)\n      resid_model <- lm(abs(init_model$residuals) ~ init_model$fitted.values)\n      final_wts   <- 1 / (resid_model$fitted.values^2)\n      model_types$WLS_weighted <- lm(formula, data = data, weights = final_wts)\n    }\n\n    # 5) Bayesian regression\n    model_types$Bayes <- arm::bayesglm(formula, data = data)\n\n    # 6) Random Forest\n    set.seed(123)\n    model_types$RF <- randomForest(\n      formula,\n      data       = data,\n      ntree      = 500,\n      importance = TRUE\n    )\n\n    # 7) PLS (LOO CV)\n    pls_loo <- plsr(formula, data = data, scale = TRUE, validation = \"LOO\")\n    best_loo <- selectNcomp(pls_loo, method = \"onesigma\", plot = FALSE)\n    model_types$PLS_LOO <- pls_loo\n    pls_meta$PLS_LOO <- list(best_ncomp = best_loo)\n\n    # 8) PLS (10-fold CV)\n    pls_cv <- plsr(formula, data = data, scale = TRUE,\n                   validation = \"CV\", segments = 10)\n    best_cv <- selectNcomp(pls_cv, method = \"onesigma\", plot = FALSE)\n    model_types$PLS_kfold <- pls_cv\n    pls_meta$PLS_kfold <- list(best_ncomp = best_cv)\n\n    pdf_pages_element <- list()\n    plot_models <- list()\n\n    # --------------------------------\n    # Process each model\n    # --------------------------------\n    for (model_name in names(model_types)) {\n\n      m <- model_types[[model_name]]\n\n      is_lm   <- model_name %in% c(\"OLS\",\"WLS_var\",\"OLS_weighted\",\"WLS_weighted\",\"Bayes\")\n      is_rf   <- model_name == \"RF\"\n      is_pls  <- model_name %in% c(\"PLS_LOO\",\"PLS_kfold\")\n\n      # ---- Predictions & residuals ----\n      if (is_lm) {\n        pred       <- as.numeric(predict(m))\n        resid_vals <- residuals(m)\n\n      } else if (is_rf) {\n        pred       <- as.numeric(predict(m))\n        resid_vals <- data[[y_col]] - pred\n\n      } else if (is_pls) {\n        best_ncomp <- pls_meta[[model_name]]$best_ncomp\n        pred       <- as.numeric(predict(m, ncomp = best_ncomp, newdata = data))\n        resid_vals <- data[[y_col]] - pred\n      } else {\n        pred       <- as.numeric(predict(m))\n        resid_vals <- data[[y_col]] - pred\n      }\n\n      # ---- Add metrics to summary ----\n      if (is_lm) {\n        model_summary <- bind_rows(\n          model_summary,\n          extract_stats(m, model_name, el)\n        )\n\n      } else if (is_rf) {\n        R2   <- cor(data[[y_col]], pred)^2\n        RMSE <- sqrt(mean((data[[y_col]] - pred)^2))\n\n        # 10-fold CV for RF\n        set.seed(123)\n        n <- nrow(data)\n        k <- 10\n        folds  <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = n))\n        obs_cv <- c()\n        pred_cv <- c()\n\n        for (fold in 1:k) {\n          train_idx <- which(folds != fold)\n          test_idx  <- which(folds == fold)\n          rf_cv <- randomForest(formula, data = data[train_idx, ], ntree = 500)\n          p_cv  <- predict(rf_cv, newdata = data[test_idx, ])\n          pred_cv <- c(pred_cv, p_cv)\n          obs_cv  <- c(obs_cv, data[[y_col]][test_idx])\n        }\n\n        RMSEP <- sqrt(mean((obs_cv - pred_cv)^2))\n\n        model_summary <- bind_rows(\n          model_summary,\n          tibble(\n            Element   = el,\n            Model     = \"RF\",\n            Intercept = NA_real_,\n            Slope     = NA_real_,\n            R2        = R2,\n            RMSE      = RMSE,\n            RMSEP     = RMSEP,\n            AIC       = NA_real_,\n            BIC       = NA_real_\n          )\n        )\n\n      } else if (is_pls) {\n        best_ncomp <- pls_meta[[model_name]]$best_ncomp\n        R2   <- cor(data[[y_col]], pred)^2\n        RMSE <- sqrt(mean((data[[y_col]] - pred)^2))\n\n        rm <- tryCatch(RMSEP(m, estimate = \"CV\"), error = function(e) NULL)\n        RMSEP_cv <- NA_real_\n        if (!is.null(rm)) {\n          RMSEP_cv <- as.numeric(rm$val[1, best_ncomp + 1, 1])\n        }\n\n        model_summary <- bind_rows(\n          model_summary,\n          tibble(\n            Element   = el,\n            Model     = model_name,\n            Intercept = NA_real_,\n            Slope     = NA_real_,\n            R2        = R2,\n            RMSE      = RMSE,\n            RMSEP     = RMSEP_cv,\n            AIC       = NA_real_,\n            BIC       = NA_real_\n          )\n        )\n      }\n\n      # For comparison plot later\n      plot_models[[model_name]] <- list(pred = pred)\n\n      # ---- check_model diagnostics (LM/Bayes only) ----\n      if (is_lm) {\n        diag_plot <- check_model(m)\n        ggsave(file.path(element_dir,\n                         paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_diagnostics.pdf\")),\n               diag_plot, width = 20, height = 20, units = \"cm\", dpi = 600)\n        pdf_pages_element[[paste0(model_name, \"_Diag\")]] <- diag_plot\n      }\n\n      # ---- Residual distribution ----\n      p_resid <- ggplot(tibble(resid = resid_vals), aes(resid)) +\n        geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = \"grey70\") +\n        geom_density(color = \"red\") +\n        theme_bw() +\n        ggtitle(paste(el, model_name, \"Residual distribution\"))\n\n      ggsave(file.path(element_dir,\n                       paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_Residuals.pdf\")),\n             p_resid, width = 20, height = 20, units = \"cm\", dpi = 600)\n      pdf_pages_element[[paste0(model_name, \"_Resid\")]] <- p_resid\n\n      # ---- Normality tests ----\n      shapiro <- tryCatch(shapiro.test(resid_vals), error = function(e) NULL)\n      ks      <- tryCatch(ks.test(scale(resid_vals), \"pnorm\"), error = function(e) NULL)\n\n      norm_df <- tibble(\n        Element   = el,\n        Model     = model_name,\n        Shapiro_W = if (!is.null(shapiro)) unname(shapiro$statistic) else NA_real_,\n        Shapiro_p = if (!is.null(shapiro)) shapiro$p.value else NA_real_,\n        KS_D      = if (!is.null(ks)) unname(ks$statistic) else NA_real_,\n        KS_p      = if (!is.null(ks)) ks$p.value else NA_real_,\n        Skewness  = psych::skew(resid_vals),\n        Kurtosis  = psych::kurtosi(resid_vals)\n      )\n\n      write.csv(\n        norm_df,\n        file.path(element_dir, paste0(el, \"_\", model_name, \"_Normality.csv\")),\n        row.names = FALSE\n      )\n\n      # PACKAGES\n  library(broom)\n  library(performance)\n  library(see)\n  library(ggplot2)\n  library(dplyr)\n  library(purrr)\n  library(boot)\n  library(psych)\n  library(lmtest)\n  library(arm)\n  library(randomForest)\n  library(pls)\n  library(ggpubr)\n\n  if (!dir.exists(save_dir)) dir.create(save_dir, recursive = TRUE)\n\n  # ====================================================\n  # MAIN LOOP\n  # ====================================================\n  for (el in elements) {\n\n    y_col <- paste0(el,\"_ICP\")\n    x_col <- el\n    var_col <- paste0(el,var_suffix)\n    sd_col  <- paste0(el,sd_suffix)\n\n    formula <- as.formula(paste0(y_col,\"~\",x_col))\n\n    element_dir <- file.path(save_dir, el)\n    dir.create(element_dir, recursive=TRUE, showWarnings=FALSE)\n\n    # FIT MODELS\n    model_types <- list()\n    pls_meta <- list()\n\n    model_types$OLS <- lm(formula, data=data)\n\n    if (var_col %in% names(data)) {\n      model_types$WLS_var <- lm(formula, data=data,\n                                weights=1/data[[var_col]])\n    }\n\n    if (sd_col %in% names(data)) {\n      wts_sd <- 1/(data[[sd_col]]^2)\n      model_types$OLS_weighted <- lm(formula, data=data, weights=wts_sd)\n    }\n\n    if (sd_col %in% names(data)) {\n      init <- lm(formula, data=data, weights=1/(data[[sd_col]]^2))\n      resid_mod <- lm(abs(init$residuals) ~ init$fitted.values)\n      model_types$WLS_weighted <-\n        lm(formula, data=data,\n           weights=1/(resid_mod$fitted.values^2))\n    }\n\n    model_types$Bayes <- bayesglm(formula, data=data)\n\n    set.seed(123)\n    model_types$RF <- randomForest(formula, data=data, ntree=500,\n                                   importance=TRUE)\n\n    pls_loo <- plsr(formula, data=data, scale=TRUE, validation=\"LOO\")\n    pls_meta$PLS_LOO <- list(best=selectNcomp(pls_loo,\"onesigma\",plot=FALSE))\n    model_types$PLS_LOO <- pls_loo\n\n    pls_cv <- plsr(formula, data=data, scale=TRUE,\n                   validation=\"CV\", segments=10)\n    pls_meta$PLS_kfold <- list(best=selectNcomp(pls_cv,\"onesigma\",plot=FALSE))\n    model_types$PLS_kfold <- pls_cv\n\n    #
